---

## HIPAA Security Rule Compliance Assessment: SOP-HR-005 (Acceptable Use Policy)

### Assessment Scope
This assessment evaluates SOP-HR-005 v4.2 against two HIPAA Security Rule standards:
- **§ 164.308(a)(3) — Workforce Security**
- **§ 164.308(a)(5) — Security Awareness and Training**

---

### 1. WORKFORCE SECURITY — § 164.308(a)(3)

The standard requires policies and procedures to ensure appropriate access to ePHI and to prevent unauthorized access. It has three addressable implementation specifications:

#### 1A. Authorization and/or Supervision (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Procedures for authorization/supervision of workforce members who work with ePHI or in locations where it might be accessed | **Section 4.1** — Principle of Least Privilege: "Users shall be granted access only to the specific Meridian Information Resources and data assets minimally necessary to perform their established job duties." Quarterly access reviews via IdentityNow certifications. **Section 3** — RACI matrix assigns responsibility for monitoring (UAM, DLP, SIEM) to IT Security (CISO). **Section 6.3.3** — DLP policies (`DLP-PROD-01`, `DLP-PROD-02`, `DLP-ENDP-03`) provide technical supervision of ePHI handling. | **COMPLIANT.** The SOP establishes both authorization (least privilege, quarterly reviews) and supervision (continuous technical monitoring via UAM, DLP, SIEM). |

#### 1B. Workforce Clearance Procedure (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Procedures to determine that workforce access to ePHI is appropriate | **Section 9.1** — Initial training gates network access provisioning behind successful completion of HIPAA & AUP training (85% pass threshold). **Section 4.1** — Role-based access reviewed quarterly. **Section 6.1, ADM-001** — AUP acknowledgment required before initial access is granted. | **COMPLIANT.** The SOP establishes a clearance procedure: training completion + policy acknowledgment before access is provisioned, with ongoing quarterly validation. |

#### 1C. Termination Procedures (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Procedures for terminating ePHI access upon employment ending or as required by clearance determinations | **Section 8.2** — Emergency escalation includes immediate account disablement, session token revocation, and endpoint quarantine. **Section 6.1, ADM-001** — Automatic access suspension after 10 business days of non-acknowledgment. **Section 9.4** — 30-day non-compliance triggers account suspension. | **PARTIAL.** The SOP addresses termination-like actions (suspension for non-compliance, emergency disablement) but does **not** explicitly describe a standard termination procedure for routine employee separations (e.g., offboarding workflow, access revocation timeline, equipment return). This is a gap. The SOP references SOP-IT-002 (Access Control and Identity Management Policy) which likely contains the detailed termination procedure, but SOP-HR-005 itself does not address this specification directly. |

---

### 2. SECURITY AWARENESS AND TRAINING — § 164.308(a)(5)

The standard requires a security awareness and training program for **all** workforce members (including management). It has four addressable implementation specifications:

#### 2A. Security Reminders (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Periodic security updates | **Section 7.3** — Quarterly "Safe Harbor" email from CHRO with simplified infographic on top 3 AUP risks. **Section 6.1, ADM-001** — Annual re-acknowledgment of AUP. | **COMPLIANT.** Quarterly reminders plus annual re-acknowledgment satisfy periodic security updates. |

#### 2B. Protection from Malicious Software (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Procedures for guarding against, detecting, and reporting malicious software | **Section 5.3.2(2)** — Strictly Prohibited: "Intentional introduction of viruses, ransomware, worms, keyloggers, or any other malicious code." Triggers immediate CSIRT escalation. **Section 6.3.1** — EDR (Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) in Active mode; stopping the service generates high-severity alert. **Section 6.3.2** — SWG (Zscaler) blocks "Hacking" and "Peer-to-Peer" categories. **Section 9.2** — Annual refresher uses real CSIRT case studies. | **COMPLIANT.** The SOP establishes guardrails (prohibition), detection (EDR, SWG), and reporting (CSIRT escalation). The training program reinforces this with real case studies. |

#### 2C. Log-in Monitoring (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Procedures for monitoring log-in attempts and reporting discrepancies | **Section 7.1** — Weekly audit log review by SOC; tier-1 analyst reviews "AUP Violations" dashboard, triages true positives, escalates to tier-2. **Section 7.2, AUP-03** — MTTR for high-severity alerts < 60 minutes, 24/7/365. **Section 6.3.2** — CASB (Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps) monitors anomalous tenant activity. | **COMPLIANT.** The SOP establishes monitoring procedures (weekly review, dashboard, CASB) and reporting/escalation pathways. |

#### 2D. Password Management (Addressable)

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Procedures for creating, changing, and safeguarding passwords | **Section 5.3.1** — Credential Sharing prohibition: "Sharing individual user account credentials... with any other person, including IT support staff or supervisors. All access must be attributable." **Section 10.1** — References SOP-IT-003 (Password and Authentication Standard) as a related policy. | **PARTIAL.** SOP-HR-005 prohibits credential sharing but does **not** itself contain procedures for password creation, changing, or safeguarding. It defers entirely to SOP-IT-003. While cross-referencing is acceptable, the AUP itself lacks any affirmative password management procedures. This is a minor gap in the AUP's self-contained coverage. |

---

### 3. CROSS-CUTTING: SANCTION POLICY — § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(C) (Required)

Although not explicitly in the request, the sanction policy is a required implementation specification that underpins both workforce security and training enforcement:

| Requirement | SOP-HR-005 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Apply appropriate sanctions against workforce members who fail to comply with security policies | **Section 6.1, ADM-002** — "Meridian operates a formal, graduated HR Sanction Policy mapped to investigation findings. Sanctions range from mandatory retraining to termination." **Section 4.3** — Zero tolerance for malicious prohibited activities: "immediate suspension of access, escalation to CSIRT, and possible summary termination." **Section 10.1** — References SOP-HR-004 (Employee Disciplinary Action SOP). | **COMPLIANT.** The SOP explicitly establishes a graduated sanction framework and cross-references the detailed disciplinary SOP. |

---

### 4. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS

| HIPAA Requirement | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **§ 164.308(a)(3)(ii)(A)** — Authorization/Supervision | ✅ Compliant | Least privilege, quarterly reviews, continuous monitoring |
| **§ 164.308(a)(3)(ii)(B)** — Workforce Clearance | ✅ Compliant | Training-gated access, acknowledgment requirement |
| **§ 164.308(a)(3)(ii)(C)** — Termination Procedures | ⚠️ **Partial** | Emergency/disciplinary suspension covered; routine offboarding not addressed in this SOP |
| **§ 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(A)** — Security Reminders | ✅ Compliant | Quarterly emails + annual re-acknowledgment |
| **§ 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B)** — Malicious Software Protection | ✅ Compliant | Prohibition, EDR, SWG, CSIRT escalation, case-study training |
| **§ 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(C)** — Log-in Monitoring | ✅ Compliant | Weekly SOC review, CASB, defined MTTR |
| **§ 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(D)** — Password Management | ⚠️ **Partial** | Credential sharing prohibited; detailed procedures deferred to SOP-IT-003 |
| **§ 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(C)** — Sanction Policy | ✅ Compliant | Graduated sanctions, zero-tolerance provisions |

---

### 5. NOTABLE STRENGTHS

1. **Training program is robust**: Initial training within 5 business days (exceeding the proposed NPRM 30-day standard), annual refresher with real case studies, role-based supplemental training, and automated gating of access behind training completion.
2. **Acknowledgment mechanism (ADM-001)** ties directly to access control — failure to acknowledge within 10 days triggers automatic suspension.
3. **Technical enforcement** (DLP, UAM, CASB, EDR) provides strong detective and preventive controls supporting both workforce security and training objectives.
4. **RACI matrix** clearly assigns responsibility for monitoring, investigation, and enforcement.

### 6. GAPS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

| Gap | Recommendation | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| **Termination Procedures**: SOP-HR-005 lacks explicit routine offboarding procedures for ePHI access termination upon normal employment separation. | Add a section or explicit cross-reference to SOP-IT-002 describing the standard offboarding workflow (access revocation timeline, equipment return, data preservation). Alternatively, incorporate a summary of termination procedures directly in Section 6.1 as a new administrative control (e.g., ADM-004). | **Medium** — The cross-reference to SOP-IT-002 mitigates this, but the AUP should at minimum state the principle explicitly. |
| **Password Management**: The AUP prohibits sharing but does not address creation, changing, or safeguarding procedures. | Add a brief affirmative statement in Section 5.2 (Permitted Use) or Section 6.1 (Administrative Controls) that workforce members must adhere to SOP-IT-003 for password lifecycle management, and summarize key requirements (e.g., minimum length, MFA requirement, prohibition on password reuse). | **Low** — Deferral to a dedicated standard is acceptable under HIPAA's documentation flexibility, but a summary statement strengthens audit readiness. |
| **NPRM Readiness**: The December 2024 proposed rule would require annual training (already met), role-based training within 30 days (already exceeded), and explicit documentation of training (already tracked via AUP-02 KPI). | No immediate action required, but monitor the final rule. SOP-HR-005 is well-positioned for the proposed changes. | **Advisory** |

---

### 7. OVERALL CONCLUSION

**SOP-HR-005 v4.2 is substantially compliant with HIPAA § 164.308(a)(3) (Workforce Security) and § 164.308(a)(5) (Security Awareness and Training).** 

The SOP demonstrates strong coverage across 6 of 8 assessed implementation specifications. Two addressable specifications — Termination Procedures and Password Management — are only partially addressed within the four corners of this SOP, relying on cross-references to other policies (SOP-IT-002 and SOP-IT-003). While HIPAA's documentation standard (§ 164.316) permits policies to be maintained across multiple documents, the AUP would benefit from at minimum a summary statement or explicit procedural reference for these two areas to ensure a reviewer can confirm coverage without chasing external documents.

**Compliance level: SUBSTANTIALLY COMPLIANT with minor gaps.**

## Findings: OCR HIPAA Enforcement Actions Targeting AI Systems Processing PHI (Past 12 Months)

**No, the HHS Office for Civil Rights has not issued any HIPAA enforcement actions in the past 12 months (approximately March 2024 – March 2025) that specifically address AI systems processing protected health information.**

### What the Record Shows

The OCR has been highly active in HIPAA enforcement during this period — announcing approximately 20–22 resolution agreements and civil monetary penalties since the beginning of 2024. However, **every one of these enforcement actions** falls into categories other than AI-specific processing of PHI:

| Category | Notable Cases | Approximate Date |
|---|---|---|
| **Ransomware / Cybersecurity** | Bryan County Ambulance Authority ($90,000); Elgon Information Systems ($80,000); Virtual Private Network Solutions ($90,000); Plastic Surgery Associates of South Dakota ($500,000); Providence Medical Institute ($240,000 CMP) | Oct 2024 – Jan 2025 |
| **Impermissible Disclosure** | Holy Redeemer Family Medicine (reproductive health PHI disclosure); Inmediata Health Group | Nov – Dec 2024 |
| **Right of Access** | Multiple Right of Access settlements (e.g., Mental Health Center, $100,000 CMP) | Nov 2024 |
| **Security Rule Risk Analysis Failures** | Seven-enforcement-action initiative targeting inadequate risk analysis | Oct 2024 – Jan 2025 |
| **Large-Scale Breaches** | Montefiore Medical Center ($4.75M); Solara Medical Supplies ($3M); Warby Parker ($1.5M CMP) | Feb – Dec 2024 |

### What OCR *Has* Done on AI

While no AI-specific enforcement actions exist, OCR has taken significant **policy and guidance steps** regarding AI and PHI:

1. **December 27, 2024** — OCR issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to modify the HIPAA Security Rule, which would strengthen cybersecurity protections for ePHI. The proposed rule has implications for AI systems that process ePHI.

2. **October 2024 OCR Cybersecurity Newsletter** — OCR specifically addressed AI-related threats, including deepfakes used for social engineering against healthcare entities.

3. **General guidance** — OCR has made clear that the HIPAA Security Rule applies to AI systems just as it does to any other ePHI system: covered entities and business associates must include AI tools in their risk analyses (§ 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)), execute Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) with clear limits on PHI use and retention, and implement technical safeguards under § 164.312 (access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, and transmission security).

### Bottom Line

As of March 2025, **there is no OCR resolution agreement or civil monetary penalty that specifically names or targets an AI system's processing of PHI as the basis for the enforcement action.** The enforcement docket remains dominated by ransomware incidents, risk analysis failures, impermissible disclosures, and right-of-access violations. That said, given OCR's stated focus on AI governance and the proposed Security Rule updates, AI-specific enforcement is widely expected to emerge in the near future.

## Gap Analysis: SOP-AIML-001 vs. EU AI Act Articles 9 and 14

Based on a thorough review of SOP-AIML-001 (v2.1) against the full text of EU AI Act Article 9 (Risk Management System) and Article 14 (Human Oversight), the following **specific controls are MISSING** from the SOP and would be required before deployment of a high-risk AI system in the EU.

---

### ARTICLE 9 — RISK MANAGEMENT SYSTEM: MISSING CONTROLS

#### 1. No Formal, Documented Risk Management *System* (Article 9(1))

**What the Act requires:** Article 9(1) mandates that a risk management system shall be **"established, implemented, documented and maintained"** as a distinct, standalone system in relation to high-risk AI systems.

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has a Risk Tier Classification (Section 4.2 / P-01 Step 1.3) and an "Adverse Impact Assessment" definition (Section 2.1), but these are project-level scoring exercises, not a **continuous, documented risk management system**. The SOP lacks a dedicated risk management system document, process, or framework that is maintained as a living artifact throughout the model lifecycle.

**Gap:** The SOP conflates risk *classification* (tiering) with risk *management*. There is no requirement to establish, document, and maintain a formal risk management system as a distinct governance artifact.

---

#### 2. No "Continuous Iterative Process" with "Regular Systematic Review and Updating" (Article 9(2))

**What the Act requires:** Article 9(2) requires the risk management system to be "a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the **entire lifecycle** of a high-risk AI system, requiring **regular systematic review and updating**."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has quarterly model reviews (Section 5.8.5) and continuous monitoring (Section 5.8), but these focus on *model performance*, not on systematic review and updating of the *risk management system itself*. The risk tier is calculated once at problem formulation (P-01 Step 1.3) with no mandated periodic reassessment of the risk management system's design or effectiveness.

**Gap:** No requirement for regular systematic review and updating of the risk management system as a whole. The quarterly review (Form F-11-QRR) covers model performance, not the risk management system's continued adequacy.

---

#### 3. Missing Step: Identification and Analysis of Risks from "Reasonably Foreseeable Misuse" (Article 9(2)(a)-(b))

**What the Act requires:** Article 9(2)(a) requires identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks when the system is used "in accordance with its intended purpose." Article 9(2)(b) goes further, requiring estimation and evaluation of risks that may emerge "under conditions of **reasonably foreseeable misuse**."

**What the SOP has:** The Risk Tier Scoring Matrix (P-01 Step 1.3) considers harm severity, scale, decision autonomy, reversibility, and data sensitivity. The RAIR (Gate 3) evaluates safety and robustness (Domain 6). However, neither process explicitly requires a structured analysis of **reasonably foreseeable misuse** scenarios — i.e., deliberate or accidental use of the system in ways not intended by the provider.

**Gap:** No requirement to systematically identify, analyze, estimate, and evaluate risks arising from reasonably foreseeable misuse. The SOP's risk assessment is use-case-centric, not misuse-scenario-centric.

---

#### 4. Missing Step: Evaluation of Risks Based on Post-Market Monitoring Data (Article 9(2)(c))

**What the Act requires:** Article 9(2)(c) requires "the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the **post-market monitoring system** referred to in Article 72."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has continuous monitoring (Section 5.8) and quarterly reviews, but the risk management process (P-01 Step 1.3) is performed entirely pre-deployment. There is no feedback loop that requires post-market monitoring data to be fed back into the risk identification and evaluation process.

**Gap:** The SOP does not require that data from post-deployment monitoring be systematically analyzed to identify new or evolving risks and fed back into the risk management system. This breaks the "continuous iterative" requirement of Article 9(2).

---

#### 5. No Formal Residual Risk Determination (Article 9(5))

**What the Act requires:** Article 9(5) requires that risk management measures shall ensure that "the relevant **residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk** of the high-risk AI systems is **judged to be acceptable**." It further requires (5)(a) elimination or reduction of risks through adequate design, (5)(b) implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures for risks that cannot be eliminated, and (5)(c) provision of information and training to deployers.

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has approval gates and the RAIR, but there is no explicit requirement to:
- Formally assess and document residual risk **per identified hazard**
- Make an explicit **acceptability judgment** on overall residual risk
- Document that risks were first addressed through design (elimination/reduction), then through control measures, and only then through information/training

**Gap:** No formal residual risk determination process. The approval gates are binary (approved/rejected) without requiring a documented judgment that residual risks are acceptable per hazard and overall.

---

#### 6. No Consideration of Adverse Impact on Persons Under 18 and Vulnerable Groups (Article 9(9))

**What the Act requires:** Article 9(9) requires that when implementing the risk management system, providers "shall give consideration to whether in view of its intended purpose the high-risk AI system is likely to have an adverse impact on **persons under the age of 18** and, as appropriate, **other vulnerable groups**."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP's fairness testing (Step 4.2) includes age as a protected attribute and mentions "disability status" and "socioeconomic indicators." However, there is no explicit requirement to assess adverse impact specifically on children/minors or to identify and consider other vulnerable groups (e.g., elderly, cognitively impaired, economically disadvantaged) in the risk management process.

**Gap:** No explicit requirement to consider adverse impacts on persons under 18 or to systematically identify and assess impacts on vulnerable groups as part of the risk management system.

---

#### 7. No Formal Post-Market Monitoring Plan as Part of Technical Documentation (Article 72, cross-referenced by Article 9(2)(c))

**What the Act requires:** Article 72(3) requires a **post-market monitoring plan** that is part of the technical documentation (Annex IV). Article 9(2)(c) ties the risk management system directly to data from this post-market monitoring system.

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has monitoring infrastructure (Section 5.8.1-5.8.2) and alerting, but there is no requirement to produce a formal **post-market monitoring plan** as a standalone document that forms part of the technical documentation. The monitoring is operational, not a documented plan meeting Article 72 requirements.

**Gap:** No requirement for a formal, documented post-market monitoring plan integrated with the technical documentation.

---

### ARTICLE 14 — HUMAN OVERSIGHT: MISSING CONTROLS

#### 8. No Requirement for Human-Machine Interface Tools Designed for Oversight (Article 14(1))

**What the Act requires:** Article 14(1) requires that high-risk AI systems "shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with **appropriate human-machine interface tools**, that they can be **effectively overseen** by natural persons during the period in which they are in use."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP mentions "human-centered design" (PS-1) and "human interaction points" (P-01 Step 1.1(c)), but there is no specific requirement that the system's **human-machine interface** be designed with oversight-specific tools. The SOP focuses on model development, not UI/UX design for oversight.

**Gap:** No requirement to design and document human-machine interface tools specifically for enabling effective human oversight. The SOP treats human interaction as a workflow consideration, not an oversight-by-design requirement.

---

#### 9. No Measures to Address Automation Bias (Article 14(4)(b))

**What the Act requires:** Article 14(4)(b) requires that natural persons assigned human oversight are enabled "to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (**automation bias**), in particular for high-risk AI systems used to provide information or recommendations for decisions to be taken by natural persons."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP does not mention automation bias anywhere. There is no requirement to train overseers on automation bias, to design interfaces that mitigate over-reliance, or to test for automation bias in user studies.

**Gap:** Complete absence of any control addressing automation bias — a specific, enumerated requirement in Article 14(4)(b).

---

#### 10. No "Stop Button" or Safe-State Interruption Mechanism (Article 14(4)(e))

**What the Act requires:** Article 14(4)(e) requires that human overseers are enabled "to intervene in the operation of the high-risk AI system or **interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure** that allows the system to come to a **halt in a safe state**."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has a rollback plan (Section 5.7.2) and decommissioning procedures (Section 5.8.6), but these are administrative/operational controls, not a real-time "stop button" or safe-state interruption mechanism built into the system for use by human overseers during operation.

**Gap:** No requirement for a real-time interruption mechanism (stop button or equivalent) that allows human overseers to bring the system to a safe state. The SOP's rollback and decommissioning are not equivalent to operational interruption capability.

---

#### 11. No Requirement That Human Oversight Measures Be Built Into the System by the Provider (Article 14(3)(a))

**What the Act requires:** Article 14(3)(a) requires that oversight measures be "identified and built, when technically feasible, **into the high-risk AI system by the provider** before it is placed on the market or put into service."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP addresses model development, testing, and deployment but does not require that human oversight measures be **built into the system itself** (as opposed to being external procedural controls). There is no design requirement for embedded oversight capabilities.

**Gap:** The SOP treats oversight as a governance/procedural function (RAIR, approvals, monitoring) rather than requiring that oversight capabilities be engineered into the system itself before deployment.

---

#### 12. No Requirement for Deployer Training on System Capacities, Limitations, and Output Interpretation (Article 14(4)(a), (c); Article 9(5)(c))

**What the Act requires:** Article 14(4)(a) requires that overseers be enabled "to properly understand the relevant **capacities and limitations** of the high-risk AI system and be able to duly monitor its operation, including in view of detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance." Article 14(4)(c) requires the ability "to correctly **interpret the high-risk AI system's output**, taking into account, for example, the interpretation tools and methods available." Article 9(5)(c) requires provision of "information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, **training to deployers**."

**What the SOP has:** The SOP has training requirements (Section 9) but these are for **internal Meridian personnel** (Model Developers, Model Owners), not for **external deployers** (the EU AI Act's "deployers" — e.g., hospitals using Meridian's clinical AI). The SOP does not require that deployer-facing training materials be created covering system capacities, limitations, anomaly detection, and output interpretation.

**Gap:** No requirement to provide training to deployers (end-users) on system capacities, limitations, anomaly detection, and output interpretation. The SOP's training program is inward-facing only.

---

#### 13. No Instructions for Use Meeting Article 13 Requirements (Article 14(4) cross-reference to Article 13)

**What the Act requires:** Article 14(4) requires that the system be "provided to the deployer in such a way that" oversight is enabled. Article 13 requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by **instructions for use** containing specific information including: identity/contact details, characteristics/capabilities/limitations, accuracy metrics, known circumstances leading to risks, technical capabilities for explaining output, performance on specific groups, input data specifications, and human oversight measures.

**What the SOP has:** The SOP requires Model Cards (PS-4, Section 5.7.2) and a Technical Specification Document (TSD), but these are internal governance artifacts. There is no requirement to produce **deployer-facing instructions for use** meeting the specific content requirements of Article 13(3)(a)-(d).

**Gap:** No requirement to produce Article 13-compliant instructions for use for deployers. Model Cards and TSDs are internal documents, not deployer-facing instructions.

---

### SUMMARY TABLE OF MISSING CONTROLS

| # | EU AI Act Reference | Missing Control | Severity |
|---|-------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | Art. 9(1) | Formal, documented, maintained risk management system as a distinct artifact | **Critical** |
| 2 | Art. 9(2) | Continuous iterative process with regular systematic review and updating of the RMS | **Critical** |
| 3 | Art. 9(2)(a)-(b) | Structured analysis of risks from reasonably foreseeable misuse | **High** |
| 4 | Art. 9(2)(c) | Feedback loop from post-market monitoring data into risk identification/evaluation | **High** |
| 5 | Art. 9(5) | Formal residual risk determination per hazard with acceptability judgment | **Critical** |
| 6 | Art. 9(9) | Consideration of adverse impact on persons under 18 and vulnerable groups | **High** |
| 7 | Art. 72(3) / Art. 9(2)(c) | Formal post-market monitoring plan as part of technical documentation | **High** |
| 8 | Art. 14(1) | Human-machine interface tools designed specifically for effective oversight | **High** |
| 9 | Art. 14(4)(b) | Measures to address automation bias (awareness, training, interface design) | **High** |
| 10 | Art. 14(4)(e) | "Stop button" or safe-state interruption mechanism built into the system | **Critical** |
| 11 | Art. 14(3)(a) | Oversight measures built into the system by the provider (not just procedural) | **High** |
| 12 | Art. 14(4)(a),(c) / Art. 9(5)(c) | Deployer training on capacities, limitations, anomaly detection, output interpretation | **High** |
| 13 | Art. 13 / Art. 14(4) | Deployer-facing instructions for use meeting Article 13 content requirements | **Critical** |

---

**Compliance level: gap**

The SOP has substantial governance infrastructure (risk tiering, RAIR, monitoring, model cards) that could serve as a foundation, but it lacks at least four critical controls (formal risk management system, residual risk determination, stop-button mechanism, and Article 13 instructions for use) and nine high-severity gaps that would need to be remediated before a high-risk AI system could be lawfully deployed in the EU. The SOP was designed primarily against NIST AI RMF 1.0 and U.S.-centric frameworks (HIPAA, SOC 2, HITRUST), and does not operationalize the specific, prescriptive requirements of EU AI Act Articles 9 and 14.

## HIPAA Privacy Rule: The "Minimum Necessary" Standard

### What It Is

The **minimum necessary standard**, codified at **45 CFR § 164.502(b)**, requires that when a covered entity or business associate **uses, discloses, or requests** protected health information (PHI), it must make **reasonable efforts to limit the PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose** of the use, disclosure, or request.

This is a foundational principle of the HIPAA Privacy Rule — it is not a "least possible" standard, but a reasonableness standard. Covered entities must implement policies and procedures to identify who needs access, what information they need, and under what conditions.

Under **§ 164.514(d)**, the rule further specifies:

- **Routine/recurring disclosures**: Must follow standard protocols that limit PHI to what is reasonably necessary.
- **Non-routine disclosures**: Must be reviewed on an individual basis against criteria designed to limit PHI.
- **Entire medical records**: Generally may **not** be used, disclosed, or requested unless the entire record is **specifically justified** as the amount reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose.
- **Reliance on others**: A covered entity may reasonably rely on representations from public officials, other covered entities, workforce professionals, or researchers (under § 164.512(i)) that the information requested is the minimum necessary.

---

### Disclosures to Which the Minimum Necessary Standard Does NOT Apply

Under **§ 164.502(b)(2)**, the minimum necessary requirement **does not apply** to the following six categories:

| # | Exception | Description |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| **(i)** | **Treatment disclosures** | Disclosures to or requests by a health care provider **for treatment** purposes. |
| **(ii)** | **Disclosures to the individual** | Uses or disclosures made **to the individual** who is the subject of the PHI (per § 164.502(a)(1)(i) or as required by § 164.502(a)(2)(i)). |
| **(iii)** | **Authorizations** | Uses or disclosures made pursuant to a valid **authorization** under § 164.508 (i.e., the individual has signed off). |
| **(iv)** | **Disclosures to the Secretary of HHS** | Disclosures made to the **Secretary of Health and Human Services** for compliance investigations and enforcement under Subpart C of Part 160. |
| **(v)** | **Required by law** | Uses or disclosures that are **required by law**, as described in § 164.512(a). |
| **(vi)** | **Compliance with HIPAA itself** | Uses or disclosures required for **compliance with the applicable requirements** of the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (this subchapter). |

---

### Key Takeaway

The minimum necessary standard is a broad, reasonableness-based obligation that applies to most uses and disclosures of PHI — but Congress and HHS carved out specific exceptions where applying the standard would be impractical or counterproductive. The most significant practical exception is **treatment**: a provider requesting or receiving PHI for treatment purposes is not constrained by the minimum necessary rule, which ensures clinical care is not impeded. Similarly, individuals are entitled to their own information without limitation, and disclosures explicitly authorized by the individual or mandated by law are exempt.

question.question: Under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, what is the maximum timeframe for notifying affected individuals after discovery of a breach, and what information must the notification contain?
question.expected_answer: Per 45 CFR §164.404, individual notification must be made without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of the breach. The written notice must include, at minimum: a brief description of what happened (including date of breach and date of discovery, if known), the types of unsecured PHI involved, steps individuals should take to protect themselves, a brief description of what the covered entity is doing to investigate/mitigate and prevent recurrence, and contact procedures.

output.answer:
## HIPAA Breach Notification Rule: Timeframe and Content Requirements

### Maximum Timeframe for Notifying Affected Individuals

Under **45 CFR § 164.404(b)**, a covered entity must provide breach notification to affected individuals **without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of the breach**.

Key points about the timeframe:

- **Discovery date** (§ 164.404(a)(2)): A breach is treated as "discovered" on the first day the breach is known to the covered entity — or, by exercising reasonable diligence, *would have been known*. Knowledge by any workforce member or agent (other than the person committing the breach) is imputed to the covered entity.

- **Law enforcement delay** (§ 164.412): If a law enforcement official provides a written statement that notification would impede a criminal investigation or damage national security, the covered entity must delay notification for the period specified. If the statement is oral, the delay is temporary and no longer than 30 days, unless a written statement is submitted during that time.

- **Business associates** (§ 164.410(b)): Business associates must notify the covered entity (not individuals directly) also within the same 60-calendar-day maximum, without unreasonable delay.

---

### Required Content of the Notification

Under **§ 164.404(c)**, the notification to individuals must include, **to the extent possible**, the following five elements:

| # | Element | Detail |
|---|---------|--------|
| **(A)** | **Description of what happened** | A brief description, including the date of the breach and the date of discovery (if known). |
| **(B)** | **Types of PHI involved** | A description of the types of unsecured protected health information involved (e.g., full name, Social Security number, date of birth, home address, account number, diagnosis, disability code, or other types). |
| **(C)** | **Steps for individuals to protect themselves** | Any steps individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach. |
| **(D)** | **What the covered entity is doing** | A brief description of what the covered entity is doing to investigate the breach, mitigate harm, and protect against further breaches. |
| **(E)** | **Contact procedures** | Contact information for individuals to ask questions or learn more, which must include a toll-free telephone number, an email address, website, or postal address. |

Additionally, under **§ 164.404(c)(2)**, the notification must be **written in plain language**.

---

### Methods of Delivery (§ 164.404(d))

- **Primary method**: First-class mail to the individual's last known address, or electronic mail if the individual has agreed to electronic notice.
- **Deceased individuals**: Written notice to the next of kin or personal representative.
- **Substitute notice**: If contact information is insufficient or out-of-date:
  - Fewer than 10 individuals: alternative written notice, telephone, or other means.
  - 10 or more individuals: a conspicuous 90-day posting on the covered entity's website homepage **and** a toll-free phone number active for at least 90 days, **or** conspicuous notice in major print or broadcast media in the affected geographic areas.
- **Urgent situations**: The covered entity may provide additional notice by telephone or other means if there is a risk of imminent misuse of the PHI.

---

### Summary

The HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR § 164.404) requires covered entities to notify affected individuals **no later than 60 calendar days** after breach discovery, and the notification must contain: (A) a description of the breach and its dates, (B) the types of PHI involved, (C) protective steps for individuals, (D) the entity's investigation and mitigation efforts, and (E) contact procedures including a toll-free number — all in plain language.

question.question: What does SOC 2 Common Criterion CC7 (System Operations / Monitoring) cover at a high level?
question.expected_answer: CC7 covers system operations and monitoring activities: detection and monitoring of configuration changes (CC7.1), monitoring of system components for anomalies (CC7.2), evaluation of security events to determine whether they could result in failure to meet objectives (CC7.3), incident response (CC7.4), and recovery from identified security incidents (CC7.5).

output.answer:
I now have a comprehensive picture of all five CC7 sub-criteria. Here's the high-level summary:

---

## SOC 2 Common Criterion CC7 — System Operations / Monitoring

**CC7** falls under the "System Operations" category of the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (Common Criteria). It addresses how an entity **detects, monitors, evaluates, responds to, and recovers from system events and security incidents** that could impair its ability to meet its service commitments and system requirements. It consists of five sub-criteria:

### CC7.1 — Vulnerability Detection & Configuration Monitoring
The entity uses detection and monitoring procedures to identify **(1) changes to configurations** that introduce new vulnerabilities and **(2) susceptibilities to newly discovered vulnerabilities**. Key points of focus include:
- Using defined configuration standards for hardening systems
- Monitoring infrastructure and software for noncompliance with standards
- Implementing change-detection mechanisms (e.g., file integrity monitoring)
- Detecting unknown or unauthorized components
- Conducting periodic vulnerability scans and remediating findings in a timely manner

### CC7.2 — Anomaly & Intrusion Detection
The entity **monitors system components and their operation for anomalies** indicative of malicious acts, natural disasters, and errors. Anomalies are analyzed to determine whether they represent security events. Key points of focus include:
- Implementing detection policies, procedures, and tools (e.g., intrusion detection, logging of unusual activity)
- Designing detection measures to identify compromises across physical, logical, and credential-based vectors
- Implementing filters to summarize and analyze anomalies
- Monitoring the effectiveness of detection tools themselves

### CC7.3 — Security Event Evaluation
The entity **evaluates security events to determine whether they constitute security incidents** (i.e., events that could or did cause a failure to meet objectives) and takes actions to prevent or address such failures. Key points of focus include:
- Responding to security incidents and periodically evaluating response procedures
- Communicating and reviewing detected security events with security program leadership
- Developing procedures to analyze incidents and determine system impact
- For confidentiality/privacy engagements: assessing impact on confidential or personal information

### CC7.4 — Incident Response
The entity responds to identified security incidents by **executing a defined incident-response program** to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents. Key points of focus include:
- Assigning roles and responsibilities (including external resources)
- Containing, mitigating, and resolving security incidents
- Restoring operations to an interim functional state
- Communicating incident information to affected parties in a timely manner
- Remediating identified vulnerabilities and documenting remediation activities
- Periodically evaluating the effectiveness of incident response

### CC7.5 — Recovery from Security Incidents
The entity **identifies, develops, and implements activities to recover** from identified security incidents. Key points of focus include:
- Restoring the affected environment to functional operation (rebuilding systems, patching, reconfiguring)
- Communicating the nature of the incident, recovery actions, and prevention steps to management and others
- Determining the root cause of the incident

---

**In summary**, CC7 establishes a complete lifecycle for security operations: from **detecting vulnerabilities and anomalies** (CC7.1–7.2), through **triage and evaluation** (CC7.3), to **incident response and containment** (CC7.4), and finally **recovery and root-cause analysis** (CC7.5). Together, these criteria ensure the entity has the operational capability to identify and respond to system events before they materially impact service commitments.

## SOC 2 CC8.1 — Change Management Requirements

**SOC 2 Common Criterion CC8.1** requires that the entity **authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes** to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures to meet its objectives.

The criterion is supported by the following **points of focus**, which describe the key characteristics of an effective change management process:

### 1. Manages Changes Throughout the System Life Cycle
A process for managing system changes throughout the life cycle of the system and its components — including infrastructure, data, software, and both manual and automated procedures — must be in place to support the achievement of entity objectives.

### 2. Authorizes Changes
A process must exist to **authorize** system and architecture changes *prior to* design, development, or acquisition and configuration. This means no change should proceed without formal approval.

### 3. Designs and Develops Changes
Changes must be **designed and developed in a secure manner** to support the achievement of entity objectives. This implies that security considerations are embedded into the change design and development process, not bolted on afterward.

### 4. Documents Changes
A process must be in place to **document** system changes to support:
- Ongoing maintenance of the system, and
- Internal and external users in performing their responsibilities.

### 5. Tests and Approves Changes (from the main criterion text)
The overarching criterion explicitly calls out that changes must be **tested** and **approved** before implementation. This means:
- Testing validates that the change works as intended and does not introduce unintended effects.
- Approval ensures appropriate sign-off before the change goes live.

### 6. Configures and Implements Changes (from the main criterion text)
Changes must be properly **configured** and **implemented** in a controlled manner, ensuring that what was designed, tested, and approved is what actually gets deployed.

---

### Summary

In essence, CC8.1 requires a **formal, end-to-end change management lifecycle** that covers:

| Phase | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Authorization | Formal approval before work begins |
| Design & Development | Secure design and build |
| Documentation | Record-keeping for maintenance and user support |
| Testing | Validation before deployment |
| Approval | Sign-off before implementation |
| Configuration & Implementation | Controlled deployment |

This criterion applies broadly across infrastructure, data, software, and procedures, and is foundational to the **Security** trust services category (and relevant to all other categories where change management affects Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, or Privacy).

question.question: Under GDPR Article 33, what is the time limit for notifying the supervisory authority of a personal data breach, and when does the clock start?
question.expected_answer: Article 33(1) requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after the controller has become aware of the breach. If the notification is later than 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay. The clock starts when the controller becomes 'aware' of the breach, which means having a reasonable degree of certainty that a personal data breach has occurred.
question.notes: Specific timeline often confused with HIPAA's 60 days.

output.answer:
## GDPR Article 33 — Notification Time Limit

Under **Article 33(1)** of the GDPR, the controller must notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach **without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours** after having become aware of it.

### When does the clock start?

The 72-hour clock starts ticking from the moment the controller **"becomes aware"** of the personal data breach. This is not when the breach *occurred*, but when the controller first has a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident involving personal data has taken place. In practice, this means the clock starts once the controller's internal detection mechanisms, employees, or third parties (e.g., a processor) bring the breach to the controller's attention.

### Key details from Article 33:

- **Exception:** Notification is not required if the breach is "unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons."
- **Late notification:** If notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be **accompanied by reasons for the delay** (Article 33(1), second sentence).
- **Processors' obligation:** Under Article 33(2), a processor must notify the controller **"without undue delay"** after becoming aware of a breach — no specific hour limit is set for processors, but the urgency is clear.
- **Phased notification:** Where it is not possible to provide all required information at once, it may be provided **in phases without undue further delay** (Article 33(4)).
- **Documentation:** Article 33(5) requires the controller to document all personal data breaches, including facts, effects, and remedial actions, to enable supervisory authority verification.

### Practical takeaway

The 72-hour window is a maximum, not a safe harbour. The primary obligation is "without undue delay," meaning controllers must act as quickly as circumstances permit. Organisations should have breach detection and escalation procedures in place to ensure they can meet this tight timeline.

question.question: What rights does GDPR Article 17 grant to data subjects, and what are the principal exemptions a controller can invoke?
question.expected_answer: Article 17 grants the 'right to erasure' / 'right to be forgotten' — the data subject has the right to obtain erasure of personal data without undue delay when: the data is no longer necessary for the purposes; consent has been withdrawn; the data subject objects; the data was unlawfully processed; or erasure is required by EU/Member State law. Principal exemptions (Article 17(3)): exercising the right of freedom of expression; compliance with a legal obligation; reasons of public interest in public health; archiving / research / statistical purposes; or establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims.

output.answer:
## GDPR Article 17 — Right to Erasure ("Right to Be Forgotten")

### Rights Granted to Data Subjects

Under Article 17(1), a data subject has the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning them **without undue delay** where one of the following six grounds applies:

1. **Purpose fulfilled** — The personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed.

2. **Consent withdrawn** — The data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based (under Article 6(1)(a) or Article 9(2)(a)), and there is no other legal ground for the processing.

3. **Objection upheld** — The data subject objects to processing under Article 21(1) and there are no overriding legitimate grounds, or the data subject objects under Article 21(2) (objection to direct marketing).

4. **Unlawful processing** — The personal data have been unlawfully processed.

5. **Legal obligation to erase** — The personal data must be erased for compliance with a legal obligation under Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject.

6. **Child's data (information society services)** — The personal data were collected in relation to the offer of information society services to a child under Article 8(1).

### Extended Obligation — Public Data (Article 17(2))

Where the controller has **made the personal data public** and is obliged to erase it under paragraph 1, the controller must take **reasonable steps**, accounting for available technology and cost of implementation, to inform **other controllers** processing the data that the data subject has requested erasure of any links to, or copies or replications of, those personal data.

### Principal Exemptions (Article 17(3))

The right to erasure does **not** apply to the extent that processing is necessary for any of the following five grounds:

1. **Freedom of expression and information** — Exercising the right to freedom of expression and information.

2. **Legal obligation / public interest task** — Compliance with a legal obligation requiring processing under Union or Member State law, or performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority.

3. **Public health** — Reasons of public interest in the area of public health, in accordance with Article 9(2)(h) and (i) and Article 9(3).

4. **Archiving / research / statistics** — Archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes under Article 89(1), insofar as the right to erasure is likely to render impossible or seriously impair the achievement of those objectives.

5. **Legal claims** — The establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims.

### Related Procedural Obligations

- **Article 12(3)** — The controller must respond without undue delay and within **one month** (extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests), and must inform the data subject of the reasons if it refuses to act.
- **Article 19** — The controller must communicate any erasure to each **recipient** to whom the data were disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort, and must inform the data subject of those recipients upon request.
- **Article 12(5)** — The controller may charge a reasonable fee or refuse to act where requests are **manifestly unfounded or excessive**, with the burden of proof on the controller.

In summary, Article 17 provides a powerful but not absolute right — it is carefully balanced against competing interests such as free expression, legal compliance, public health, research, and the defence of legal claims.

question.question: Under the EU AI Act, by what mechanism is an AI system classified as 'high-risk'?
question.expected_answer: Per Article 6, an AI system is high-risk if either: (1) it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment; or (2) it falls within the use cases listed in Annex III (e.g. biometric identification, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration/asylum/border, administration of justice and democratic processes). Annex III categories can be amended via delegated acts.

---

## How an AI System Is Classified as "High-Risk" Under the EU AI Act

The EU AI Act establishes **two principal pathways** for classifying an AI system as high-risk, both set out in **Article 6** of the Regulation. There is also a critical derogation mechanism and an amendment procedure.

---

### Pathway 1: AI as a Safety Component or Product Under Annex I Legislation (Article 6(1))

An AI system is classified as high-risk where **both** of the following conditions are met:

1. **(a)** The AI system is intended to be used as a **safety component of a product**, or the AI system **is itself a product**, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in **Annex I** (e.g., medical devices, machinery, lifts, toys, radio equipment, etc.); **and**

2. **(b)** The product whose safety component the AI system is, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a **third-party conformity assessment** under that relevant Annex I legislation.

This pathway captures AI systems embedded in already strictly regulated products.

---

### Pathway 2: AI Systems Listed in Annex III (Article 6(2))

In addition to Pathway 1, **AI systems referred to in Annex III** are considered high-risk. Annex III lists AI systems in **eight specific areas** (insofar as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law):

| Area | Examples |
|------|----------|
| **1. Biometrics** | Remote biometric identification systems (excluding biometric verification); biometric categorisation based on sensitive/protected attributes; emotion recognition systems |
| **2. Critical Infrastructure** | AI systems used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or supply of water, gas, heating, and electricity |
| **3. Education & Vocational Training** | AI systems determining access, admission, or assignment to educational institutions; evaluating learning outcomes; assessing the appropriate level of education |
| **4. Employment, Workers Management & Access to Self-Employment** | AI systems for recruitment or selection; making decisions on promotion, termination, or task allocation; monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour of workers |
| **5. Access to Essential Services & Benefits** | AI systems used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services; creditworthiness evaluation or credit scoring (except for fraud detection); risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance |
| **6. Law Enforcement** | AI systems for assessing the risk of a natural person becoming a victim of criminal offences; use as polygraphs and similar tools; assessing the reliability of evidence; predicting the occurrence or reoccurrence of criminal offences; profiling of natural persons during criminal investigations |
| **7. Migration, Asylum & Border Control** | AI systems used as polygraphs and similar tools; assessing security, irregular migration, or health risks; examining applications for asylum, visa, or residence permits; detecting, recognising, or identifying natural persons (except verification of travel documents) |
| **8. Administration of Justice & Democratic Processes** | AI systems intended to assist judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts and the law, and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts; AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum or voting behaviour |

---

### The Derogation: When an Annex III System Is *Not* High-Risk (Article 6(3))

By derogation from Article 6(2), an AI system referred to in Annex III **shall not be considered high-risk** where it does **not pose a significant risk of harm** to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by **not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making**. This derogation applies only where **any** of the following four conditions is fulfilled:

- **(a)** The AI system performs a **narrow procedural task**;
- **(b)** The AI system is intended to **improve the result of a previously completed human activity**;
- **(c)** The AI system is intended to **detect decision-making patterns or deviations** from prior decision-making patterns and is **not meant to replace or influence** the previously completed human assessment, **without proper human review**; or
- **(d)** The AI system performs a **preparatory task** to an assessment relevant for the purposes of the Annex III use cases.

**Critical caveat:** Notwithstanding the derogation, an Annex III AI system **shall always be considered high-risk** if it performs **profiling of natural persons** (Article 6(3), final subparagraph).

**Documentation obligation (Article 6(4)):** A provider who considers that an Annex III AI system is *not* high-risk must **document its assessment** before the system is placed on the market or put into service.

---

### Amendments to Annex III (Article 7)

The European Commission is empowered to adopt **delegated acts** (under Article 97) to:

- **Add** AI systems to Annex III where they pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights, based on criteria including the intended purpose, extent of use, potential harm, and existing remedies.
- **Remove** AI systems from Annex III where they no longer pose significant risks and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection.

---

### Summary of the Classification Mechanism

| Mechanism | Legal Basis | Key Trigger |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| Safety component / product under Annex I | Article 6(1) | AI is a safety component of (or is itself) a regulated product requiring third-party conformity assessment |
| Listed in Annex III | Article 6(2) | AI falls within one of the eight high-risk areas |
| Derogation from Annex III | Article 6(3) | System poses no significant risk + meets one of four narrow conditions (but never applies if profiling) |
| Commission amendment | Article 7 | Delegated acts to add or remove systems from Annex III |

---

**Sources:**

- Annex III, EU AI Act — [Annex III text](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3)
- Article 7, EU AI Act — [Amendments to Annex III](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/7)

**Article 11: Technical Documentation**
### Article 11: Technical Documentation

1. The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date. The technical documentation shall be drawn up in such a way as to demonstrate that the high-risk AI system complies with the requirements set out in this Section and to provide national competent authorities and notified bodies with the necessary information in a clear and comprehensive form to assess the compliance of the AI system with those requirements. It shall contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV. SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the elements of the technical documentation specified in Annex IV in a simplified manner. 2. Where a high-risk AI system related to a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I is placed on the market or put into service, a single set of technical documentation shall be drawn up containing all the information set out in paragraph 1, as well as the information required under those legal acts.

3. ### Article 23: Obligations of Importers

1. Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, importers shall ensure that the system is in conformity with this Regulation by verifying that:

(a) the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 has been carried out by the provider of the high-risk AI system;

(b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV;

(c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and instructions for use;

5. **Article 10: Data and Data Governance**
### Article 10: Data and Data Governance

1. High-risk AI systems which make use of techniques involving the training of AI models with data shall be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet the quality criteria referred to in paragraphs 2 to 5 whenever such data sets are used.

2. Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Those practices shall concern in particular:

(a) the relevant design choices;

(b) data collection processes and the origin of data, and in the case of personal data, the original purpose of the data collection;

(c) relevant data-preparation processing operations, such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation;

(d) the formulation of assumptions, in particular with respect to the information that the data are supposed to measure and represent;

(e) an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets that are needed;

(f) examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, especially where data outputs influence inputs for future operations;

(g) appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate possible biases identified according to point (f);

(h) the identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance with this Regulation, and how those gaps and shortcomings can be addressed.

3. Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They shall have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. Those characteristics of the data sets may be met at the level of individual data sets or at the level of a combination thereof.

4. Data sets shall take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements that are particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used.

## The Four Core Functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

The NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023) organizes its "Core" around four functions: **GOVERN**, **MAP**, **MEASURE**, and **MANAGE**. Here's what each covers at a high level:

---

### 1. GOVERN

**GOVERN** applies across *all* stages of an organization's AI risk management process and provides the foundational scaffolding. It focuses on establishing the organizational structures, policies, and culture needed for effective AI risk management. Key categories include:

- **GOVERN 1** — Policies, processes, and procedures for AI risk management are established, documented, and aligned with organizational values and legal/regulatory requirements. This includes ongoing monitoring, periodic review, AI system inventories, and decommissioning procedures.
- **GOVERN 2** — Accountability structures ensure the right teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks. Executive leadership takes responsibility for AI risk decisions.
- **GOVERN 3** — Workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility are prioritized in AI risk management, with diverse teams informing decisions and clear policies for human-AI configurations.
- **GOVERN 4** — A culture of critical thinking and safety-first mindset is fostered to minimize potential negative impacts.
- **GOVERN 5** — Policies and procedures are in place for third-party AI risks, including supply chain and procurement considerations.
- **GOVERN 6** — Policies and procedures address transparency, documentation, and information sharing with relevant AI actors.

> *Source: NIST AI 100-1, Part 2, §5.1, Table 1 (pp. 21–24)*

---

### 2. MAP

**MAP** establishes the contextual knowledge needed to identify and understand AI risks. It is the foundation for the MEASURE and MANAGE functions. Without contextual awareness, risk management is difficult to perform. Key categories include:

- **MAP 1** — Context is established and understood: intended purposes, beneficial uses, legal/normative expectations, deployment settings, user types, potential impacts, and organizational risk tolerances are documented.
- **MAP 2** — The AI system is categorized: specific tasks and methods (e.g., classifiers, generative models), knowledge limits, human oversight, and scientific integrity/TEVV considerations are documented.
- **MAP 3** — AI capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and expected benefits/costs are compared against appropriate benchmarks. This includes examining potential benefits, non-monetary costs, application scope, and operator proficiency.
- **MAP 4** — Risks and benefits are mapped for all components, including third-party software and data, with internal risk controls identified.
- **MAP 5** — Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized, including likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact.

> *Source: NIST AI 100-1, Part 2, §5.2, Table 2 (pp. 24–27)*

---

### 3. MEASURE

**MEASURE** employs quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method tools, techniques, and methodologies to analyze, assess, benchmark, and monitor AI risk and related impacts. It uses knowledge from MAP and informs MANAGE. Key categories include:

- **MEASURE 1** — Appropriate methods and metrics are identified and applied, starting with the most significant risks. Metrics and controls are regularly reassessed, and independent assessors are involved.
- **MEASURE 2** — AI systems are evaluated for trustworthy characteristics: validity and reliability, safety, security and resilience, transparency and accountability, explainability and interpretability, privacy, fairness and bias, and environmental impact. This includes pre-deployment testing and ongoing production monitoring.
- **MEASURE 3** — Mechanisms for tracking identified AI risks over time are in place, including tracking emergent risks and situations where metrics are not yet available. Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities are established.
- **MEASURE 4** — Feedback about the efficacy of measurement is gathered and assessed, with input from domain experts and affected communities to validate performance.

> *Source: NIST AI 100-1, Part 2, §5.3, Table 3 (pp. 28–31)*

---

### 4. MANAGE

**MANAGE** entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on a regular basis, as defined by the GOVERN function. It covers risk treatment, response, recovery, and communication. Key categories include:

- **MANAGE 1** — AI risks are prioritized based on impact, likelihood, and available resources. Prioritization is informed by the MAP and MEASURE functions.
- **MANAGE 2** — Risks are responded to, with treatment options including avoidance, mitigation, transfer, or acceptance. Responses are documented and aligned with organizational risk tolerance.
- **MANAGE 3** — Benefits and potential negative impacts of AI risks and risk treatments are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities.
- **MANAGE 4** — Risk treatments, including response and recovery, and communication plans are documented and monitored regularly. This includes post-deployment monitoring, incident response, decommissioning, change management, and continual improvement.

> *Source: NIST AI 100-1, Part 2, §5.4, Table 4 (pp. 31–33)*

---

### How the Functions Relate

The framework is designed so that **GOVERN** applies across the entire AI lifecycle, while **MAP → MEASURE → MANAGE** form a logical operational sequence: you first understand the context and identify risks (MAP), then quantitatively or qualitatively assess them (MEASURE), and finally treat, monitor, and communicate about them (MANAGE). The outputs of each function feed into the next, and the entire cycle is iterative — organizations are expected to revisit each function as contexts, capabilities, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

> *Source: NIST AI 100-1, Part 2, §5 (p. 20)*

Value Chain and Component Integration GAI value chains involve many third-party components such as procured datasets, pre-trained models, and software libraries. These components might be improperly obtained or not properly vetted, leading to diminished transparency or accountability for downstream users. While this is a risk for traditional AI systems and some other digital technologies, the risk is exacerbated for GAI due to the scale of the training data, which may be too large for humans to vet; the diﬃculty of training foundation models, which leads to extensive reuse of limited numbers of models; and the extent to which GAI may be integrated into other devices and services. ## SR 11-7: Three Foundational Elements of Model Risk Management

SR 11-7 ("Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management," issued jointly by the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC) articulates **three foundational elements** of an effective model risk management framework:

### 1. Model Development, Implementation, and Use

This element addresses the full lifecycle of model creation and deployment. As stated in the guidance (Section IV), *"Sound model development activities are aligned with model purpose, business use, and banking organization policy. Model development is not purely a technical exercise. The developer's judgment influences the model's conceptual design and soundness, inputs…"* It encompasses documenting the model's purpose, design theory, logic, methodologies, data inputs, testing, and ensuring proper implementation and ongoing use.

### 2. Model Validation

The guidance emphasizes that model validation is a critical, independent review function. The retrieved text highlights that *"Sound model risk management also involves 'effective challenge,' which refers to the critical analysis conducted by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring."* Validation must be performed by individuals with appropriate expertise, sufficient independence, and organizational standing to effect change. This also extends to vendor and third-party models (Section VII).

### 3. Governance, Policies, and Controls

The governance element establishes the oversight structure, including clear roles and responsibilities, a comprehensive model inventory, adequate documentation, and board/senior management oversight. As the guidance notes, *"Organizations benefit from clearly defining roles and responsibilities when delegating these activities"* and *"an effective model inventory includes sufficient information to understand model risks, so as to support effective model risk management at the individual and aggregate levels."*

---

Together, these three pillars — **development/implementation/use**, **validation**, and **governance** — form the core of the SR 11-7 framework, all underpinned by the principle of **"effective challenge"** and tailored to the size, complexity, and risk profile of each banking organization.

**Sources:**
- SR 11-7 (April 17, 2026), Sections III, IV, VII — Federal Reserve / FDIC / OCC
- [ModelOp — SR 11-7 Model Risk Management](https://www.modelop.com/ai-governance/ai-regulations-standards/sr-11-7)
- [Apparity — What is SR 11-7 Guidance?](https://apparity.com/euc-resources/spreadsheet-euc-risk-blog/what-is-sr-11-7-guidance)

There are a variety of ways for a banking organization to structure model risk 
management practices. Not all models present the same level of risk, and a similar model at two 
different banking organizations may present different risks. As such, practices that are 
appropriate and effective for one banking organization may be inappropriate and ineffective for a 
banking organization with a different risk profile or that uses a model for a different purpose. 
Although this guidance may be useful for any type of model, the general expectation is 
that it will be most useful for models supporting a banking organization’s significant business 
lines, operations, services, and functions. This guidance does not set forth enforceable standards 
or prescriptive requirements; accordingly, non-compliance with this guidance will not result in 
supervisory criticism against a banking organization.1  
II. PURPOSE AND SCOPE 
Based on supervisory experience and industry feedback, as well as technological 
advancements in modeling over the past several years, the Office of the Comptroller of the 
Currency, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and Federal Deposit Insurance 
Corporation (the “agencies”) are issuing this revised model risk management guidance to clarify 
model risk management principles, and to set forth a risk-based approach to model risk 
management, tailored to a banking organization’s model risk profile and the size and complexity 
of its operations. 
This guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 
billion in total assets.2 Models used by banking organizations with total assets of $30 billion or

For the purposes of this guidance, the term “model” refers to a complex quantitative 
method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, or financial theories to process 
input data into quantitative estimates. The term “model” in this guidance excludes simple 
arithmetic calculations, such as those found within spreadsheets, as well as deterministic rule-
based processes and software where there are no statistical, economic, or financial theories 
underpinning their design or use.3  
III. OVERVIEW OF MODEL RISK AND MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT 
Models are simplified representations of real-world relationships among observed 
characteristics, values, and events; they are based on assumptions that make them useful in 
estimating values and predicting events, but which also can have limitations and create model 
risk. The term “model risk” refers to the potential for adverse financial consequences associated 
with models, which may result from decisions made based on model output. Model risk is 
influenced by a model’s inherent risk, exposure, purpose, and use, each of which are discussed 
below.  
 
3 Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this 
guidance. Nonetheless, a banking organization’s risk management and governance practices should guide the 
determination of appropriate governance and controls for any tools, processes, or systems not covered in this

and non-generative, non-agentic AI models.

SUPERVISORY GUIDANCE ON  
MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT 
 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Use of models within the banking and financial services industries continues to grow in 
complexity and scope. Advances in technology along with increased competition have driven 
banking organizations to leverage innovative approaches to improve efficiencies, better mitigate 
risks, and help maximize profits. Continued use of models is essential to maintaining the 
competitiveness of banking organizations in the financial system. 
Use of models also can present substantial risk. Such risk, generally referred to as “model 
risk” for purposes of this guidance, can lead to financial loss, errors in financial statements and 
reporting, and flawed financial and risk management decisions, among other types of risk events. 
Model risk can be mitigated through active and appropriate risk management, recognizing that 
the relevance of model risk depends on the nature, scale, and use of the models in relation to the 
associated business risks.  
This guidance highlights sound principles for effective model risk management. As 
reflected in this guidance, model risk management practices vary from banking organization to 
banking organization. Each banking organization ultimately is responsible for adopting model 
risk management practices that are appropriate and effective for managing the specific risks the 
banking organization faces or is likely to face.

5  
Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate. 
Aggregate risk reflects interactions and dependencies among models; reliance on common 
assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely affect several 
models and their outputs simultaneously.   
Sound model risk management also involves “effective challenge,” which refers to the 
critical analysis conducted by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate 
changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring. 
Effective challenge is performed by individuals with the appropriate expertise to conduct a 
critical and objective challenge, sufficient independence to maintain objectivity, as well as the 
organizational standing and influence to effect any change. 
The size and complexity of the banking organization’s operations also may influence the 
range of model risk management. A banking organization with simple operations may not 
conduct model risk management with the same rigor as an organization with relatively more 
complex operations. Furthermore, a banking organization may tailor portions of its model risk 
management practices that are relevant to the risks posed by a particular model and with a level 
of rigor commensurate with that risk. Effective model risk management therefore warrants 
consideration of model risk in the context of the broader business risks that models support or 
influence.

Model Development 
Sound model development activities are aligned with model purpose, business use, and 
banking organization policy. Model development is not purely a technical exercise. The 
developer’s judgment influences the model’s conceptual design and soundness, inputs,

11  
broader model risk management activities. Organizations benefit from clearly defining roles and 
responsibilities when delegating these activities.
