## Most Recent Significant GDPR Fine — AI / Automated Decision-Making

| Detail | Information |
|---|---|
| **Case** | Automated credit card application rejections without meaningful transparency |
| **Authority** | **Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information** (*Hamburgische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit* — HmbBfDI) |
| **Fine Amount** | **€492,000** |
| **Date** | **30 September 2025** (announced 1 October 2025) |
| **Company** | An unnamed financial company (the DPA has not publicly disclosed the company's identity) |

### What Happened

The Hamburg DPA found that the financial company was using a fully automated decision-making system to process credit card applications — rejecting applicants **even when they had good credit ratings**, and doing so **without any human intervention** ("*ohne menschliches Eingreifen*"). When affected customers sought explanations, the company responded with **boilerplate, generic responses** rather than providing meaningful, intelligible information about the logic involved in the automated decision.

### GDPR Violations

The fine was grounded in violations of:

- **Article 22** (Automated individual decision-making, including profiling) — the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects, and the corresponding obligation to provide suitable safeguards including the right to human intervention, to express one's point of view, and to contest the decision.
- **Articles 13–15** (transparency / information obligations) — the controller failed to provide meaningful information about the existence of automated decision-making, the logic involved, and the significance and envisaged consequences.
- **Article 5(1)(a)** (lawfulness, fairness, and transparency principle).

### Significance

This is the most recent major GDPR enforcement action specifically targeting AI/automated decision-making. It also sits at the intersection of the GDPR and the **EU AI Act**, whose first provisions on prohibited AI practices and AI literacy took effect in February 2025, with further obligations coming into force on **2 August 2025**. The case signals that European DPAs are increasingly scrutinizing algorithmic opacity in consumer-facing decisions.

Based on my research, here is a comprehensive summary of what the European Commission and the AI Office have published in the past 12 months regarding the EU AI Act's general-purpose AI (GPAI) obligations:

---

## Yes — Three Major Instruments Published (July 2025)

The European Commission and the AI Office published three significant instruments in July 2025, all within the past 12 months:

---

### 1. GPAI Code of Practice — Published 10 July 2025

The **final version of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** was published by the AI Office on **10 July 2025**. This is the most significant instrument. Key details:

- **Legal basis**: Article 56 of the EU AI Act, which tasks the AI Office with encouraging and facilitating codes of practice at Union level.
- **Scope**: It covers the obligations in **Article 53** (transparency, copyright, training data summaries) and **Article 55** (systemic risk obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk).
- **Nature**: Voluntary — providers may rely on it to demonstrate compliance until harmonised standards are published (per Articles 53(4) and 55(2)).
- **Status**: The Commission and the AI Board have assessed the Code as **adequate**. It was developed with a wide range of stakeholders.
- **Enforcement**: The GPAI obligations became applicable on **2 August 2025**, with enforcement by the AI Office.

> Source: [Jones Day](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2025/08/eu-ai-act-european-commission-publishes-generalpurpose-ai-code-of-practice); [SCL](https://www.scl.org/eu-general-purpose-ai-code-of-practice-now-available); [Covington / Global Policy Watch](https://www.globalpolicywatch.com/2025/07/ai-office-publishes-final-version-of-the-code-of-practice-for-general-purpose-ai-models)

---

### 2. Guidelines on the Scope of GPAI Obligations — Published 18 July 2025

The European Commission published **non-binding Guidelines** clarifying key provisions of the AI Act applicable to GPAI models on **18 July 2025** (approved by the Commission on 19 July 2025). These Guidelines address:

- The **definition and scope** of what constitutes a GPAI model under Article 3(63).
- **Lifecycle obligations** for providers.
- **Systemic risk criteria** and classification thresholds.
- **Notification duties** for providers.
- Practical implementation guidance under Article 96(1) of the AI Act.

The Guidelines were published as a draft and will be formally adopted once translated into all EU languages.

> Source: [WilmerHale](https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/blogs/wilmerhale-privacy-and-cybersecurity-law/20250724-european-commission-issues-guidelines-for-providers-of-general-purpose-ai-models); [Paul Weiss](https://www.paulweiss.com/insights/client-memos/eu-commission-publishes-guidelines-on-general-purpose-ai-obligations-as-well-as-training-data-disclosure-template-further-clarity-as-the-countdown-to-enforcement-begins); [EU AI Act Portal](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/gpai-guidelines-overview)

---

### 3. Template for Public Summary of Training Content — Published 24 July 2025

The AI Office published the **mandatory template** (with an accompanying Explanatory Notice) for the public summary of training content required under **Article 53(1)(d)**. Key details:

- Providers must use this template to disclose a "sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training of the general-purpose AI model."
- It provides a **common minimal baseline** for information to be made publicly available.
- It assists copyright holders and other parties with legitimate interests in exercising their rights under Union law (linked to Article 53(1)(c) on copyright compliance).
- **Deadline**: Providers have until **2 August 2027** to publish summaries for models placed on the market before 2 August 2025.

> Source: [European Commission Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/explanatory-notice-and-template-public-summary-training-content-general-purpose-ai-models); [WilmerHale](https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/blogs/wilmerhale-privacy-and-cybersecurity-law/european-commission-releases-mandatory-template-for-public-disclosure-of-ai-training-data)

---

### What Has *Not* Yet Been Published

- **No formal implementing acts** specific to GPAI obligations have been adopted. The instruments above are guidelines, a voluntary code, and a template — not implementing acts under Article 291 TFEU.
- **No delegated acts** under Article 53(5) or 53(6) (on measurement/calculation methodologies or amendments to Annexes XI and XII) have been published yet.
- **No harmonised standards** have been published for GPAI obligations — the Code of Practice serves as an interim mechanism until those standards exist.

---

### Summary Table

| Instrument | Date | Legal Basis | Binding? |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPAI Code of Practice (final) | 10 July 2025 | Art. 56 AI Act | Voluntary (but Commission-assessed) |
| Guidelines on GPAI Obligations | 18 July 2025 | Art. 96(1) AI Act | Non-binding |
| Training Data Summary Template | 24 July 2025 | Art. 53(1)(d) AI Act | Mandatory (form of disclosure) |

---

## Supervisory Guidance, Speeches, and Enforcement Actions Interpreting SR 11-7 for AI/ML Model Risk Management (Past 12 Months)

### 1. KEY SPEECHES BY FEDERAL RESERVE GOVERNORS

#### Governor Michelle W. Bowman — November 22, 2024
**"Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System"** — 27th Annual Symposium on Building the Financial System of the 21st Century, Washington, D.C.

Bowman made the most directly relevant remarks on SR 11-7 and AI. She stated that **"while AI may be on the frontier of technology, it does not operate outside the existing legal framework,"** and that banks are relying on existing risk-management frameworks — including SR 11-7 — to guide their use of AI. She emphasized that regulators must assess **"whether our supervisory guidance is fit for the future"** and called for a **dynamic supervisory approach** to address AI's rapid evolution. She also highlighted cybersecurity risks amplified by AI and the need for international regulatory coordination.

- Source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/bowman20241122a.htm

#### Vice Chair for Supervision Michael S. Barr — February 18, 2025
**"Artificial Intelligence: Hypothetical Scenarios for the Future"** — Council on Foreign Relations, New York

Barr discussed AI's implications for financial stability and model risk. He emphasized that banks must **"think through AI liability questions"** and that existing model risk management guidance (SR 11-7) provides the foundational framework. He stressed that banks need clear agreements with fintech partners on data ownership, model transparency, and liability — a direct extension of SR 11-7's vendor/third-party model principles.

- Source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/barr20250218a.htm

#### Governor Lisa D. Cook — July 17, 2025
**"AI: A Fed Policymaker's View"** — NBER Summer Institute 2025

Cook focused primarily on AI's macroeconomic impact and the Fed's own use of AI for research and operations. While less directly tied to SR 11-7, her speech signaled the Fed's internal embrace of AI tools, which implicitly reinforces the relevance of model risk management principles to AI systems.

- Source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/cook20250717a.htm

---

### 2. REGULATORY GUIDANCE & BULLETINS

#### OCC Bulletin 2025-26 — September 2025
**"Model Risk Management: Clarification for Community Banks"**

This bulletin directly interprets SR 11-7 for community banks. Key clarifications:
- **Annual model validation is not required** — frequency and scope should be risk-based.
- Examiners **will not criticize a bank solely** for choosing less frequent or less extensive validation where reasonable.
- Community banks have **flexibility to tailor MRM practices** to their specific risk exposures, business activities, and model complexity.

While the bulletin does not use the terms "AI" or "machine learning," it is understood that AI/ML applications fall under the MRM framework, and this clarification signals OCC's effort to reduce barriers to AI adoption for smaller institutions.

- Source: https://www.occ.gov (OCC Bulletin 2025-26)

#### OCC Fall 2025 Semiannual Risk Perspective (SARP)
The Fall 2025 SARP explicitly addresses AI:
- Notes banks are **deploying sophisticated models for credit underwriting, fraud detection, and customer personalization**.
- Generative AI use cases are **largely internal-facing** (coding, call center assistance, document summarization).
- States: **"While the opportunities of AI are broad, appropriate governance and risk management should be in place commensurate with the risk."**
- Reflects a **clear shift in OCC posture** — innovation is now a **"promoted imperative"** rather than something banks pursue with caution.

- Source: https://www.occ.gov/publications-and-resources/publications/semiannual-risk-perspective/files/pub-semiannual-risk-perspective-fall-2025.pdf

#### OCC Spring 2026 Semiannual Risk Perspective
- Confirms that **GenAI and agentic AI models are not within the scope of the revised MRM guidance** (SR 26-02).
- The agencies **plan to issue a request for information (RFI)** addressing model risk management for banks' use of AI, including GenAI, agentic AI, and AI-based models.
- The OCC is **"actively reviewing supervisory expectations"** for AI.

- Source: https://www.occ.gov/publications-and-resources/publications/semiannual-risk-perspective/files/pub-semiannual-risk-perspective-spring-2026.pdf

#### FDIC — May 15, 2025 Meeting on Artificial Intelligence
The FDIC communicated to banks that they need an AI policy covering:
- Legal compliance, risk tolerance, assumptions and parameters
- Third-party risk management, data governance, and trustworthiness
- Fair lending testing
- The FDIC stated it **"does not expect to see [new] guidance around artificial intelligence"** in the immediate term, implying SR 11-7 remains the operative framework.

- Source: https://www.lba.org/common/Uploaded%20files/Peer-group-documents/FDIC%20Notes%20May%202025.pdf

---

### 3. THE SR 11-7 REPLACEMENT: SR 26-02 (April 17, 2026)

Although slightly beyond a strict 12-month window, the most significant development is the **April 17, 2026 joint issuance of SR 26-02** (Federal Reserve SR 26-02, OCC Bulletin 2026-13, FDIC adoption), which **supersedes SR 11-7 entirely**. Key AI/ML-relevant provisions:

- **GenAI and agentic AI are explicitly excluded** from the scope of the revised guidance: *"Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this guidance."*
- Traditional statistical/quantitative models and **non-generative, non-agentic AI models remain in scope**.
- The guidance is explicitly **non-enforceable** — it "does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements."
- Emphasizes a **risk-based, principles-based approach** rather than prescriptive checklists.
- The agencies plan to issue a forthcoming **RFI on AI-specific model risk management**.

- Source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.pdf

---

### 4. ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS

**No public enforcement actions in the past 12 months were identified that specifically cite AI/ML model risk deficiencies under SR 11-7.** 

The OCC's enforcement actions during this period focused on:
- Concentration risk management (commercial real estate) — May 2025
- Strategic plan, board/management oversight, liquidity, interest rate risk, credit risk, audit, and IT deficiencies — various 2024-2025 formal agreements

While model risk management deficiencies are commonly cited in enforcement actions, none of the publicly available orders in the past 12 months specifically interpret or apply SR 11-7 in the context of AI/ML models. This is consistent with the fact that the agencies are still developing their AI-specific supervisory approach, as evidenced by the planned RFI.

---

### 5. SUMMARY TABLE

| Date | Agency/Official | Type | Key AI/ML SR 11-7 Signal |
|------|----------------|------|--------------------------|
| Nov 22, 2024 | Gov. Bowman (FRB) | Speech | SR 11-7 applies to AI; assess if "fit for future" |
| Feb 18, 2025 | VC Barr (FRB) | Speech | SR 11-7 framework applies; focus on third-party AI |
| May 15, 2025 | FDIC | Meeting | No new AI guidance expected; SR 11-7 governs |
| Jul 17, 2025 | Gov. Cook (FRB) | Speech | Fed internally embracing AI tools |
| Sep 2025 | OCC | Bulletin 2025-26 | Community bank MRM flexibility (enables AI adoption) |
| Fall 2025 | OCC | SARP | AI governance must be "commensurate with risk" |
| Apr 17, 2026 | FRB/OCC/FDIC | SR 26-02 | **Replaces SR 11-7**; GenAI/agentic AI excluded; RFI forthcoming |
| Spring 2026 | OCC | SARP | GenAI/agentic AI out of scope; RFI planned |

### Bottom Line

The agencies have been actively interpreting SR 11-7 for AI/ML through speeches and bulletins rather than enforcement. The consistent message is that **SR 11-7's principles-based framework applies to AI/ML models** (except GenAI/agentic AI, which are explicitly carved out of SR 26-02), but the agencies acknowledge the framework needs updating. The planned RFI will be the next major milestone. No AI-specific enforcement actions have been made public.

Use of models within the banking and financial services industries continues to grow in

reporting, and flawed financial and risk management decisions, among other types of risk events. 
Model risk can be mitigated through active and appropriate risk management, recognizing that 
the relevance of model risk depends on the nature, scale, and use of the models in relation to the 
associated business risks.  
This guidance highlights sound principles for effective model risk management. As 
reflected in this guidance, model risk management practices vary from banking organization to 
banking organization. Each banking organization ultimately is responsible for adopting model 
risk management practices that are appropriate and effective for managing the specific risks the 
banking organization faces or is likely to face.

There are a variety of ways for a banking organization to structure model risk 
management practices. Not all models present the same level of risk, and a similar model at two

appropriate and effective for one banking organization may be inappropriate and ineffective for a 
banking organization with a different risk profile or that uses a model for a different purpose.

that it will be most useful for models supporting a banking organization’s significant business

complex operations. Furthermore, a banking organization may tailor portions of its model risk 
management practices that are relevant to the risks posed by a particular model and with a level 
of rigor commensurate with that risk. Effective model risk management therefore warrants 
consideration of model risk in the context of the broader business risks that models support or 
influence. 
IV. MODEL DEVELOPMENT AND MODEL USE 
Model Development 
Sound model development activities are aligned with model purpose, business use, and 
banking organization policy. Model development is not purely a technical exercise. The 
developer’s judgment influences the model’s conceptual design and soundness, inputs,

11  
broader model risk management activities. Organizations benefit from clearly defining roles and 
responsibilities when delegating these activities.  
Model Inventory 
It is common industry practice for banking organizations to maintain a comprehensive set 
of information for models under development or in use to support effective model risk 
management. While the inventory may contain varying levels of information to reflect different 
levels of model complexity and a banking organization’s overall level of model usage, an 
effective model inventory includes sufficient information to understand model risks, so as to 
support effective model risk management at the individual and aggregate levels.  
Documentation 
Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management. For 
example, documentation can help maximize the likelihood of continuity of operations, including 
supporting the tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions; it can also be used to 
more effectively help manage any model remediation efforts.   
VII. VENDOR AND OTHER THIRD-PARTY PRODUCTS 
The widespread use of customized vendor and other third-party products—including 
data, parameter values, or complete models—can present unique challenges for validation and 
other model risk management activities. Additionally, because certain components may be 
proprietary, banking organizations may not receive from the vendor the underlying code, data, or 
methodology that they would have if a model were developed internally. Nevertheless, the 
principles of model risk management remain applicable. 
An important element of model risk management is the validation of vendor products, 
either by internal or outside parties. Sound practice includes developing an understanding of the

12  
vendor model, including its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance. 
Similarly, sound practice involves conducting ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to 
assess whether vendor models are accurate, remain fit for purpose, and continue to be reliable. 
Such analysis can also be used to support any overlay or adjustment to model output. In cases 
where vendor models are customized to fit a banking organization’s specific business needs, 
sound practice also involves appropriately documenting, justifying, and evaluating adjustments 
made to customize the model as part of model validation.

## Gap Analysis: SOP-AIML-009 vs. EU AI Act Articles 9, 27, and 49

Based on a thorough review of SOP-AIML-009 (Algorithmic Bias Detection and Mitigation) against the EU AI Act's requirements for high-risk AI systems, here are the **specific missing procedures and artefacts**, organized by Article:

---

### ARTICLE 9 — Risk Management System

**What Article 9 requires (paras. 1–9):** A documented, continuous, iterative risk management system spanning the *entire lifecycle* of the high-risk AI system, comprising: (a) identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights; (b) estimation and evaluation of risks from intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; (c) evaluation of risks arising from post-market monitoring data; (d) adoption of suitable risk management measures; and (e) ensuring residual risks are acceptable and communicated to the deployer.

**What SOP-AIML-009 covers:** The SOP is focused narrowly on *algorithmic bias* — a subset of fairness risk. It does not constitute a comprehensive risk management system as required by Article 9.

**MISSING procedures and artefacts:**

| # | Missing Item | Article 9 Reference | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Comprehensive Risk Identification & Analysis Procedure** | Art. 9(2)(a) | The SOP only identifies bias-related risks. There is no procedure for identifying and analyzing *all* known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights (e.g., accuracy failures, robustness issues, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, feedback loops, automation bias). |
| 2 | **Reasonably Foreseeable Misuse Risk Assessment** | Art. 9(2)(b) | No procedure exists to estimate and evaluate risks arising from *reasonably foreseeable misuse* of the AI system. The SOP only addresses intended-use bias. |
| 3 | **Post-Market Data Integration into Risk Evaluation** | Art. 9(2)(c) | While Section 5.6 covers bias drift monitoring, there is no procedure for feeding post-market monitoring data back into the *overall risk evaluation* cycle (beyond bias metrics). Article 9 requires evaluation of "other risks possibly arising" from post-market data. |
| 4 | **Residual Risk Acceptability Determination** | Art. 9(5) | No procedure exists for determining whether the *overall residual risk* (including non-bias risks) is "judged to be acceptable" for the intended purpose. The SOP only checks fairness thresholds. |
| 5 | **Residual Risk Communication to Deployer** | Art. 9(5) | No procedure requires communicating residual risks to the deployer/user. The Model Card (Section 5.4) mentions "known limitations" but does not mandate residual risk communication per Article 9(5). |
| 6 | **Vulnerable Group Impact Assessment (Minors)** | Art. 9(9) | Article 9(9) requires specific consideration of adverse impact on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups. The SOP mentions protected attributes but has no dedicated procedure for assessing impact on minors or vulnerability-specific risk analysis. |
| 7 | **Risk Management System Documentation (Standalone)** | Art. 9(1) | The SOP itself is a bias detection SOP, not a documented risk management *system*. Article 9 requires the system to be "established, implemented, documented and maintained" as a distinct artefact. SOP-AIML-001 (Model Risk Management) is referenced but not integrated here. |
| 8 | **Systematic Review & Update Cycle for Risk Management** | Art. 9(2) | Article 9 requires "regular systematic review and updating" of the entire risk management system. The SOP has an annual policy review (Section 7.2) but no procedure for systematic review of the risk management system itself triggered by new evidence, incidents, or post-market data. |

---

### ARTICLE 27 — Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)

**What Article 27 requires:** Before deploying a high-risk AI system (Annex III, except point 2), deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, or deployers of systems under Annex III points 5(b) and (c) must perform a FRIA covering: (a) description of deployer's processes; (b) period and frequency of use; (c) categories of affected persons; (d) specific risks of harm; (e) human oversight measures; (f) measures in case risks materialize, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms. The deployer must notify the market surveillance authority using the Article 27(5) template.

**What SOP-AIML-009 covers:** The SOP does not mention, reference, or operationalize a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment at all.

**MISSING procedures and artefacts:**

| # | Missing Item | Article 27 Reference | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | **FRIA Procedure / Trigger** | Art. 27(1) | No procedure exists requiring or guiding the performance of a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment prior to deploying a high-risk AI system. This is a standalone obligation. |
| 10 | **Affected Persons Categorization** | Art. 27(1)(c) | No procedure requires identifying and documenting "categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected" by the AI system in its specific deployment context. |
| 11 | **Specific Risks of Harm Documentation** | Art. 27(1)(d) | No procedure requires documenting "specific risks of harm likely to have an impact" on identified categories of persons, taking into account the provider's Article 13 information. |
| 12 | **Human Oversight Measures Description** | Art. 27(1)(e) | While SOP Section 4.3 mentions human-in-the-loop for Critical/High-risk models, there is no procedure requiring a *description of the implementation of human oversight measures according to the instructions for use* as part of a FRIA. |
| 13 | **Risk Materialization Measures & Complaint Mechanism** | Art. 27(1)(f) | No procedure requires documenting "measures to be taken in the case of the materialisation of those risks, including the arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms." |
| 14 | **FRIA Notification to Market Surveillance Authority** | Art. 27(3) | No procedure exists for notifying the market surveillance authority of FRIA results. |
| 15 | **FRIA Update Trigger** | Art. 27(2) | No procedure requires updating the FRIA when any element changes or is no longer up to date. |
| 16 | **FRIA-DPIA Complementarity** | Art. 27(4) | The SOP references DPIAs (SOP-PRI-008) but does not establish how the FRIA complements the DPIA where obligations overlap. |
| 17 | **FRIA Template / Artefact** | Art. 27(5) | No FRIA template or structured output document is defined. The AI Office template (expected by 2026) is not anticipated or referenced. |

---

### ARTICLE 49 — Registration

**What Article 49 requires:** Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market or putting it into service, providers (and their authorized representatives) must register themselves and the system in the EU database (Article 71). Deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, or persons acting on their behalf must also register their use (Art. 49(3)). The information required is specified in Annex VIII, Sections A, B, and C.

**What SOP-AIML-009 covers:** The SOP makes no reference to EU database registration obligations whatsoever.

**MISSING procedures and artefacts:**

| # | Missing Item | Article 49 / Annex VIII Reference | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | **EU Database Registration Procedure (Provider)** | Art. 49(1), Annex VIII §§A–B | No procedure requires the provider to register the high-risk AI system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service. Required information includes: provider name/address/contact, trade name, system intended purpose, system status, Member States of availability, description of data used, etc. |
| 19 | **EU Database Registration Procedure (Deployer)** | Art. 49(3), Annex VIII §C | For Meridian as a deployer (if acting as a public authority or on behalf of one, e.g., in clinical settings), no procedure exists to register use in the EU database. Required: deployer name/address/contact, URL of provider's EU database entry, FRIA summary, DPIA summary. |
| 20 | **Registration as a Pre-Deployment Gate** | Art. 49(1), 49(3) | The SOP's pre-deployment approval (Section 5.4) does not include EU database registration as a gating condition. The `BiasComplianceCheck` script checks for Bias Testing Plan, FairnessAssessment, data lineage, Model Card, and Privacy Ticket — but not EU database registration. |
| 21 | **Non-High-Risk Determination Registration** | Art. 49(2) | If Meridian concludes a system is *not* high-risk under Article 6(3), Article 49(2) still requires registration of that determination. No procedure addresses this. |
| 22 | **Registration Information Maintenance** | Art. 49, Annex VIII | No procedure requires keeping registration information up to date in the EU database. |

---

### CROSS-CUTTING GAPS

| # | Missing Item | Reference | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23 | **Conformity Assessment Integration** | Art. 16(f), Art. 43 | The SOP does not integrate with or reference the conformity assessment procedure required before placing a high-risk AI system on the market. |
| 24 | **EU Declaration of Conformity** | Art. 16(g), Art. 47 | No procedure requires drawing up an EU declaration of conformity. |
| 25 | **CE Marking** | Art. 16(h), Art. 48 | No procedure addresses CE marking requirements. |
| 26 | **Quality Management System Integration** | Art. 17 | While SOP-AIML-001 is referenced, the SOP does not demonstrate how bias procedures integrate into the broader QMS required by Article 17 (covering design control, quality assurance, data management systems, accountability framework, etc.). |
| 27 | **Serious Incident Reporting** | Art. 73 | Section 5.6 covers P0 bias drift incidents but does not address the Article 73 obligation to report "serious incidents" (death, serious harm to health, critical infrastructure disruption, fundamental rights infringement) to market surveillance authorities. |
| 28 | **Instructions for Use** | Art. 13 | The SOP does not require producing "instructions for use" as specified in Article 13, which must include accuracy levels, known limitations, and human oversight measures. |

---

### SUMMARY

SOP-AIML-009 is a well-structured bias detection and mitigation procedure, but it addresses only a narrow slice of what the EU AI Act requires for high-risk AI system deployment. The most critical gaps are:

- **No comprehensive risk management system** (Article 9) — the SOP covers bias risk only, not the full spectrum of risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights.
- **No Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment procedure** (Article 27) — this is an entirely absent obligation.
- **No EU database registration procedure** (Article 49) — neither for providers nor deployers.
- **No integration with conformity assessment, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, or serious incident reporting** obligations.

**Compliance level: gap**

### Article 14: Human Oversight

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.

2. Human oversight shall aim to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular where such risks persist despite the application of other requirements set out in this Section.

3. The oversight measures shall be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use of the high-risk AI system, and shall be ensured through either one or both of the following types of measures:

(a) measures identified and built, when technically feasible, into the high-risk AI system by the provider before it is placed on the market or put into service;

(b) measures identified by the provider before placing the high-risk AI system on the market or putting it into service and that are appropriate to be implemented by the deployer.

4. For the purpose of implementing paragraphs 1, 2 and 3, the high-risk AI system shall be provided to the deployer in such a way that natural persons to whom human oversight is assigned are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate:

(a) to properly understand the relevant capacities and limitations of the high-risk AI system and be able to duly monitor its operation, including in view of detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance;

(b) to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias), in particular for high-risk AI systems used to provide information or recommendations for decisions to be taken by natural persons;

(c) to correctly interpret the high-risk AI system's output, taking into account, for example, the interpretation tools and methods available;

(d) to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system;

(e) to intervene in the operation of the high-risk AI system or interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state.

**Article 26: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 26: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems

1. Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the systems, pursuant to paragraphs 3 and 6.

2. Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.

3. The obligations set out in paragraphs 1 and 2, are without prejudice to other deployer obligations under Union or national law and to the deployer's freedom to organise its own resources and activities for the purpose of implementing the human oversight measures indicated by the provider.

4. Without prejudice to paragraphs 1 and 2, to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data, that deployer shall ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.

5. Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, inform providers in accordance with Article 72. Where deployers have reason to consider that the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions may result in that AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system. Where deployers have identified a serious incident, they shall also immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities of that incident. If the deployer is not able to reach the provider, Article 73 shall apply mutatis mutandis.

This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers of AI systems which are law enforcement authorities.

For deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation set out in the first subparagraph shall be deemed to be fulfilled by complying with the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial service law.

6. Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.

**Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity**
### Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.

2. To address the technical aspects of how to measure the appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness set out in paragraph 1 and any other relevant performance metrics, the Commission shall, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies.

3. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.

4. High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates, in particular due to their interaction with natural persons or other systems. Technical and organisational measures shall be taken in this regard.

The robustness of high-risk AI systems may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans.

High-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service shall be developed in such a way as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops), and as to ensure that any such feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures.

5. High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions aiming to ensure the cybersecurity of high-risk AI systems shall be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

The technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws.

## Gap Analysis: SOP-AIML-002 vs. GDPR Articles 6, 7, and Chapter V

### Overview

SOP-AIML-002 is a well-structured training data management SOP that addresses many operational and technical controls. However, when assessed against GDPR Articles 6 (Lawfulness of Processing), 7 (Conditions for Consent), and Chapter V (International Data Transfers), several **critical gaps** emerge. The SOP was clearly designed with HIPAA, SOC 2, and the EU AI Act in mind, but GDPR-specific privacy controls are largely absent or only superficially referenced.

---

### MISSING CONTROLS AND DOCUMENTS

---

#### GAP 1: No Lawful Basis Determination Process (Article 6)

**What Article 6 requires:** Every processing of personal data must be grounded in one of six lawful bases: consent (6(1)(a)), contract (6(1)(b)), legal obligation (6(1)(c)), vital interests (6(1)(d)), public task (6(1)(e)), or legitimate interests (6(1)(f)). The controller must determine and document the lawful basis *before* processing begins.

**What the SOP contains:** The SOP mentions "legal basis check" once in the Tier 3 access control table (Section 6.1.1) and references "verification that data use aligns with the original collection purpose and applicable notices" for internal data sources (Section 5.1.2). However, there is **no systematic lawful basis determination process** for training data. The Data Sourcing Request (Section 5.1.1) does not require identification or documentation of the GDPR lawful basis.

**Missing:**
- A **Lawful Basis Determination procedure** integrated into the sourcing workflow
- A requirement to document the specific Article 6(1) basis for each dataset containing personal data
- A **Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA)** template and process — particularly critical given EDPB Opinion 28/2024, which confirms legitimate interest *can* be a lawful basis for AI model training but requires a rigorous three-step assessment (identify interest, necessity test, balancing test)
- No mention of the EDPB's requirement that the LIA be documented and demonstrable per the accountability principle (Article 5(2))

---

#### GAP 2: No Consent Management Framework (Article 7)

**What Article 7 requires:** Where consent is the lawful basis, the controller must be able to *demonstrate* consent was given (7(1)). Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and distinguishable from other matters (7(2)). Data subjects must be able to withdraw consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw as to give (7(3)).

**What the SOP contains:** The word "consent" does not appear anywhere in the SOP. There is no consent collection, recording, or withdrawal mechanism described. The SOP references "applicable notices" (Section 5.1.2) but does not operationalize consent management for training data.

**Missing:**
- A **Consent Management Procedure** for training datasets where consent is the lawful basis
- A **Consent Record** system capable of demonstrating who consented, when, to what, and how (Article 7(1))
- A **Consent Withdrawal Mechanism** integrated into the data pipeline — if a data subject withdraws consent, how is their data removed from training datasets and, critically, from already-trained models?
- No mention of the requirement that consent requests be "clearly distinguishable" from other matters (Article 7(2))
- No assessment of whether consent is "freely given" in healthcare contexts where there may be power imbalances (Article 7(4))

---

#### GAP 3: No Data Subject Rights Procedure for Training Data (Articles 12–22, particularly Articles 16, 17, 21)

**What the GDPR requires:** Data subjects have rights to access (Art. 15), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), data portability (Art. 20), and objection (Art. 21). These rights extend to personal data used in training datasets.

**What the SOP contains:** SOP-PRIV-003 (Data Subject Access Request Handling) is listed as a related document (Section 10.1), but the SOP itself contains **no operational procedure** for handling data subject rights requests that involve training data. There is no mechanism to:
- Identify and extract a specific data subject's records from versioned training datasets
- Rectify inaccurate personal data in immutable versioned datasets (which creates a tension with the immutability principle in Section 4.5)
- Erase personal data from training datasets and retrain or adjust models accordingly
- Handle objections to processing under Article 21(1)

**Missing:**
- A **Data Subject Rights in Training Data Procedure** addressing the intersection of immutable versioned datasets and the rights to rectification (Art. 16) and erasure (Art. 17)
- A documented process for model retraining or adjustment when training data must be removed
- No mention of the notification obligation under Article 19 (informing recipients of rectification/erasure)

---

#### GAP 4: No Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) Requirement (Article 35)

**What Article 35 requires:** Where processing using new technologies is likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms of natural persons, a DPIA must be carried out *prior* to processing. Given that Meridian processes special category data (health data — Article 9) on a large scale for AI/ML training, a DPIA is **mandatory** under Article 35(3)(b).

**What the SOP contains:** The Data Card (Section 5.8) includes a Section 9 for "Legal and Compliance" that references "Privacy impact assessment reference (if conducted)." The word "if" is the problem — for high-risk AI systems processing health data, a DPIA is not optional. There is no requirement that a DPIA be completed before data sourcing approval.

**Missing:**
- A **mandatory DPIA gate** in the sourcing workflow (Section 5.1.1) for any dataset containing personal data, especially special category data
- Integration of DPIA findings into the Sourcing Approval Package
- A requirement for prior consultation with the supervisory authority (Article 36) when the DPIA indicates unmitigated high risk
- No mention of the DPIA content requirements from Article 35(7): systematic description, necessity/proportionality assessment, risk assessment, and mitigation measures

---

#### GAP 5: No Article 30 Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) for Training Data

**What Article 30 requires:** Controllers must maintain a record of processing activities including: controller/DPO contact details, purposes of processing, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients (including third countries), transfer safeguards, and retention periods.

**What the SOP contains:** The Data Card (Section 5.8) captures some overlapping information, but it is not structured as an Article 30 ROPA. There is no requirement to maintain a centralized ROPA that covers all training data processing activities. The SOP does not reference Article 30 at all.

**Missing:**
- A **Training Data ROPA** or integration of training data processing activities into Meridian's enterprise ROPA
- Documentation of categories of data subjects (not just data types)
- Envisaged time limits for erasure of different categories of data (Article 30(1)(f))
- The ROPA must be made available to supervisory authorities on request (Article 30(4))

---

#### GAP 6: No Transparency / Information Notice Framework (Articles 13 & 14)

**What Articles 13 & 14 require:** Data subjects must be provided with specific information about processing, including: controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, transfer intentions, retention periods, and their rights. Article 14 applies when data is not obtained directly from the data subject — which is the typical case for healthcare AI training data sourced from EHR systems.

**What the SOP contains:** Section 5.1.2 mentions "verification that data use aligns with the original collection purpose and applicable notices" for internal data sources, but there is no procedure for ensuring Article 14 information is provided to data subjects whose data is repurposed for AI/ML training. The SOP does not address the Article 14(3)(a) requirement to provide information within a reasonable period (max one month).

**Missing:**
- An **Article 14 Transparency Procedure** for notifying data subjects when their data is used for AI/ML training, including all required information elements
- Assessment of whether the "research exemption" under Article 14(5)(b) applies (disproportionate effort) and documentation of that assessment
- No mention of the Article 13/14 requirement to inform data subjects about automated decision-making (Article 22), which is directly relevant to Meridian's clinical AI and financial scoring models

---

#### GAP 7: No Transfer Mechanism Documentation (Chapter V — Articles 44–49)

**What Chapter V requires:** Any transfer of personal data to a third country requires either an adequacy decision (Art. 45), appropriate safeguards (Art. 46 — e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses, Binding Corporate Rules), or a derogation (Art. 49). Transfers must be documented, and the level of protection must not be undermined (Art. 44).

**What the SOP contains:** The SOP acknowledges international operations (Boston, London, Berlin, Singapore, Toronto — Section 1.2) and mentions "Cross-Border Transfer Review" in the RACI matrix (Section 3.1) with the CPO/DPO as Accountable. Section 6.1.1 includes "geo-fencing" and "geo-restricted" controls for Tier 3 data. However, there is **no substantive procedure** for international transfer compliance:

**Missing:**
- A **Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA)** requirement — mandatory since *Schrems II* for any transfer relying on Article 46 safeguards
- Identification of which specific transfer mechanisms are used (SCCs? BCRs? Adequacy decisions?) for each data flow — e.g., EU patient data in eu-west-1 accessed from Boston/Singapore/Toronto
- No documentation of whether the UK adequacy decision covers London operations post-Brexit
- No mention of the requirement to document transfers in the Article 30 ROPA (Article 30(1)(e))
- The "Cross-Border Transfer Review" in the RACI is listed but never operationalized in the detailed procedures (Section 5)
- No procedure for assessing whether onward transfers (e.g., from EU to US cloud infrastructure) comply with Chapter V
- No mention of the 2021 EU SCCs or the UK International Data Transfer Agreement
- No mention of Binding Corporate Rules (Article 47) as a potential mechanism for intra-group transfers across Meridian's global offices

---

#### GAP 8: No Special Category Data Safeguards (Article 9)

**What Article 9 requires:** Processing of health data, genetic data, and biometric data is prohibited unless a specific exception applies (explicit consent, substantial public interest, health/social care, research, etc.). Additional safeguards are required.

**What the SOP contains:** The SOP handles clinical data extensively but never references Article 9 or the requirement for an Article 9(2) exception. The Data Sourcing Request does not require identification of whether special category data is involved or which Article 9(2) exception applies.

**Missing:**
- An **Article 9 Exception Determination** integrated into the sourcing workflow
- Documentation of which Article 9(2) condition is relied upon for each dataset containing health data
- No mention of Member State law variations under Article 9(4) (e.g., German Federal Data Protection Act additional requirements for Berlin office)
- No reference to the requirement for "suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and interests of the data subject" under Article 9(2)(h)-(j)

---

#### GAP 9: No Data Protection by Design and by Default Integration (Article 25)

**What Article 25 requires:** Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to implement data protection principles (data minimization, purpose limitation, etc.) and ensure that, by default, only necessary personal data is processed.

**What the SOP contains:** Section 4.6 addresses "Data Minimization" as a policy statement, requiring justification for each data field. However, this is framed as a model fitness concern rather than a GDPR obligation. There is no reference to Article 25 or the concept of "data protection by design and by default."

**Missing:**
- Explicit integration of Article 25 principles into the preprocessing pipeline design
- A requirement that data protection by default be verified at each stage gate
- No mention of pseudonymization as a design measure (Article 25(1) explicitly references pseudonymization)

---

#### GAP 10: No Processor Due Diligence or Article 28 Contractual Requirements for Data Vendors

**What Article 28 requires:** When engaging a processor, the controller must use only processors providing sufficient guarantees and must have a contract containing specific mandatory terms (Article 28(3)).

**What the SOP contains:** Section 5.1.3 addresses third-party data sources with requirements for vendor security assessments, DUAs, and quality warranties. However, there is no distinction between third parties as *data sources* vs. third parties as *processors*. If a vendor processes personal data on Meridian's behalf (e.g., labeling vendors, annotation platforms), Article 28 processor contracts are required.

**Missing:**
- A **Processor vs. Controller determination** for each third-party relationship
- Article 28-compliant Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) for labeling vendors and annotation platforms
- No requirement that processors assist with data subject rights requests (Article 28(3)(e))
- No requirement that processors delete or return data at contract end (Article 28(3)(g))

---

### SUMMARY TABLE OF MISSING CONTROLS

| # | GDPR Article(s) | Missing Control / Document | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Art. 6 | Lawful Basis Determination Procedure + LIA template | **Critical** |
| 2 | Art. 7 | Consent Management Framework (collection, recording, withdrawal) | **Critical** |
| 3 | Arts. 16, 17, 19, 21 | Data Subject Rights Procedure for training data (rectification, erasure, objection in immutable datasets) | **Critical** |
| 4 | Art. 35 | Mandatory DPIA gate in sourcing workflow | **Critical** |
| 5 | Art. 30 | Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) for training data | **Critical** |
| 6 | Arts. 13, 14, 22 | Transparency/Information Notice Procedure for AI/ML training purposes | **High** |
| 7 | Arts. 44–49 (Chapter V) | Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA), documented transfer mechanisms (SCCs/BCRs), onward transfer controls | **Critical** |
| 8 | Art. 9 | Special Category Data exception determination + additional safeguards | **Critical** |
| 9 | Art. 25 | Data Protection by Design and by Default integration into pipeline design | **High** |
| 10 | Art. 28 | Processor DPA requirements for labeling vendors and annotation platforms | **High** |

---

**Compliance level: gap**

The SOP lacks ten material GDPR controls across Articles 6, 7, 9, 13–14, 16–17, 19, 21, 25, 28, 30, 35, and Chapter V (Articles 44–49). The most critical deficiencies are: (1) no lawful basis determination process for training data processing, (2) no consent management framework, (3) no operational procedure for handling data subject rights (erasure/rectification) in immutable versioned datasets, (4) no mandatory DPIA gate, (5) no Article 30 ROPA for training data activities, (6) no documented international transfer mechanisms (SCCs, BCRs, or TIAs) despite global operations spanning the EU, UK, US, Singapore, and Canada, and (7) no Article 9 special category data exception determination despite processing health data at scale. The SOP's strong operational controls for data quality, bias, and versioning are commendable but do not substitute for these GDPR-specific legal and procedural requirements.

## Gap Analysis: SOP-COPS-001 vs. SOC 2 CC7 (System Operations) and CC8 (Change Management)

Based on a detailed review of SOP-COPS-001 (v5.2, July 2025) against the full text of SOC 2 CC7.1–CC7.5 and CC8.1, I've identified the following **missing or insufficiently evidenced controls** that an auditor would flag.

---

### CC7.1 — Vulnerability Detection & Configuration Monitoring

**What the SOP covers:** Section 6.2 mentions AWS KMS key rotation, Netskope CASB, and Microsoft Purview DLP. Section 7.2 describes HIPAA log review (PHI read events, access elevation).

**MISSING CONTROLS:**

| # | Gap | SOC 2 Point of Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **No vulnerability scanning program is documented.** The SOP is silent on infrastructure/software vulnerability scans — frequency, tooling, remediation SLAs, or reporting. CC7.1 explicitly requires "conducts vulnerability scans… on a periodic basis and after significant changes." | *Conducts Vulnerability Scans* |
| 2 | **No file integrity monitoring (FIM) or change-detection mechanism.** There is no mention of tools (e.g., AWS Config, OSSEC, Tripwire) that alert on unauthorized modifications to critical system files, configuration files, or content files. | *Implements Change-Detection Mechanisms* |
| 3 | **No defined configuration hardening standards.** The SOP references a "Technical Security Baseline (TSB)" defined by the CISO but never specifies what it contains, how it's enforced, or how noncompliance is detected. | *Uses Defined Configuration Standards* |
| 4 | **No procedure to detect unknown/unauthorized components.** No mention of asset discovery, unauthorized software detection, or rogue device identification. | *Detects Unknown or Unauthorized Components* |

---

### CC7.2 — Anomaly Detection & Security Event Monitoring

**What the SOP covers:** Section 7.2 describes weekly HIPAA log reviews (Snowflake `QUERY_HISTORY`, Okta access elevation events). Splunk dashboard `HIPAA-Compliance-DB` exists. Netskope block events generate instant alerts to CISO.

**MISSING CONTROLS:**

| # | Gap | SOC 2 Point of Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | **No defined detection policies, procedures, and tools for the full spectrum of threats.** The SOP's monitoring is narrowly scoped to PHI read events and access elevation. There is no mention of: intrusion detection systems (IDS/IPS), network traffic anomaly detection, malware detection, or behavioral analytics. | *Implements Detection Policies, Procedures, and Tools* |
| 6 | **No use of threat intelligence sources.** The SOP does not reference any intelligence feeds (e.g., ISACs, CVE feeds, vendor bulletins) used to identify newly discovered threats. | *Implements Detection Policies, Procedures, and Tools* (sub-point 2) |
| 7 | **Detection measures are not designed across the full threat taxonomy.** CC7.2 requires detection measures for: (1) compromise of physical barriers, (2) unauthorized actions of authorized personnel, (3) compromised credentials, (4) external unauthorized access, (5) compromise of authorized external parties, and (6) unauthorized hardware/software. The SOP only addresses #2 (access elevation) and partially #4 (Netskope blocks). | *Designs Detection Measures* |
| 8 | **No documented procedure to filter, summarize, and analyze anomalies.** The SOP describes raw log review but no tiered analysis, correlation rules, or SIEM use-case documentation. | *Implements Filters to Analyze Anomalies* |
| 9 | **No process to monitor and maintain the effectiveness of detection tools.** No mention of tuning detection rules, testing detection coverage, or validating that monitoring tools are functioning. | *Monitors Detection Tools for Effective Operation* |

---

### CC7.3 — Security Incident Evaluation & Response

**What the SOP covers:** Section 8.2 describes breach escalation — contact `security-hotline@meridian.com`, CIRT activates SOP-IR-002. Section 7.2 references SOP-IR-004 for bulk data anomaly response.

**MISSING CONTROLS:**

| # | Gap | SOC 2 Point of Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | **No documented procedure for evaluating whether security events constitute incidents.** The SOP jumps directly from "suspect a breach" to "activate CIRT." There is no triage process, severity classification matrix, or impact assessment procedure for security events that may or may not be incidents. | *Develops and Implements Procedures to Analyze Security Incidents* |
| 11 | **No periodic evaluation of incident response procedures.** CC7.3 requires that procedures for responding to security incidents be evaluated for effectiveness on a periodic basis. The SOP mentions bi-annual tabletop exercises (Section 9) but does not describe a process for incorporating lessons learned into procedure updates. | *Responds to Security Incidents* (periodic evaluation) |
| 12 | **No documented process for communicating detected security events to security program management.** The SOP describes alerts to CISO for PHI transmission violations but lacks a general process for security event communication and review by responsible individuals. | *Communicates and Reviews Detected Security Events* |

---

### CC7.4 — Incident Response Mitigation & Post-Incident Analysis

**What the SOP covers:** Section 8.2 references SOP-IR-002 (HIPAA Breach Response) and mentions CIRT activation. Section 9 includes bi-annual tabletop exercises.

**MISSING CONTROLS:**

| # | Gap | SOC 2 Point of Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 13 | **No periodic evaluation of incidents to identify patterns and root causes.** CC7.4 requires management to periodically review incidents and identify the need for system changes based on incident patterns and root causes. The SOP has no mention of trend analysis, post-incident review meetings, or a lessons-learned repository. | *Periodically Evaluates Incidents* |
| 14 | **No documented process for implementing changes to prevent/detect recurrences.** While SOP-IR-002 may cover this, SOP-COPS-001 itself does not reference a feedback loop from incident findings into preventive control improvements. | *Implements Changes to Prevent and Detect Recurrences* |

---

### CC7.5 — Incident Recovery

**What the SOP covers:** The SOP does not address recovery activities at all. It references SOP-IR-002 for breach response but recovery is outside its scope.

**MISSING CONTROLS:**

| # | Gap | SOC 2 Point of Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 15 | **No documented recovery procedures.** No mention of restoring affected environments, rebuilding systems, patching, or modifying configurations post-incident. | *Restores the Affected Environment* |
| 16 | **No root cause determination process.** CC7.5 explicitly requires root cause determination for incidents. Not addressed. | *Determines Root Cause of the Incident* |
| 17 | **No incident-recovery plan testing.** CC7.5 requires periodic testing of incident-recovery plans including threat-based scenarios, consideration of key personnel unavailability, and revision of resilience posture based on test results. The SOP mentions tabletop exercises for "Incident Reporting Drill" but not recovery-specific testing. | *Implements Incident-Recovery Plan Testing* |
| 18 | **No communication procedure for incident recovery.** No process for communicating recovery actions taken and prevention activities to management and external parties. | *Communicates Information About the Incident* |

---

### CC8.1 — Change Management

**What the SOP covers:** The SOP is almost entirely silent on change management. Section 5.1 describes data access request provisioning (a narrow access-change workflow). Section 11 has a revision history for the SOP itself. Section 8.1 describes exception handling.

**MISSING CONTROLS — This is the most significant gap area:**

| # | Gap | SOC 2 Point of Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 19 | **No change management process for infrastructure, data, software, or procedures.** The SOP does not describe how changes to production systems, code, configurations, or data structures are authorized, developed, tested, approved, and deployed. This is a foundational CC8.1 requirement. | *Manages Changes Throughout the System Life Cycle* |
| 20 | **No change authorization process.** No mention of a Change Advisory Board (CAB), change request ticketing, or pre-authorization workflow before design/development begins. | *Authorizes Changes* |
| 21 | **No secure design/development process for changes.** No reference to secure SDLC, code review, or security impact analysis for changes. | *Designs and Develops Changes* |
| 22 | **No change documentation requirements.** No requirement to document what changed, why, and how — beyond the SOP's own revision history. | *Documents Changes* |
| 23 | **No change tracking mechanism.** No ticketing system or register for tracking changes prior to implementation. | *Tracks System Changes* |
| 24 | **No software configuration management.** No mention of configuration parameters, baseline configurations, or monitoring of configuration drift for developed/acquired software. | *Configures Software* |
| 25 | **No testing of system changes before production.** No requirement for unit, integration, regression, or security testing of changes prior to deployment. | *Tests System Changes* |
| 26 | **No approval process for system changes prior to implementation.** No second-party approval, peer review, or management sign-off gate. | *Approves System Changes* |
| 27 | **No segregation of duties for deployment.** No restriction preventing a single individual from both developing and deploying changes. This is one of the most commonly cited SOC 2 findings. | *Deploys System Changes* |
| 28 | **No baseline configuration of IT technology.** The TSB is referenced but never defined or operationalized in the SOP. No mention of creating or maintaining a baseline configuration. | *Creates Baseline Configuration of IT Technology* |
| 29 | **No emergency change process.** No defined procedure for urgent changes that bypass normal controls, including mandatory after-the-fact review. | *Provides for Changes Necessary in Emergency Situations* |
| 30 | **No process to identify changes needed to remediate incidents.** No linkage between incident findings and the change management process. | *Identifies Changes in Infrastructure, Data, Software, and Procedures Required to Remediate Incidents* |

---

### Summary of Findings

| Criterion | Gaps Identified | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **CC7.1** (Vulnerability Detection) | 4 gaps — no vuln scanning, no FIM, no config standards, no unknown component detection | **High** |
| **CC7.2** (Anomaly Detection) | 5 gaps — narrow detection scope, no threat intel, incomplete detection design, no filtering/analysis procedure, no tool effectiveness monitoring | **High** |
| **CC7.3** (Incident Evaluation) | 3 gaps — no triage/classification, no periodic procedure evaluation, no security event communication process | **Medium** |
| **CC7.4** (Incident Mitigation) | 2 gaps — no periodic incident review/trending, no preventive change feedback loop | **Medium** |
| **CC7.5** (Incident Recovery) | 4 gaps — no recovery procedures, no root cause process, no recovery plan testing, no recovery communication | **High** |
| **CC8.1** (Change Management) | 12 gaps — virtually the entire change management lifecycle is undocumented | **Critical** |

---

### What an Auditor Would Specifically Need to See

For a SOC 2 Type 2 examination, an auditor would require **operating evidence** — not just policy statements — for each point of focus. The most urgent missing evidence categories are:

1. **Change management tickets** showing authorization → testing → approval → deployment with segregation of duties (CC8.1)
2. **Vulnerability scan reports** with remediation tracking (CC7.1)
3. **SIEM correlation rules and detection use-case documentation** (CC7.2)
4. **Incident response test results and after-action reports** (CC7.3, CC7.5)
5. **Post-incident review meeting minutes** showing trend analysis and control improvements (CC7.4)
6. **Emergency change records** with retroactive review evidence (CC8.1)
7. **Configuration baseline documentation** and drift monitoring reports (CC8.1, CC7.1)

The SOP is strong on HIPAA-specific operational controls (access requests, PHI handling, encryption, disposal) but was clearly not designed with SOC 2 CC7/CC8 in mind. The change management and system operations domains are almost entirely dependent on external documents (SOP-IR-002, SOP-IR-004, the TSB) that are referenced but whose content is not incorporated or summarized.

---

**Compliance level: gap**

Trust Services Categories .12 The table in paragraph .29 presents the trust services criteria and the related points of focus. In that table, the trust services criteria are classified into the following categories: a. Security. Information and systems are protected against unauthorized access, unauthorized dis- closure of information, and damage to systems that could compromise the availability, integrity, confidentiality, and privacy of information or systems and affect the entity’s ability to achieve its objectives. Security refers to the protection of i. information during its collection or creation, use, processing, transmission, and storage and ii. systems that use electronic information to process, transmit or transfer, and store infor- mation to enable the entity to meet its objectives. Controls over security prevent or detect the breakdown and circumvention of segregation of duties, system failure, incorrect pro- cessing, theft or other unauthorized removal of information or system resources, misuse of software, and improper access to or use of, alteration, destruction, or disclosure of in- formation. b. Availability. Information and systems are available for operation and use to meet the entity’s ob- jectives. Availability refers to the accessibility of information used by the entity’s systems as well as the products or services provided to its customers. The availability objective does not, in itself, set a minimum acceptable performance level; it does not address system functionality (the specific functions a system performs) or usability (the ability of users to apply system functions to the performance of specific tasks or problems). However, it does address whether systems include controls to support accessibility for operation, monitoring, and maintenance. c. Processing integrity (over the provisioning of services or the production, manufacturing, or dis- tribution of goods). System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized to meet the entity’s objectives. Processing integrity refers to the completeness, validity, accuracy, timeliness, and authorization of system processing.
