Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me synthesize the analysis.

---

## Assessment: SOP-LEGC-001 vs. EU AI Act Regulatory Change Monitoring Expectations

### The EU AI Act's Relevant Obligations

The EU AI Act does not contain a single, standalone article that says "providers must track regulatory developments." Instead, the obligation to monitor and adapt to regulatory change is **embedded across multiple, interconnected provisions** that collectively create a duty of continuous regulatory vigilance:

**1. Article 17(1)(a) — Quality Management System: Regulatory Compliance Strategy**
This is the most direct hook. Article 17(1)(a) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to include in their QMS *"a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system."* A "strategy for regulatory compliance" inherently implies an ongoing capability to identify, assess, and respond to regulatory changes — not a one-time compliance snapshot.

**2. Article 9 — Risk Management System (Continuous Iterative Process)**
Article 9(2) mandates that the risk management system be *"a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating."* This lifecycle-wide obligation necessarily requires the provider to incorporate new regulatory risks as they emerge.

**3. Article 72 — Post-Market Monitoring**
Article 72(2) requires providers to *"actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data... to evaluate the continuous compliance of AI systems with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2."* Continuous compliance evaluation cannot be performed without awareness of how the regulatory baseline itself may have shifted.

**4. Article 16 — General Provider Obligations**
Article 16(a) and (j) require providers to ensure ongoing compliance and take corrective actions — duties that presuppose awareness of regulatory evolution.

**5. Recital-level and Guidance Expectations**
External guidance (e.g., from the Future of Privacy Forum, Nemko, and Hyperproof) consistently interprets these articles as imposing a duty on providers to monitor the regulatory landscape and adapt their compliance posture accordingly.

---

### SOP-LEGC-001: What It Gets Right

The SOP is, in many respects, **well-aligned** with the EU AI Act's expectations:

| EU AI Act Expectation | SOP-LEGC-001 Alignment |
|---|---|
| Regulatory compliance strategy (Art. 17(1)(a)) | §5.1 Horizon Scanning with daily/weekly monitoring of EU Official Journal, EC AI Office, EDPB |
| Continuous, iterative risk process (Art. 9(2)) | §5.2 Impact Assessment with structured gap analysis and materiality scoring |
| Post-market monitoring (Art. 72) | Referenced in §10.1 via SOP-LEGC-002 (EU AI Act Conformity Assessment and Post-Market Monitoring) |
| Traceability / audit trail (Art. 17(1)(k)) | POL-LEGC-001-C mandates full traceability from regulation → Impact Assessment → Jira → validated control |
| Documentation and record-keeping (Art. 17(1)(k)) | §5.4.2 requires a complete evidence package before RCI closure |
| Accountability framework (Art. 17(1)(m)) | §3 RACI matrix with named roles; §4 policy statements |
| Management of modifications (Art. 17(1)(a)) | §5.3 Implementation Planning with SLA-governed remediation |
| Communication with competent authorities (Art. 17(1)(j)) | §5.1.2 "Applicable & Urgent" path escalates to CCO/GC within 4 hours |

---

### Gaps and Partial Compliance Areas

Despite the SOP's strengths, several gaps exist when measured against the EU AI Act's full expectations:

**GAP 1: No Explicit "Regulatory Monitoring" as a QMS Element (Partial)**
Article 17(1)(a) requires a *"strategy for regulatory compliance."* While the SOP's Horizon Scanning (§5.1) is operationally robust, the SOP does not explicitly frame this as part of the **Quality Management System** required by Article 17. The QMS under Article 17 must be a single, coherent, documented system. SOP-LEGC-001 references SOP-LEGC-002 for conformity assessment and post-market monitoring, but the integration between the RCM process and the formal QMS documentation is not explicitly cross-referenced as an Article 17 QMS component. The SOP should explicitly state that the RCM program serves as the "regulatory compliance strategy" element of the Article 17 QMS.

**GAP 2: Horizon Scanning Sources — No Direct AI Office Monitoring (Partial)**
§5.1.1 lists "EC AI Office announcements" under EU Official Publications, but the monitoring method is described as "Automated RSS Feeds integrated into CUBE; manual review of CUBE-curated summaries." The EU AI Office is the primary governance and enforcement body under the AI Act (Article 3(47)), and its guidance, codes of practice, and implementing acts will be critical. The SOP should specify a **dedicated, direct monitoring line** for AI Office publications (e.g., the AI Office's dedicated webpage, codes of practice consultations, and delegated/implementing acts under Articles 51-56), rather than subsuming it under a general EUR-Lex feed.

**GAP 3: No Explicit Trigger for "Substantial Modification" Reassessment (Gap)**
Article 3(23) defines "substantial modification" and Article 17(1)(a) requires procedures for managing modifications. When a regulatory change requires a modification to a high-risk AI system, the provider must assess whether that change constitutes a "substantial modification" requiring a new conformity assessment under Article 43(4). The SOP's Impact Assessment (§5.2.2) includes an Operational Gap Analysis, but it does not explicitly include a step to determine whether the required remediation constitutes a "substantial modification" under Article 3(23) that would trigger re-assessment. This is a meaningful gap.

**GAP 4: Post-Market Monitoring Integration Is Only Referential (Partial)**
Article 72 post-market monitoring and the RCM process are interdependent: regulatory changes may reveal new monitoring obligations, and monitoring data may reveal regulatory non-compliance. The SOP references SOP-LEGC-002 (§10.1) but does not describe a **feedback loop** between post-market monitoring findings and the Horizon Scanning / Impact Assessment process. For example, if post-market monitoring reveals a systemic performance issue, that should feed back into the RCM process as a potential regulatory risk.

**GAP 5: No Explicit Procedure for Monitoring Implementing/Delegated Acts (Partial)**
The EU AI Act empowers the Commission to adopt numerous implementing and delegated acts (e.g., Article 72(3) post-market monitoring plan template by February 2026; Article 51 delegated acts on systemic risk criteria). The Horizon Scanning sources (§5.1.1) do not explicitly call out monitoring for these forthcoming Commission acts, which will be critical compliance documents.

---

### Conclusion

SOP-LEGC-001 is a **well-structured, operationally mature** regulatory change management framework that aligns substantially with the EU AI Act's expectation that providers track and adapt to regulatory developments. The four-phase lifecycle (Horizon Scanning → Impact Assessment → Implementation → Tracking & Closure) with SLA-governed timelines, named accountability, and full audit trail traceability directly satisfies the spirit of Articles 9, 16, 17, and 72.

However, the SOP falls short of full compliance in three specific areas: (1) it does not explicitly position itself as the "regulatory compliance strategy" element of the Article 17 QMS; (2) it lacks an explicit "substantial modification" determination step in the Impact Assessment procedure; and (3) it does not establish a formal feedback loop between post-market monitoring outputs and the RCM horizon scanning intake. These are remediable gaps rather than fundamental design flaws.

**Compliance level: partial**

# Chapter I: General Provisions (Articles 1-4)

## Article 1: Subject Matter

1. The purpose of this Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and supporting innovation.

2. This Regulation lays down:

(a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union;

(b) prohibitions of certain AI practices;

(c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems;

(d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems;

(e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models;

(f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement;

(g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including startups.

## Article 2: Scope

1. This Regulation applies to:

(a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country;

(b) deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union;

(c) providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union;

(d) importers and distributors of AI systems;

(e) product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark;

(f) authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union;

(g) affected persons that are located in the Union.

**Article 16: Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 16: Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems

Providers of high-risk AI systems shall:

(a) ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2;

(b) indicate on the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, as applicable, their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, the address at which they can be contacted;

(c) have a quality management system in place which complies with Article 17;

(d) keep the documentation referred to in Article 18;

(e) when under their control, keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as referred to in Article 19;

(f) ensure that the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure as referred to in Article 43, prior to its being placed on the market or put into service;

(g) draw up an EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47;

(h) affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, to indicate conformity with this Regulation, in accordance with Article 48;

(i) comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1);

(j) take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20;

(k) upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2;

(l) ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.

**Article 72: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 72: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems

1. Providers shall establish and document a post-market monitoring system in a manner that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system.

2. The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime, and which allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of AI systems with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. Where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law enforcement authorities.

3. The post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV. The Commission shall adopt an implementing act laying down detailed provisions establishing a template for the post-market monitoring plan and the list of elements to be included in the plan by 2 February 2026. That implementing act shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2).

4. For high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, where a post-market monitoring system and plan are already established under that legislation, in order to ensure consistency, avoid duplications and minimise additional burdens, providers shall have a choice of integrating, as appropriate, the necessary elements described in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 using the template referred in paragraph 3 into systems and plans already existing under that legislation, provided that it achieves an equivalent level of protection.

The first subparagraph of this paragraph shall also apply to high-risk AI systems referred to in point 5 of Annex III placed on the market or put into service by financial institutions that are subject to requirements under Union financial services law regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes.

## Analysis: SOP-AIML-014 vs. SR 11-7 Model Documentation Standards

### Preliminary Note: SR 11-7 Has Been Superseded

Before addressing the core question, it is critical to note that **SR 11-7 was superseded by SR 26-2 on April 17, 2026** (Federal Reserve SR 26-2 / OCC Bulletin 2026-13). The SOP (version 2.9, dated December 20, 2025) was drafted before this transition and references SR 11-7 throughout. SR 26-2 preserves the core intellectual architecture — conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis, ongoing monitoring, effective challenge, and documentation standards — but is more principles-based and streamlined. The SOP's SR 11-7 references are now technically outdated, though the substantive requirements largely carry forward. I will assess the SOP against SR 11-7 as asked, but flag the transition risk.

---

### 1. Documentation Sufficiency Standard

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** "Documentation of model development and validation should be sufficiently detailed so that parties unfamiliar with a model can understand how the model operates, its limitations, and its key assumptions." (SR 11-7, Section on Documentation; also carried forward in SR 26-2).

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:** Section 4.2 explicitly incorporates this exact standard: "documentation must be sufficiently detailed to allow parties unfamiliar with the model to understand the model's functioning, limitations, and key assumptions." The SOP's Model Card template (Section 4.3, detailed in Appendix A) requires 10 minimum content sections that collectively address this. **Compliant.**

---

### 2. Conceptual Soundness (SR 11-7 Section III.A / Model Development)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Documentation must include a comprehensive description of theory, logic, and assumptions; justification for methodology choice relative to alternatives; description of theoretical relationships between inputs and outputs; and documentation of expert judgment or qualitative adjustments.

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:**

| SR 11-7 Requirement | SOP Provision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Theory, logic, assumptions | Section 4.2(a): "detailed exposition of the mathematical and statistical methodology employed" | **Compliant** |
| Justification vs. alternatives | Section 5.1.2(3): "Algorithm Selection Rationale" requiring comparison of at least two candidate approaches | **Compliant** |
| Input-output relationships | Section 4.2(c): "description of the theoretical relationship between input variables and predicted outcomes" | **Compliant** |
| Expert judgment / qualitative adjustments | Section 4.2(d): "documentation of all expert judgment or qualitative adjustments applied" | **Compliant** |

Additionally, Section 5.1.2 requires a Development Log with EDA summary, feature engineering log, and hyperparameter tuning record — all supporting conceptual soundness documentation. **Compliant.**

---

### 3. Data Integrity Documentation (SR 11-7 Section III.B)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Documentation of data source, quality, and relevance; provenance of training/validation/test datasets; descriptive statistics; preprocessing steps; representativeness assessment; and proxy variable documentation.

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:**

| SR 11-7 Requirement | SOP Provision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Data provenance | Section 4.2(a): "provenance of all training, validation, and test datasets" | **Compliant** |
| Descriptive statistics | Section 4.2(b): "descriptive statistics for all input features, including counts of missing values and extreme observations" | **Compliant** |
| Preprocessing steps | Section 4.2(c): "data preprocessing and transformation steps applied" | **Compliant** |
| Representativeness | Section 4.2(d): "assessment of data representativeness relative to the target population" | **Compliant** |
| Proxy variables | Section 4.2(e): "documentation of any proxy variables used when ideal data was unavailable" | **Compliant** |

Section 5.1.1(3) also requires pre-development documentation of data sources in the Data Source Registry. Section 5.1.3(5) requires a Data Quality Certificate with >95% completeness for SR 11-7 models. **Compliant.**

---

### 4. Model Performance Testing (SR 11-7 Section III.C)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Sensitivity analysis, back-testing, benchmarking against alternatives, stability analysis, and stress testing.

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:**

| SR 11-7 Requirement | SOP Provision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Sensitivity analysis | Section 4.2(a): "sensitivity analysis demonstrating model behavior across a plausible range of input values" | **Compliant** |
| Back-testing | Section 4.2(b): "back-testing results where historical data is available" | **Compliant** |
| Benchmarking | Section 4.2(c): "benchmarking against alternative models or industry standards" | **Compliant** |
| Stability analysis | Section 4.2(d): "stability analysis assessing the sensitivity of model outputs to small perturbations in inputs" | **Compliant** |
| Stress testing | Section 4.2(e): "stress testing results under adverse scenarios defined in SOP-RISK-004" | **Compliant** |

Section 5.1.3 further operationalizes these with specific metrics: confusion matrix, ROC-AUC with 95% CI, calibration curve, stratified performance, KS statistic, and stability tests at 1%, 5%, and 10% perturbation levels. **Compliant.**

---

### 5. Outcomes Analysis (SR 11-7 Section IV)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Framework for ongoing outcomes analysis including key metrics, trigger thresholds, monitoring cadence, and responsible parties.

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:**

| SR 11-7 Requirement | SOP Provision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Key metrics to track | Section 4.2(a): "key metrics to be tracked on an ongoing basis" | **Compliant** |
| Trigger thresholds | Section 4.2(b): "thresholds that trigger investigation or remediation" | **Compliant** |
| Monitoring cadence | Section 4.2(c): "minimum monthly for Critical Models, quarterly for all other SR 11-7 Models" | **Compliant** |
| Responsible party | Section 4.2(d): "the responsible party for conducting and reviewing outcomes analysis" | **Compliant** |

Section 5.4 operationalizes this with specific drift thresholds (ROC-AUC degradation >5pp, F1 >7pp, KS <30% for credit models) and the annual recertification process. **Compliant.**

---

### 6. Model Inventory (SR 11-7 Governance Section)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** "It is common industry practice for banking organizations to maintain a comprehensive set of information for models under development or in use... an effective model inventory includes sufficient information to understand model risks."

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:** Section 5.2 establishes the Meridian Model Inventory System with unique Model IDs, version-controlled Model Cards, full audit trail, automated workflow routing, and searchable metadata. The system is required for all production models. **Compliant.**

---

### 7. Effective Challenge / Independent Validation (SR 11-7 Core Principle)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** "Effective challenge" requires critical analysis by objective experts with appropriate expertise, sufficient independence, and organizational standing to effect change.

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:**

- Section 6.2 enforces segregation of duties: no individual may serve as both Model Owner and Model Validator for the same model.
- For SR 11-7 Models, the validation function reports to the Chief Compliance Officer, not the AI/ML Engineering organization — ensuring organizational independence.
- Section 5.1.4 requires a dedicated SR 11-7 Compliance Review by a Senior Model Validator (7 business days).
- Approval requires signatures from both the Accountable Executive (business) and an independent validator.

**Compliant.**

---

### 8. Vendor / Third-Party Models (SR 11-7 Section VII)

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** "Sound practice includes developing an understanding of the vendor model, including its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance... conducting ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis."

**SOP-AIML-014 Alignment:** Section 5.5 requires: pre-procurement assessment, contractual documentation requirements, internal Model Card creation within 45 days, gap analysis, and risk acceptance memoranda for un-remediated gaps. Annual updated performance reports benchmarked against Meridian-specific data are contractually required for SR 11-7 vendor models. **Compliant.**

---

### 9. Identified Gaps and Concerns

Despite strong overall alignment, I identify the following issues:

#### Gap 1: SR 11-7 Is Superseded — SOP References Are Stale
The SOP (v2.9, December 2025) references SR 11-7 throughout. SR 11-7 was superseded by **SR 26-2 on April 17, 2026**. The SOP's Section 4.2 is titled "SR 11-7 Compliance" and all sub-references point to SR 11-7 sections (III.A, III.B, III.C, IV). While SR 26-2 preserves the core framework, the SOP has not been updated to reflect the new guidance. This is a **governance/documentation currency gap**. The SOP should be revised to reference SR 26-2 and confirm alignment with any new or modified expectations.

#### Gap 2: Appendix A Not Provided
Section 4.3 states that "Detailed specifications for each section are provided in Appendix A." The SOP text reviewed does not include Appendix A (the Model Card template). Without reviewing the actual template, I cannot confirm that each of the 10 minimum content sections is operationalized with sufficient granularity. This is a **procedural completeness risk** — the policy framework is strong, but the actual template must be reviewed to confirm full alignment.

#### Gap 3: No Explicit Reference to Aggregate Model Risk
SR 11-7 (and SR 26-2) emphasize that "Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate." The SOP focuses entirely on individual model documentation. While aggregate risk assessment may be covered in other SOPs (e.g., SOP-RISK-003), the Model Card itself does not appear to require documentation of model dependencies, interactions, or common assumptions shared across models. This is a **minor gap** in the documentation framework.

#### Gap 4: Internal Audit Role Not Explicitly Defined in Documentation Review
SR 11-7 contemplates internal audit's role in model risk management. The SOP's RACI matrix (Section 3) does not include Internal Audit as a stakeholder. While the Model Validation team performs independent review, internal audit's periodic assessment of the overall documentation framework is not addressed. Under SR 26-2, internal audit's involvement is framed conditionally, but the absence of any reference is notable.

---

### Summary Assessment

| SR 11-7 Domain | SOP-AIML-014 Status |
|---|---|
| Documentation sufficiency (unfamiliar-party standard) | **Compliant** |
| Conceptual soundness (III.A) | **Compliant** |
| Data integrity (III.B) | **Compliant** |
| Performance testing (III.C) | **Compliant** |
| Outcomes analysis (IV) | **Compliant** |
| Model inventory | **Compliant** |
| Effective challenge / independence | **Compliant** |
| Vendor / third-party models (VII) | **Compliant** |
| Governance, policies, controls | **Compliant** |
| SR 11-7 → SR 26-2 transition | **Gap — SOP not updated** |
| Appendix A (Model Card template) | **Unable to verify — not in record** |
| Aggregate model risk documentation | **Minor gap** |
| Internal audit role | **Minor gap** |

---

### Conclusion

**SOP-AIML-014 substantially satisfies SR 11-7's expectations for model documentation standards.** The SOP is comprehensive, well-structured, and directly maps its requirements to SR 11-7's core documentation domains (conceptual soundness, data integrity, performance testing, and outcomes analysis). It operationalizes these through detailed procedures, defined roles (RACI), segregation of duties, an auditable inventory system, and specific quantitative thresholds.

However, the SOP requires **updating to reference SR 26-2** (which superseded SR 11-7 on April 17, 2026), and the actual Model Card template (Appendix A) should be reviewed to confirm operational completeness. Two minor gaps — aggregate model risk documentation and internal audit's role — should be addressed in the next revision.

**Overall Rating: Compliant with minor findings.**

---

**Compliance level: Compliant**

---

## Compliance Assessment: SOP-FIN-010 vs. SR 11-7 Expectations for Regulatory Capital Models

### Overall Assessment

SOP-FIN-010 is a **comprehensive and well-structured** document that demonstrates substantial alignment with SR 11-7's core expectations. However, several gaps and areas of partial compliance exist. Below is a detailed analysis organized by SR 11-7's key domains.

---

### 1. Model Validation (SR 11-7 Section V — "Model Validation and Monitoring")

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Validation must evaluate whether models perform as expected, assess reliability and limitations, and occur prior to first use. Validation should include conceptual soundness assessment and outcomes analysis. The nature and rigor should align with model materiality.

| SR 11-7 Element | SOP-FIN-010 Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Independent validation** | Section 3.3 establishes structural independence: separate reporting lines (MRM → CRO, not model development), compensation independence, 36-month validation firewall, and external validation mandate (RC-P-002). | **Compliant** |
| **Annual validation** | RC-P-001 requires annual independent validation for all regulatory capital models, with reports to the Model Risk Committee within 45 days. Ctl-010 operationalizes this. | **Compliant** |
| **Biennial external validation** | RC-P-002 and Ctl-012 require biennial external validation of A-IRB models by KPMG LLP, with scope covering all model components, data inputs, and theoretical foundations. | **Compliant** |
| **Pre-use validation** | SR 11-7 states validation should occur prior to first use. The SOP does not explicitly address pre-use validation for new or materially changed models. Section 5.3 references model versions (e.g., v3.1, v2.8) but does not mandate MRM sign-off before a new version enters production. | **Gap** — The SOP lacks an explicit gate requiring MRM validation sign-off before a new model version is promoted to production. Ctl-022 requires peer review for code changes, and the MLflow registry requires MRM sign-off for staging-to-production promotion (Section 6.3), but this is framed as a system access control rather than a formal validation gate. |
| **Conceptual soundness** | RC-P-003 requires documentation of theoretical basis, mathematical specifications, data sources, development sample, estimation results, and limitations. Ctl-023 requires TRDs no older than 18 months. | **Compliant** |
| **Outcomes analysis** | RC-P-004 and Ctl-031 through Ctl-035 require back-testing (binomial test at 95% confidence), AUROC/AR, PSI, Hosmer-Lemeshow, and K-S statistics. | **Compliant** |

---

### 2. Ongoing Monitoring (SR 11-7 Section V — "Ongoing Monitoring")

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Ongoing monitoring should verify that models continue to perform as expected, using outcomes analysis and comparison to benchmarks. Monitoring reports should be commensurate with model materiality.

| SR 11-7 Element | SOP-FIN-010 Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Quarterly monitoring** | RC-P-004 and Section 5.10 require quarterly MPM reports within 20 business days of quarter-end. | **Compliant** |
| **Back-testing** | Ctl-031: binomial test at 95% confidence comparing realized defaults to PD estimates. | **Compliant** |
| **Benchmarking** | RC-P-004(b) explicitly requires "benchmarking against alternative models." However, the detailed procedures in Section 5.10 do not operationalize this — there is no specification of which alternative models, how benchmarking is performed, or what thresholds apply. | **Partial** — Benchmarking is stated as a policy requirement but lacks procedural detail. |
| **Stability assessment** | Ctl-033 (PSI) and Ctl-035 (K-S statistic) provide distributional stability monitoring. | **Compliant** |
| **Threshold-based escalation** | RC-P-005 and Section 6.4 define green/amber/red thresholds with mandatory 10-business-day response for red breaches. Ctl-038 operationalizes this. | **Compliant** |
| **Fit-for-purpose assessment** | RC-P-005 and Ctl-038 require assessment of whether the model remains fit for purpose upon red threshold breach. | **Compliant** |

---

### 3. Governance and Controls (SR 11-7 Section VI — "Governance and Controls")

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Clear roles, responsibilities, and accountability; effective policies; model inventory; and internal audit evaluation of the MRM framework.

| SR 11-7 Element | SOP-FIN-010 Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Clear roles and responsibilities** | Section 3 provides a detailed RACI matrix and role definitions. | **Compliant** |
| **Board and senior management oversight** | The Model Risk Committee (chaired by CRO) and Board Risk Committee are referenced throughout. However, the SOP does not explicitly describe the Board's role in approving the model risk management framework or receiving regular reporting on model risk, as SR 11-7 contemplates. | **Partial** — Board-level engagement is implied (escalation paths, quarterly reporting) but not explicitly defined as an affirmative governance responsibility. |
| **Model inventory** | Ctl-021 requires a Model Inventory Record (MIR) with model ID, name, version, owner, tier, development date, validation dates, and status. | **Compliant** |
| **Internal audit** | Section 7.4 requires annual independent review of the control environment by Internal Audit. SR 11-7 notes that internal audit should evaluate whether MRM practices are rigorous and effective — the SOP frames the audit as a control effectiveness review, which aligns. | **Compliant** |
| **Conflict of interest management** | Section 3.3 addresses structural independence, compensation independence, and the validation firewall. | **Compliant** |

---

### 4. Documentation (SR 11-7 Section VI — "Documentation")

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Adequate documentation supports continuity, tracks recommendations and exceptions, and aids remediation.

| SR 11-7 Element | SOP-FIN-010 Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Comprehensive model documentation** | RC-P-003 requires six specific documentation elements. Ctl-020 through Ctl-025 operationalize documentation requirements. | **Compliant** |
| **Data lineage** | Ctl-024 requires data lineage documentation in Collibra tracing each input variable to its Snowflake source. | **Compliant** |
| **Code repository** | Ctl-022 requires Git-based version control with peer review and branch protection. | **Compliant** |
| **Exception tracking** | Section 8.3 requires all exceptions documented on Form FIN-010-EXCEPTION and logged in Archer. | **Compliant** |

---

### 5. Model Overlays and Overrides (SR 11-7 Section VI — "Model Operating Controls")

**SR 11-7 Expectation:** Overlays and adjustments should be documented, justified, and subject to governance.

| SR 11-7 Element | SOP-FIN-010 Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Override documentation** | RC-P-007 and Ctl-050 require documentation with business rationale, capital impact quantification, and approval. | **Compliant** |
| **Override governance** | RC-P-007 requires approval by model owner, Head of MRM, and CRO; quarterly review by Model Risk Committee; and 12-month sunset provisions. | **Compliant** |
| **Override limits** | Ctl-052 caps cumulative override impact at 25 bps of CET1 ratio. | **Compliant** |

---

### 6. Identified Gaps and Concerns

#### Gap 1: Pre-Use Validation Gate (Moderate Severity)
SR 11-7 states: "Validation generally occurs prior to a model's first use." While the MLflow registry (Section 6.3) requires MRM sign-off for staging-to-production promotion, the SOP does not explicitly require a formal validation report sign-off before a new model version is used for regulatory capital calculations. The annual validation cycle (RC-P-001) could theoretically allow a model to operate for up to 12 months before its first independent validation if it were deployed mid-cycle. **Recommendation:** Add an explicit control requiring MRM validation sign-off before any new model version is promoted to production for regulatory capital use.

#### Gap 2: Benchmarking Operationalization (Low Severity)
RC-P-004(b) requires "benchmarking against alternative models," but Section 5.10's MPM procedures do not specify which alternative models, the benchmarking methodology, or acceptable deviation thresholds. SR 11-7's outcomes analysis discussion contemplates comparison to alternative models and benchmarks. **Recommendation:** Specify the alternative models/challenger models used for benchmarking and define thresholds for acceptable deviation.

#### Gap 3: Board-Level Governance Definition (Low Severity)
SR 11-7 contemplates that the board of directors (or board committee) should approve the model risk management framework and receive regular reporting. The SOP references the Board Risk Committee in escalation paths but does not explicitly define the Board's affirmative role in approving the MRM framework or receiving regular (non-escalation) model risk reporting. **Recommendation:** Add explicit language describing the Board Risk Committee's role in approving the model risk management framework and receiving quarterly model risk reports.

#### Gap 4: Contingency for Urgent Pre-Validation Use (Low Severity)
SR 11-7 acknowledges that "certain circumstances (e.g., an urgent business need) may necessitate using the model before validation is completed" and states that in such cases, "sound practice involves greater attention to the model's limitations... informing relevant stakeholders... and determining appropriate controls (e.g., placing limits on model use or more closely monitoring its performance)." The SOP does not address this contingency scenario. **Recommendation:** Add a procedure for conditional pre-validation use with enhanced controls.

#### Gap 5: Vendor Model Risk Management (Low Severity)
SR 11-7 Section VII addresses vendor and third-party products, noting that "the principles of model risk management remain applicable" and that sound practice includes "developing an understanding of the vendor model, including its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance." The SOP references SAS Institute Inc. as the platform provider and KPMG as the external validator, but does not explicitly address how SR 11-7's vendor model principles apply to the SAS Regulatory Capital Engine itself (which contains embedded quantitative methods). **Recommendation:** Clarify whether the SAS engine contains embedded models subject to SR 11-7 and, if so, how vendor model risk management principles are applied.

---

### Summary Table

| SR 11-7 Domain | Compliance Status |
|---|---|
| Model Validation — Independence | Compliant |
| Model Validation — Annual/Biennial Cycle | Compliant |
| Model Validation — Pre-Use Gate | **Gap** |
| Model Validation — Conceptual Soundness | Compliant |
| Model Validation — Outcomes Analysis | Compliant |
| Ongoing Monitoring — Frequency & Metrics | Compliant |
| Ongoing Monitoring — Benchmarking | **Partial** |
| Ongoing Monitoring — Thresholds & Escalation | Compliant |
| Governance — Roles & Responsibilities | Compliant |
| Governance — Board Oversight | **Partial** |
| Governance — Model Inventory | Compliant |
| Governance — Internal Audit | Compliant |
| Documentation | Compliant |
| Model Overlays & Overrides | Compliant |
| Vendor Model Risk Management | **Partial** |
| Contingency for Urgent Pre-Validation Use | **Gap** |

---

**Compliance level: partial**

The SOP is strong in its core architecture — independence, validation cycles, monitoring metrics, documentation, and override governance all align well with SR 11-7. However, the absence of an explicit pre-use validation gate, incomplete operationalization of benchmarking, and lack of explicit board-level governance definition and vendor model risk management provisions prevent a finding of full compliance. These gaps are moderate to low in severity and are remediable through targeted SOP amendments.

Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management. For 
example, documentation can help maximize the likelihood of continuity of operations, including

The widespread use of customized vendor and other third-party products—including 
data, parameter values, or complete models—can present unique challenges for validation and

proprietary, banking organizations may not receive from the vendor the underlying code, data, or

Models are simplified representations of real-world relationships among observed

question.question: Is SOP-CLIN-006 (Clinical AI Human Override Procedures) compliant with HIPAA's expectations for ePHI access control and audit when clinicians override AI outputs?
question.expected_answer: Compliant. The SOP implements role-based access control to ePHI (§164.312(a)) for the clinician override interface, automatic audit logging of every override event including user, timestamp, reason code, and PHI accessed (§164.312(b) audit controls), and integrity controls (§164.312(c)) so that override actions cannot alter the underlying ePHI record. The override procedure preserves the minimum-necessary standard (§164.502(b)) and ties into the workforce-training programme (§164.308(a)(5)). PHI accessed via override pathways is included in accounting-of-disclosures procedures where required.

## Compliance Analysis: SOP-CLIN-006 vs. HIPAA ePHI Access Control & Audit Requirements

### Overview

SOP-CLIN-006 (v5.3, effective 2025-08-15) establishes Meridian's framework for human override of AI-generated clinical recommendations. The analysis below evaluates the SOP against HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164, Subpart C) and Privacy Rule (45 CFR Part 164, Subpart E) requirements for ePHI access control and audit controls when clinicians override AI outputs.

---

### 1. Access Control — 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(1)

**What HIPAA requires:** Covered entities and business associates must "implement technical policies and procedures for electronic information systems that maintain electronic protected health information to allow access only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights as specified in § 164.308(a)(4)."

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**

| HIPAA Implementation Specification | SOP-CLIN-006 Control | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Unique User Identification (Required)** — § 164.312(a)(2)(i) | Section 6.1: RBAC via `ClarityClinicalUser` role; IAM integrated with customer AD/LDAP via SAML 2.0. Unique user IDs enforced. | **Compliant.** The SOP explicitly ties override actions to unique, authenticated user identities. |
| **Emergency Access Procedure (Required)** — § 164.312(a)(2)(ii) | Section 8.2: Emergency Model Disablement pathway; Clinical Safety Hotline 24/7/365. However, the SOP does not address *emergency access to ePHI* when normal access controls are unavailable (e.g., system outage preventing override). | **Partial gap.** Section 8.1 addresses technical exceptions (local browser storage, manual EHR documentation), but does not explicitly establish an emergency access procedure for obtaining necessary ePHI when the Clarity platform is unavailable. The SOP assumes the EHR remains available as a fallback, but does not document a formal emergency access procedure as required by § 164.312(a)(2)(ii). |
| **Automatic Logoff (Addressable)** — § 164.312(a)(2)(iii) | Section 6.2 compliance mapping table states: "Automatic logoff after 15 minutes of inactivity." | **Compliant.** The SOP documents this control. |
| **Encryption and Decryption (Addressable)** — § 164.312(a)(2)(iv) | Section 6.2: TLS 1.3 for data in transit; PHI within override rationale encrypted over HTTPS. Cryptographic signing of audit records. | **Compliant.** |

**Information Access Management — § 164.308(a)(4):**

| Implementation Specification | SOP-CLIN-006 Control | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Access Authorization (Addressable)** — § 164.308(a)(4)(ii)(B) | Section 6.1: RBAC gating; only `ClarityClinicalUser` role can execute Accept/Modify/Reject. Read-only roles do not expose override buttons. | **Compliant.** |
| **Access Establishment and Modification (Addressable)** — § 164.308(a)(4)(ii)(C) | Section 6.1 references SOP-ISEC-008 (Access Control Standard) for role assignment management. Section 9.2: automatic suspension of `ClarityClinicalUser` role for non-recertification. | **Compliant.** The SOP references the governing access control SOP and includes a mechanism for role suspension. |

---

### 2. Audit Controls — 45 CFR § 164.312(b)

**What HIPAA requires:** "Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information."

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**

The SOP's Section 6.2 ("Audit Logging") is the most directly relevant section. It provides:

- A detailed logged-events table covering: Override Dialog Opened, Modify Saved, Reject Saved, Explicit Accept, Tacit Accept, and Override Rationale Edited.
- Each event captures: Timestamp, User ID, Patient ID, Session ID, Action, Override Event ID, AI Model ID, AI Recommendation ID, Pre-Override State, Post-Override State, Rationale, and Outcome (Success/Failure).
- Immutable audit trail with cryptographic signing via internal PKI.
- No deletion API for the Override Audit Trail table.
- Corrections via supplementary note (not alteration of original).
- 6-year minimum retention.

**Assessment against HIPAA audit requirements:**

| Element | SOP-CLIN-006 | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| User Identification | ✓ User ID captured for every event | **Compliant** |
| Date/Time | ✓ Timestamp captured for every event | **Compliant** |
| Action Description | ✓ Modify, Reject, Accept, Accept-Tacit, Rationale Edited | **Compliant** |
| Object/Resource Accessed | ✓ Patient ID, AI Model ID, AI Recommendation ID | **Compliant** |
| Pre/Post State | ✓ Captured for all override events | **Compliant** |
| Outcome | ✓ Success/Failure captured | **Compliant** |
| Immutability | ✓ Cryptographic signing; no deletion API; supplementary-note-only corrections | **Compliant** |
| Retention | ✓ 6 years minimum | **Compliant** |

**Information System Activity Review — § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Required):**

The SOP addresses this through:
- Section 7.1: KPIs monitored daily on rolling windows, formally reviewed monthly.
- Section 7.2: Dashboards at clinician, site, and corporate levels.
- Section 3.1 RACI: Monthly audit trail integrity verification by Clinical AI Product Team (R) and CCO (A).
- Section 7.3: HIPAA accounting of disclosures for audit trail exports containing PHI.

**Assessment: Compliant.** The SOP establishes regular review of audit logs and override patterns.

---

### 3. Integrity Controls — 45 CFR § 164.312(c)(1)

**What HIPAA requires:** "Implement policies and procedures to protect electronic protected health information from improper alteration or destruction."

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**
- Section 6.1: Cryptographic signing of audit records; immutability; no deletion API.
- Section 6.2: Message authentication codes applied to data at rest in PostgreSQL audit tables.
- Corrections only via supplementary note, preserving original record.

**Assessment: Compliant.** The SOP's controls exceed the minimum for integrity protection.

---

### 4. Person or Entity Authentication — 45 CFR § 164.312(d)

**What HIPAA requires:** "Implement procedures to verify that a person or entity seeking access to electronic protected health information is the one claimed."

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**
- Section 6.1: MFA required for every session initiation.
- Section 6.2 compliance mapping: "MFA enforced. Unique user IDs required."
- Version 5.3 (2025-08-15): Added MFA re-authentication requirement for post-hoc rationale edits.

**Assessment: Compliant.** MFA at session initiation and for sensitive post-hoc edits is a strong control.

---

### 5. Transmission Security — 45 CFR § 164.312(e)(1)

**What HIPAA requires:** "Implement technical security measures to guard against unauthorized access to electronic protected health information that is being transmitted over an electronic communications network."

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**
- Section 6.2: TLS 1.3 for all data in transit; PHI within override rationale encrypted over HTTPS.

**Assessment: Compliant.**

---

### 6. Minimum Necessary Standard — 45 CFR § 164.502(b)

**What HIPAA requires:** When using or disclosing PHI, covered entities must make reasonable efforts to limit PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose.

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**
- The SOP does not explicitly address the minimum necessary standard in the context of override workflows. The override rationale field (Section 5.2, 5.3) is free-text and could contain more PHI than necessary. The SOP requires a minimum character count (20 for Modify, 50 for Reject) but does not include guidance or controls to limit PHI in rationale text to the minimum necessary.
- Section 7.3 addresses accounting of disclosures for audit trail exports containing PHI, but this is about disclosure accounting, not about limiting PHI collection at the point of override.

**Assessment: Partial gap.** The SOP does not include a minimum-necessary limitation on PHI collected in override rationale free-text fields. Clinicians could inadvertently include excessive PHI in rationale text. This is a recognized risk given that the rationale text is stored in the audit trail and may be exported to external parties.

---

### 7. Accounting of Disclosures — 45 CFR § 164.528

**What HIPAA requires:** Individuals have a right to an accounting of disclosures of PHI made in the six years prior to the request (excluding disclosures for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations).

**What SOP-CLIN-006 provides:**
- Section 7.3: Explicitly addresses this. The Meridian Privacy Officer maintains a centralized disclosure log. Accounting provided within 30 days (extendable by 30 days). The SOP correctly identifies that exports to non-TPO recipients (external auditors without BAA, regulators requesting identifiable data) trigger accounting requirements.

**Assessment: Compliant.** The SOP correctly identifies the trigger condition and establishes a process.

---

### 8. 2025 Proposed HIPAA Security Rule Considerations

The January 2025 HHS NPRM proposes eliminating the distinction between "required" and "addressable" implementation specifications and strengthening audit logging requirements. While not yet final, the proposed rule signals the direction of enforcement. SOP-CLIN-006 v5.3 already treats several "addressable" specifications as implemented (automatic logoff, encryption, integrity controls), which positions it well for the proposed changes. However, the **emergency access procedure gap** noted above would become more significant if the addressable/required distinction is eliminated.

---

### Summary of Findings

| HIPAA Requirement | SOP-CLIN-006 Status |
|---|---|
| Access Control (§ 164.312(a)(1)) — RBAC, Unique User ID | ✅ Compliant |
| Emergency Access Procedure (§ 164.312(a)(2)(ii)) | ⚠️ Partial — no formal emergency ePHI access procedure documented |
| Automatic Logoff (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iii)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Encryption (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iv)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Audit Controls (§ 164.312(b)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Information System Activity Review (§ 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Integrity (§ 164.312(c)(1)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Person/Entity Authentication (§ 164.312(d)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Transmission Security (§ 164.312(e)(1)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Information Access Management (§ 164.308(a)(4)) | ✅ Compliant |
| Minimum Necessary (§ 164.502(b)) | ⚠️ Partial — no controls limiting PHI in override rationale free-text |
| Accounting of Disclosures (§ 164.528) | ✅ Compliant |

---

### Gaps Identified

1. **Emergency Access Procedure (§ 164.312(a)(2)(ii)):** SOP-CLIN-006 Section 8.1 addresses technical failure recovery (local browser storage, manual EHR fallback) but does not establish a formal emergency access procedure for obtaining necessary ePHI when the Clarity platform is unavailable. The SOP should either cross-reference an existing emergency access procedure (e.g., from SOP-ISEC-008 or a disaster recovery SOP) or include one directly.

2. **Minimum Necessary in Override Rationale (§ 164.502(b)):** The free-text override rationale fields (Sections 5.2 and 5.3) have no controls, guidance, or warnings to clinicians about limiting PHI to the minimum necessary. Given that rationale text is stored in the audit trail and may be exported to non-TPO recipients (triggering accounting of disclosures under Section 7.3), the SOP should include: (a) a warning or guidance in the override dialog about avoiding unnecessary PHI in rationale text, and/or (b) a periodic review of rationale text for minimum necessary compliance.

---

**Compliance level: partial**

The SOP is strong on audit controls, integrity, authentication, and transmission security. The two gaps — absence of a formal emergency access procedure and lack of minimum-necessary controls on override rationale free-text — prevent a finding of full compliance. These are addressable gaps that do not undermine the overall framework but should be remediated, particularly given the 2025 proposed HIPAA Security Rule changes that would eliminate the addressable/required distinction.

## Alignment Analysis: SOP-AIML-007 vs. NIST AI RMF MEASURE and MANAGE Functions

### Overview

SOP-AIML-007 (v3.8, effective 2024-05-17) is a mature, well-structured SOP that demonstrates substantial alignment with the NIST AI RMF 1.0's MEASURE and MANAGE functions. However, there are specific gaps — particularly around **emergent risk identification** and **structured feedback integration** — that prevent a finding of full alignment. Below is the detailed subcategory-by-subcategory analysis.

---

## MEASURE FUNCTION

### MEASURE 1: Appropriate methods and metrics are identified and applied.

| Subcategory | RMF Requirement | SOP Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MEASURE 1.1** | Approaches and metrics for measurement of AI risks enumerated during MAP are selected; risks that cannot be measured are documented. | **Strong.** Section 5.1.2 defines six drift metrics (PSI, KS, AUC-ROC, PR-AUC, Chi-squared, KL Divergence) with explicit thresholds. Section 5.1.3 defines performance-based triggers with model-type-specific metrics. Section 7.1 defines 8 KPIs. | **Compliant.** The SOP enumerates specific, quantitative metrics tied to identified risks. |
| **MEASURE 1.2** | Appropriateness of AI metrics and effectiveness of existing controls are regularly assessed and updated. | **Partial.** Section 7.3 defines quarterly AI Governance Reports that review KPIs and NIST AI RMF alignment. The revision history shows periodic threshold refinement (v3.8 refined drift thresholds based on 12-month telemetry). However, there is no explicit, documented cadence for formally reassessing whether the *metrics themselves* remain appropriate. | **Partial.** Periodic review exists but lacks a formal "metrics appropriateness review" process. |
| **MEASURE 1.3** | Internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers and/or independent assessors are involved in regular assessments. | **Strong.** Section 6.2.3 explicitly states Model Validation operates with independence from development teams, reporting through separate management chains (CRO for financial, CMIO for clinical). Section 5.5.2 defines independent approval authorities. | **Compliant.** |

### MEASURE 2: AI systems are evaluated for trustworthy characteristics.

| Subcategory | RMF Requirement | SOP Alignment | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MEASURE 2.1** | Test sets, metrics, and details about tools used during TEVV are documented. | **Strong.** Section 5.2.2 defines train/validation/test split configuration. Section 5.3.3 requires comprehensive training metadata (SHA-256 hashes, hyperparameters, hardware config, dependency manifests). Section 5.4.1 requires side-by-side testing on identical test sets. | **Compliant.** |
| **MEASURE 2.3** | AI system performance or assurance criteria are measured and demonstrated for conditions similar to deployment setting(s). | **Strong.** Section 5.4.4 mandates shadow deployment for Tier 1 and Tier 2 models (minimum 14 days, 100% traffic mirroring). Section 5.6 requires canary deployment (10% traffic, 4-hour bake) before full promotion. | **Compliant.** |
| **MEASURE 2.4** | The functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components – as identified in the MAP function – are monitored when in production. | **Strong.** Section 5.1.2 defines continuous drift monitoring via Evidently AI on AWS EKS. ## Overall Assessment

**SOP-AIML-007 demonstrates strong alignment with the NIST AI RMF MEASURE and MANAGE functions for handling distributional drift.** The SOP's drift detection framework (Section 5.1.2) is comprehensive, with six statistical metrics, rolling windows, tiered priorities, and explicit MTTD/MTTR KPIs. The retraining pipeline, validation gate, shadow deployment, canary promotion, and rollback procedures collectively address the core of MEASURE 2.4 (production monitoring), MANAGE 2.2 (sustaining value), and MANAGE 2.4 (deactivation/disengagement).

**However, the SOP has a material gap in handling emergent risks** — risks that fall outside the predefined drift and performance degradation taxonomy. NIST AI RMF MEASURE 3.1 explicitly requires tracking of "unanticipated and emergent AI risks," and MEASURE 3.2 requires consideration of risks "difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques." The SOP's monitoring framework is excellent at detecting *known* degradation patterns but provides no structured mechanism for discovering *unknown* failure modes. Additionally, the absence of end-user feedback integration (MEASURE 3.3) means the organization may miss risks that manifest in user experience before they appear in telemetry.

**Alignment finding: SUBSTANTIALLY ALIGNED with identified gaps.**

The SOP would benefit from: (1) an emergent risk scanning process (e.g., periodic red-teaming, adversarial stress testing beyond FGSM, cross-model anomaly correlation); (2) a structured end-user feedback channel integrated into retraining triggers; and (3) a qualitative risk tracking supplement for risks not captured by quantitative metrics.

**Compliance level: Substantially Aligned (with specific, remediable gaps in emergent risk identification and stakeholder feedback integration).**

5.3 Measure
The MEASURE function employs quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method tools, tech-
niques, and methodologies to analyze, assess, benchmark, and monitor AI risk and related
impacts. It uses knowledge relevant to AI risks identified in the MAP function and informs
the MANAGE function. AI systems should be tested before their deployment and regu-
larly while in operation. AI risk measurements include documenting aspects of systems’
functionality and trustworthiness.
Measuring AI risks includes tracking metrics for trustworthy characteristics, social impact,
and human-AI configurations. Processes developed or adopted in the MEASURE function
should include rigorous software testing and performance assessment methodologies with
associated measures of uncertainty, comparisons to performance benchmarks, and formal-
ized reporting and documentation of results. Processes for independent review can improve
the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases and potential conflicts of inter-
est.
Where tradeoffs among the trustworthy characteristics arise, measurement provides a trace-
able basis to inform management decisions. Options may include recalibration, impact
mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodolo-
gies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and trans-
parent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will en-
hance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is in-
cumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms, roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be ef- fective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addi- tion, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and resources. 2. Audience Identifying and managing AI risks and potential impacts – both positive and negative – re- quires a broad set of perspectives and actors across the AI lifecycle. Ideally, AI actors will represent a diversity of experience, expertise, and backgrounds and comprise demograph- ically and disciplinarily diverse teams. The AI RMF is intended to be used by AI actors across the AI lifecycle and dimensions. The OECD has developed a framework for classifying AI lifecycle activities according to five key socio-technical dimensions, each with properties relevant for AI policy and gover- nance, including risk management [OECD (2022) OECD Framework for the Classification of AI systems — OECD Digital Economy Papers]. Figure 2 shows these dimensions, slightly modified by NIST for purposes of this framework. The NIST modification high- lights the importance of test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) processes throughout an AI lifecycle and generalizes the operational context of an AI system. AI dimensions displayed in Figure 2 are the Application Context, Data and Input, AI Model, and Task and Output. AI actors involved in these dimensions who perform or manage the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems and drive AI risk management efforts are the primary AI RMF audience. Representative AI actors across the lifecycle dimensions are listed in Figure 3 and described in detail in Appendix A. Within the AI RMF, all AI actors work together to manage risks and achieve the goals of trustworthy and responsible AI. AI actors with TEVV-specific expertise are integrated throughout the AI lifecycle and are especially likely to benefit from the Framework. Performed regularly, TEVV tasks can provide insights relative to technical, societal, legal, and ethical standards or norms, and can assist with anticipating impacts and assessing and tracking emergent risks. As a regular process within an AI lifecycle, TEVV allows for both mid-course remediation and post-hoc risk management. Human Factors tasks and activities are found throughout the dimensions of the AI life- cycle. They include human-centered design practices and methodologies, promoting the active involvement of end users and other interested parties and relevant AI actors, incor- porating context-specific norms and values in system design, evaluating and adapting end user experiences, and broad integration of humans and human dynamics in all phases of the AI lifecycle. Human factors professionals provide multidisciplinary skills and perspectives to understand context of use, inform interdisciplinary and demographic diversity, engage in consultative processes, design and evaluate user experience, perform human-centered evaluation and testing, and inform impact assessments. A transparent system is not necessarily an accurate, privacy-enhanced, secure, or fair system. However, it is difficult to determine whether an opaque system possesses such characteristics, and to do so over time as complex systems evolve. The role of AI actors should be considered when seeking accountability for the outcomes of AI systems. The relationship between risk and accountability associated with AI and tech- nological systems more broadly differs across cultural, legal, sectoral, and societal contexts. When consequences are severe, such as when life and liberty are at stake, AI developers and deployers should consider proportionally and proactively adjusting their transparency and accountability practices. Maintaining organizational practices and governing structures for harm reduction, like risk management, can help lead to more accountable systems. Measures to enhance transparency and accountability should also consider the impact of these efforts on the implementing entity, including the level of necessary resources and the need to safeguard proprietary information. Maintaining the provenance of training data and supporting attribution of the AI system’s decisions to subsets of training data can assist with both transparency and accountability. Training data may also be subject to copyright and should follow applicable intellectual property rights laws. As transparency tools for AI systems and related documentation continue to evolve, devel- opers of AI systems are encouraged to test different types of transparency tools in cooper- ation with AI deployers to ensure that AI systems are used as intended. 3.5 Explainable and Interpretable Explainability refers to a representation of the mechanisms underlying AI systems’ oper- ation, whereas interpretability refers to the meaning of AI systems’ output in the context of their designed functional purposes. Together, explainability and interpretability assist those operating or overseeing an AI system, as well as users of an AI system, to gain deeper insights into the functionality and trustworthiness of the system, including its out- puts. The underlying assumption is that perceptions of negative risk stem from a lack of ability to make sense of, or contextualize, system output appropriately. Explainable and interpretable AI systems offer information that will help end users understand the purposes and potential impact of an AI system. Risk from lack of explainability may be managed by describing how AI systems function, with descriptions tailored to individual differences such as the user’s role, knowledge, and skill level. Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human inter- vention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality. AI safety risk management approaches should take cues from efforts and guidelines for safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or application-specific guidelines or standards. 3.3 Secure and Resilient AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be re- silient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their envi- ronment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted from: ISO /IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples, data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Manage- ment Framework are among those which are applicable here. Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the abil- ity to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes re- silience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data. 3.4 Accountable and Transparent Trustworthy AI depends upon accountability. Accountability presupposes transparency. By promoting higher levels of understanding, transparency increases confidence in the AI system. 1.2 Challenges for AI Risk Management
Several challenges are described below. They should be taken into account when managing
risks in pursuit of AI trustworthiness.
1.2.1 Risk Measurement
AI risks or failures that are not well-defined or adequately understood are difficult to mea-
sure quantitatively or qualitatively. The inability to appropriately measure AI risks does not
imply that an AI system necessarily poses either a high or low risk. Some risk measurement
challenges include:
Risks related to third-party software, hardware, and data: Third-party data or systems
can accelerate research and development and facilitate technology transition. They also
may complicate risk measurement. Risk can emerge both from third-party data, software or
hardware itself and how it is used. Risk metrics or methodologies used by the organization
developing the AI system may not align with the risk metrics or methodologies uses by
the organization deploying or operating the system. Also, the organization developing
the AI system may not be transparent about the risk metrics or methodologies it used. Risk
measurement and management can be complicated by how customers use or integrate third-
party data or systems into AI products or services, particularly without sufficient internal
governance structures and technical safeguards. Regardless, all parties and AI actors should
manage risk in the AI systems they develop, deploy, or use as standalone or integrated
components.
Tracking emergent risks: Organizations’ risk management efforts will be enhanced by
identifying and tracking emergent risks and considering techniques for measuring them.

## Assessment: SOP-AIML-019 vs. NIST AI RMF MANAGE Function

### Overview

SOP-AIML-019 (v5.2, 2026-06-05) explicitly states in its revision history that it was updated to "align with NIST AI RMF 1.0 MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions." I have evaluated the SOP against all four MANAGE categories and their subcategories. Below is the detailed mapping.

---

### MANAGE 1: Risk Prioritization, Response, and Management

| Subcategory | NIST Requirement | SOP-AIML-019 Coverage | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MANAGE 1.1** — Determination of whether AI system achieves intended purpose and whether deployment should proceed | The organization must determine whether the AI system achieves its intended purpose and whether development/deployment should proceed. | **Strongly addressed.** Section 5.4 (Phase 4: Closure and Rollout Decision) requires: (a) DSRB review of statistical validity, SRM absence, observation period adequacy, and a **Practical Significance Assessment** (Step 11); (b) CAIO Go/No-Go authorization with CSO co-sign for clinical models (Step 12); (c) explicit "Roll Out," "Do Not Roll Out," or "Gather More Data" decision recorded in Guild Tracker. | ✅ Compliant |
| **MANAGE 1.2** — Treatment of documented AI risks prioritized based on impact, likelihood, and available resources | Risks must be prioritized by impact, likelihood, and resources. | **Partially addressed.** POL-019-03 mandates guardrail metrics for high-risk models (fairness, stability, safety). The Safety Assessment Checklist (Appendix A, §5.1.1 item 6) covers bias, patient impact, privacy, and hallucination risk. However, the SOP does not explicitly require a **risk prioritization matrix** (impact × likelihood) or tie risk treatment to resource availability. Risk classification is deferred to SOP-RISK-001. | ⚠️ Partial |
| **MANAGE 1.3** — Responses to high-priority AI risks are developed, planned, and documented (mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept) | Risk response options must be documented for high-priority risks. | **Addressed.** Section 5.1.3 (Clinical/Fiscal Safety Review) allows the CSO to impose additional guardrail metrics. Section 5.3.2 mandates Root Cause Analysis within 48 hours of guardrail breach. Section 6.1 provides technical controls (Zero-Traffic Kill Switch, Latency Circuit Breaker, automated pause). However, the SOP does not explicitly categorize responses as mitigate/transfer/avoid/accept. | ⚠️ Partial |
| **MANAGE 1.4** — Negative residual risks to downstream acquirers and end users are documented | Residual risks must be documented. | **Gap.** The SOP does not explicitly require documentation of negative residual risks after mitigations are applied. The Practical Significance Assessment (§5.4.1) weighs statistical effect against operational cost but does not address residual risk communication to downstream acquirers or end users. | ❌ Gap |

---

### MANAGE 2: Strategies to Maximize Benefits and Minimize Negative Impacts

| Subcategory | NIST Requirement | SOP-AIML-019 Coverage | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MANAGE 2.1** — Resources to manage AI risks considered alongside viable non-AI alternatives | Resources and non-AI alternatives must be considered. | **Gap.** The SOP does not require consideration of non-AI alternative systems, approaches, or methods as part of the experiment design or rollout decision. The EDD template (§5.1.1) does not include a field for non-AI alternatives. | ❌ Gap |
| **MANAGE 2.2** — Mechanisms to sustain the value of deployed AI systems | Mechanisms must sustain value of deployed AI systems. | **Addressed.** Section 7.1 defines KPIs including False Discovery Rate (FDR) — measuring whether "successful" experiments degrade post-rollout — with a <10% threshold triggering DSRB methodological review. ### NIST AI RMF

NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms, roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be ef- fective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addi- tion, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and resources. 2. Audience Identifying and managing AI risks and potential impacts – both positive and negative – re- quires a broad set of perspectives and actors across the AI lifecycle. Ideally, AI actors will represent a diversity of experience, expertise, and backgrounds and comprise demograph- ically and disciplinarily diverse teams. The AI RMF is intended to be used by AI actors across the AI lifecycle and dimensions. The OECD has developed a framework for classifying AI lifecycle activities according to five key socio-technical dimensions, each with properties relevant for AI policy and gover- nance, including risk management [OECD (2022) OECD Framework for the Classification of AI systems — OECD Digital Economy Papers]. Figure 2 shows these dimensions, slightly modified by NIST for purposes of this framework. The NIST modification high- lights the importance of test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) processes throughout an AI lifecycle and generalizes the operational context of an AI system. AI dimensions displayed in Figure 2 are the Application Context, Data and Input, AI Model, and Task and Output. AI actors involved in these dimensions who perform or manage the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems and drive AI risk management efforts are the primary AI RMF audience. Representative AI actors across the lifecycle dimensions are listed in Figure 3 and described in detail in Appendix A. Within the AI RMF, all AI actors work together to manage risks and achieve the goals of trustworthy and responsible AI. AI actors with TEVV-specific expertise are integrated throughout the AI lifecycle and are especially likely to benefit from the Framework. Performed regularly, TEVV tasks can provide insights relative to technical, societal, legal, and ethical standards or norms, and can assist with anticipating impacts and assessing and tracking emergent risks. As a regular process within an AI lifecycle, TEVV allows for both mid-course remediation and post-hoc risk management. The People & Planet dimension at the center of Figure 2 represents human rights and the broader

2 This work was informed by public feedback and consultations with diverse stakeholder groups as part of NIST’s Generative AI Public Working Group (GAI PWG). The GAI PWG was an open, transparent, and collaborative process, facilitated via a virtual workspace, to obtain multistakeholder input on GAI risk management and to inform NIST’s approach. The focus of the GAI PWG was limited to four primary considerations relevant to GAI: Governance, Content Provenance, Pre-deployment Testing, and Incident Disclosure (further described in Appendix A). As such, the suggested actions in this document primarily address these considerations. Future revisions of this proﬁle will include additional AI RMF subcategories, risks, and suggested actions based on additional considerations of GAI as the space evolves and empirical evidence indicates additional risks. A glossary of terms pertinent to GAI risk management will be developed and hosted on NIST’s Trustworthy & Responsible AI Resource Center (AIRC), and added to The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms. This document was also informed by public comments and consultations from several Requests for Information. 2. Overview of Risks Unique to or Exacerbated by GAI In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability (or likelihood) of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event. Some risks can be assessed as likely to materialize in a given context, particularly those that have been empirically demonstrated in similar contexts. Other risks may be unlikely to materialize in a given context, or may be more speculative and therefore uncertain. AI risks can diﬀer from or intensify traditional software risks. Likewise, GAI can exacerbate existing AI risks, and creates unique risks. GAI risks can vary along many dimensions: • Stage of the AI lifecycle: Risks can arise during design, development, deployment, operation, and/or decommissioning. • Scope: Risks may exist at individual model or system levels, at the application or implementation levels (i.e., for a speciﬁc use case), or at the ecosystem level – that is, beyond a single system or organizational context. Examples of the latter include the expansion of “algorithmic monocultures,3” resulting from repeated use of the same model, or impacts on access to opportunity, labor markets, and the creative economies.4 • Source of risk: Risks may emerge from factors related to the design, training, or operation of the GAI model itself, stemming in some cases from GAI model or system inputs, and in other cases, from GAI system outputs. Value Chain and Component Integration GAI value chains involve many third-party components such as procured datasets, pre-trained models, and software libraries. These components might be improperly obtained or not properly vetted, leading to diminished transparency or accountability for downstream users. While this is a risk for traditional AI systems and some other digital technologies, the risk is exacerbated for GAI due to the scale of the training data, which may be too large for humans to vet; the diﬃculty of training foundation models, which leads to extensive reuse of limited numbers of models; and the extent to which GAI may be integrated into other devices and services. As GAI systems often involve many distinct third-party components and data sources, it may be diﬃcult to attribute issues in a system’s behavior to any one of these sources. Errors in third-party GAI components can also have downstream impacts on accuracy and robustness. For example, test datasets commonly used to benchmark or validate models can contain label errors. Inaccuracies in these labels can impact the “stability” or robustness of these benchmarks, which many GAI practitioners consider during the model selection process.
