Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are distinct characteristics that support each other. Transparency can answer the question of “what happened” in the system. Ex- plainability can answer the question of “how” a decision was made in the system. Inter- pretability can answer the question of “why” a decision was made by the system and its meaning or context to the user. 3.6 Privacy-Enhanced Privacy refers generally to the norms and practices that help to safeguard human autonomy, identity, and dignity. These norms and practices typically address freedom from intrusion, limiting observation, or individuals’ agency to consent to disclosure or control of facets of their identities (e.g., body, data, reputation). (See The NIST Privacy Framework: A Tool for Improving Privacy through Enterprise Risk Management.) Privacy values such as anonymity, confidentiality, and control generally should guide choices for AI system design, development, and deployment. Privacy-related risks may influence security, bias, and transparency and come with tradeoffs with these other characteristics. Like safety and security, specific technical features of an AI system may promote or reduce privacy. AI systems can also present new risks to privacy by allowing inference to identify individuals or previously private information about individuals. Privacy-enhancing technologies (“PETs”) for AI, as well as data minimizing methods such as de-identification and aggregation for certain model outputs, can support design for privacy-enhanced AI systems. 6 2.2. Confabulation “Confabulation” refers to a phenomenon in which GAI systems generate and conﬁdently present erroneous or false content in response to prompts. Confabulations also include generated outputs that diverge from the prompts or other input or that contradict previously generated statements in the same context. These phenomena are colloquially also referred to as “hallucinations” or “fabrications.” Confabulations can occur across GAI outputs and contexts.9,10 Confabulations are a natural result of the way generative models are designed: they generate outputs that approximate the statistical distribution of their training data; for example, LLMs predict the next token or word in a sentence or phrase. While such statistical prediction can produce factually accurate and consistent outputs, it can also produce outputs that are factually inaccurate or internally inconsistent. This dynamic is particularly relevant when it comes to open-ended prompts for long-form responses and in domains which require highly contextual and/or domain expertise. Risks from confabulations may arise when users believe false content – often due to the conﬁdent nature of the response – leading users to act upon or promote the false information. This poses a challenge for many real-world applications, such as in healthcare, where a confabulated summary of patient information reports could cause doctors to make incorrect diagnoses and/or recommend the wrong treatments. Risks of confabulated content may be especially important to monitor when integrating GAI into applications involving consequential decision making. GAI outputs may also include confabulated logic or citations that purport to justify or explain the system’s answer, which may further mislead humans into inappropriately trusting the system’s output. For instance, LLMs sometimes provide logical steps for how they arrived at an answer even when the answer itself is incorrect. Similarly, an LLM could falsely assert that it is human or has human traits, potentially deceiving humans into believing they are speaking with another human. The extent to which humans can be deceived by LLMs, the mechanisms by which this may occur, and the potential risks from adversarial prompting of such behavior are emerging areas of study. Given the wide range of downstream impacts of GAI, it is diﬃcult to estimate the downstream scale and impact of confabulations. Environmental Impacts Training, maintaining, and operating (running inference on) GAI systems are resource-intensive activities, with potentially large energy and environmental footprints. Energy and carbon emissions vary based on what is being done with the GAI model (i.e., pre-training, ﬁne-tuning, inference), the modality of the content, hardware used, and type of task or application. Current estimates suggest that training a single transformer LLM can emit as much carbon as 300 round- trip ﬂights between San Francisco and New York. In a study comparing energy consumption and carbon emissions for LLM inference, generative tasks (e.g., text summarization) were found to be more energy- and carbon-i ntensive th an discriminative or non-generative tasks (e.g., text classiﬁcation). Methods for creating smaller versions of trained models, such as model distillation or compression, could reduce environmental impacts at inference time, but training and tuning such models may still contribute to their environmental impacts. Currently there is no agreed upon method to estimate environmental impacts from GAI. Trustworthy AI Characteristics: Accountable and Transparent, Safe 2.6. Harmful Bias and Homogenization Bias exists in many forms and can become ingrained in automated systems. AI systems, including GAI systems, can increase the speed and scale at which harmful biases manifest and are acted upon, potentially perpetuating and amplifying harms to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society. For example, when prompted to generate images of CEOs, doctors, lawyers, and judges, current text-to-image models underrepresent women and/or racial minorities, and people with disabilities. Image generator models have also produced biased or stereotyped output for various demographic groups and have diﬃculty producing non-stereotyped content even when the prompt speciﬁcally requests image features that are inconsistent with the stereotypes. Harmful bias in GAI models, which may stem from their training data, can also cause representational harms or perpetuate or exacerbate bias based on race, gender, disability, or other protected classes. 6. AI RMF Profiles
AI RMF use-case profiles are implementations of the AI RMF functions, categories, and
subcategories for a specific setting or application based on the requirements, risk tolerance,
and resources of the Framework user: for example, an AI RMF hiring profile or an AI
RMF fair housing profile. Profiles may illustrate and offer insights into how risk can be
managed at various stages of the AI lifecycle or in specific sector, technology, or end-use
applications. AI RMF profiles assist organizations in deciding how they might best manage
AI risk that is well-aligned with their goals, considers legal/regulatory requirements and
best practices, and reflects risk management priorities.
AI RMF temporal profiles are descriptions of either the current state or the desired, target
state of specific AI risk management activities within a given sector, industry, organization,
or application context. An AI RMF Current Profile indicates how AI is currently being
managed and the related risks in terms of current outcomes. A Target Profile indicates the
outcomes needed to achieve the desired or target AI risk management goals.
Comparing Current and Target Profiles likely reveals gaps to be addressed to meet AI risk
management objectives. Action plans can be developed to address these gaps to fulfill
outcomes in a given category or subcategory. Prioritization of gap mitigation is driven by
the user’s needs and risk management processes. This risk-based approach also enables
Framework users to compare their approaches with other approaches and to gauge the
resources needed (e.g., staffing, funding) to achieve AI risk management goals in a cost-
effective, prioritized manner.

negative risk or harms include the reality that development of metrics is often an institu-
tional endeavor and may inadvertently reflect factors unrelated to the underlying impact. In
addition, measurement approaches can be oversimplified, gamed, lack critical nuance, be-
come relied upon in unexpected ways, or fail to account for differences in affected groups
and contexts.
Approaches for measuring impacts on a population work best if they recognize that contexts
matter, that harms may affect varied groups or sub-groups differently, and that communities
or other sub-groups who may be harmed are not always direct users of a system.
Risk at different stages of the AI lifecycle: Measuring risk at an earlier stage in the AI
lifecycle may yield different results than measuring risk at a later stage; some risks may
be latent at a given point in time and may increase as AI systems adapt and evolve. Fur-
thermore, different AI actors across the AI lifecycle can have different risk perspectives.
For example, an AI developer who makes AI software available, such as pre-trained mod-
els, can have a different risk perspective than an AI actor who is responsible for deploying
that pre-trained model in a specific use case. Such deployers may not recognize that their
particular uses could entail risks which differ from those perceived by the initial developer.
All involved AI actors share responsibilities for designing, developing, and deploying a
trustworthy AI system that is fit for purpose.
Risk in real-world settings: While measuring AI risks in a laboratory or a controlled
environment may yield important insights pre-deployment, these measurements may differ
from risks that emerge in operational, real-world settings.
Inscrutability: Inscrutable AI systems can complicate risk measurement. Inscrutability
can be a result of the opaque nature of AI systems (limited explainability or interpretabil-
ity), lack of transparency or documentation in AI system development or deployment, or
inherent uncertainties in AI systems.
Human baseline: Risk management of AI systems that are intended to augment or replace
human activity, for example decision making, requires some form of baseline metrics for
comparison. This is difficult to systematize since AI systems carry out different tasks – and
perform tasks differently – than humans.

Sustainability refers to the “state of the global system, including environmental, social, and economic aspects, in which the needs of the present are met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs” ( ISO /IEC TR 24368:2022). Responsible AI is meant to result in technology that is also equitable and accountable. The expectation is that organizational practices are carried out in accord with “professional responsibility,” defined by ISO as an approach that “aims to ensure that professionals who design, develop, or deploy AI systems and applications or AI-based products or systems, recognize their unique position to exert influence on people, society, and the future of AI” (ISO /IEC TR 24368:2022). As directed by the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 (P.L. 116-283), the goal of the AI RMF is to offer a resource to the organizations designing, developing, deploying, or using AI systems to help manage the many risks of AI and promote trustwor- thy and responsible development and use of AI systems. ---

## Gap Analysis: SOP-AIML-009 vs. GDPR Article 35 (DPIA) and Article 22 (Automated Decision-Making)

### Summary of Findings

SOP-AIML-009 is a well-structured bias detection and mitigation framework, but it contains **significant procedural gaps** when measured against GDPR Articles 35 and 22. Below I identify each missing procedure, organized by regulatory obligation.

---

## MISSING PROCEDURES — GDPR Article 35 (DPIA)

### 1. No Mandatory DPIA Trigger for Algorithmic Bias as a "High Risk" Factor

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(1) mandates a DPIA *prior to processing* whenever processing — particularly using new technologies — is "likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons." Article 35(3)(a) explicitly identifies "a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects… or similarly significantly affect the natural person" as a mandatory DPIA trigger.

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 references DPIAs only tangentially. Section 3 (Roles) states the EU DPO "reviews Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) where algorithmic bias creates a high risk to individuals." Section 5.1.5 requires a Privacy Consultation Ticket (category `Bias-Testing-DPIA`) for PII/PHI use in bias testing. However, **there is no procedure that mandates a DPIA be conducted — or updated — specifically because an AI/ML system performs automated decision-making that could produce biased outcomes affecting individuals' rights.** The SOP treats DPIA as a privacy consultation checkbox for bias testing data use, not as a mandatory, standalone assessment triggered by the automated decision-making itself.

**Missing Procedure:** A mandatory step in Phase 1 (Pre-Development) or the Model Risk Tier classification process requiring that any model classified as Critical or High risk — or any model making consequential decisions about individuals — automatically triggers a full DPIA under Article 35, with the bias risk assessment integrated as a core component.

---

### 2. No Systematic Description of Processing Operations and Purposes (Article 35(7)(a))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(7)(a) requires "a systematic description of the envisaged processing operations and the purposes of the processing, including, where applicable, the legitimate interest pursued by the controller."

**What's Missing:** The SOP's Bias Testing Plan (Section 5.1) captures the decision context, protected attributes, fairness metrics, and thresholds. However, it does **not** require a systematic description of: (i) the full data processing operations (collection, storage, processing, sharing), (ii) the categories of data subjects affected, (iii) the categories of personal data processed (including special category data under Article 9), (iv) the retention periods for data used in both training and inference, (v) the recipients of model outputs, or (vi) any international transfers of personal data (relevant given Meridian's global operations in London, Berlin, Singapore, Toronto). The Bias Testing Plan is a fairness document — not a DPIA-compliant processing description.

**Missing Procedure:** A requirement that the DPIA (referenced as SOP-PRI-008) must be cross-linked to the Bias Testing Plan and must contain a complete Article 35(7)(a) processing description that specifically addresses how personal data flows through the algorithmic system.

---

### 3. No Assessment of Necessity and Proportionality (Article 35(7)(b))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(7)(b) requires "an assessment of the necessity and proportionality of the processing operations in relation to the purposes." This operationalizes the data minimization principle (Article 5(1)(c)).

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 addresses data minimization only in the narrow context of bias testing (Section 4.4: "use de-identified or pseudonymized datasets for bias analysis whenever possible"). There is **no procedure requiring an assessment of whether the automated processing itself is necessary and proportionate** — e.g., whether the specific protected attributes or proxy variables being processed are strictly necessary for the model's purpose, whether less intrusive alternatives exist, or whether the scale of data collection is proportionate to the stated purpose.

**Missing Procedure:** A mandatory necessity and proportionality assessment within the DPIA framework that evaluates: (i) whether each category of personal data (including inferred/proxy data) is necessary for the model's purpose, (ii) whether less data-intensive approaches could achieve the same objective, and (iii) whether the benefits of automated decision-making justify the privacy intrusion, particularly for Critical and High-risk models.

---

### 4. No DPIA Risk Assessment Specific to Algorithmic Bias Harms (Article 35(7)(c))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(7)(c) requires "an assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects." This must go beyond technical model performance to assess risks to individuals' legal rights, economic interests, health, dignity, and non-discrimination.

**What's Missing:** The SOP's risk framework is organized around Model Risk Tiers (Critical, High, Standard, Low) based on "potential severity of harm from biased or erroneous outputs." The fairness metrics (SPD, EOD, AOD) and the 80% Rule assess *statistical* bias. However, there is **no procedure requiring a qualitative, rights-based risk assessment** that evaluates: (i) the specific rights and freedoms at stake (e.g., right to health, right to non-discrimination, right to access financial services), (ii) the likelihood and severity of harm to specific vulnerable groups, (iii) the cumulative or systemic effects of biased decisions across multiple models, or (iv) the risk of function creep (data collected for one purpose being used for algorithmic decision-making in another context).

**Missing Procedure:** A structured rights-and-freedoms risk assessment, integrated into the DPIA, that maps each model's potential biased outcomes to specific GDPR rights and fundamental freedoms at risk, with severity and likelihood ratings per affected group.

---

### 5. No Procedure Requiring DPIA Documentation of "Measures Envisaged to Address the Risks" (Article 35(7)(d))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(7)(d) requires documentation of "the measures envisaged to address the risks, including safeguards, security measures and mechanisms to ensure the protection of personal data and to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation taking into account the rights and legitimate interests of data subjects and other persons concerned."

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 has extensive technical and administrative controls (Section 6), but these are **not mapped to specific DPIA-identified risks** in a way that demonstrates how each control mitigates a particular risk to data subjects' rights and freedoms. The controls are presented as standalone governance measures, not as a risk-treatment plan within a DPIA framework.

**Missing Procedure:** A requirement that each bias-related risk identified in the DPIA be explicitly linked to one or more specific mitigating measures (technical, administrative, or procedural), with residual risk ratings documented after mitigation.

---

### 6. No Procedure for Seeking Data Subject Views (Article 35(9))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(9) states: "Where appropriate, the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing, without prejudice to the protection of commercial or public interests or the security of processing operations."

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 contains **no procedure whatsoever** for consulting data subjects, patient representatives, consumer advocacy groups, or civil society organizations about the intended algorithmic processing. The IRB (Section 3) comprises internal Meridian personnel only (CAIO, VP of Engineering, Chief Compliance Officer, rotating Product lead). There is no patient advisory council, no consumer panel, and no external stakeholder consultation mechanism.

**Missing Procedure:** A procedure for seeking the views of data subjects or their representatives (e.g., patient advocacy groups for Clinical AI, consumer groups for HealthPay) on high-risk algorithmic processing, with documentation of how those views were considered in the DPIA and bias mitigation strategy.

---

### 7. No Procedure for DPIA Review When Risk Changes (Article 35(11))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 35(11) states: "Where necessary, the controller shall carry out a review to assess if processing is performed in accordance with the data protection impact assessment at least when there is a change of the risk represented by processing operations."

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 has continuous monitoring for *bias drift* (Section 5.6) with P0 incidents triggered when fairness metrics deviate by >20%. However, there is **no procedure requiring a DPIA review** when: (i) a model is retrained on new data, (ii) a model's scope expands to new populations, (iii) new protected attributes are identified, (iv) a P0 bias drift incident occurs, or (v) the model's risk tier changes. The 30-day and 180-day re-validation cycles (Section 5.6.3) assess bias metrics only — not the broader DPIA risk profile.

**Missing Procedure:** A mandatory DPIA review trigger linked to: model retraining, scope expansion, P0 bias incidents, risk tier reclassification, and at minimum on the same cadence as the bias re-validation schedule (30 days for High/Critical, 180 days for Standard).

---

### 8. No Procedure for Prior Consultation with Supervisory Authority (Article 36)

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 36(1) states: "The controller shall consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk."

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 contains **no reference whatsoever** to Article 36 prior consultation. Given that Meridian's Clinical AI Platform processes special category health data at scale for automated risk scoring and diagnostic decisions — processing that is highly likely to trigger Article 36 obligations — the complete absence of a prior consultation procedure is a critical gap. The IRB and CAIO approval gates (Section 5.4.3) are purely internal and do not substitute for supervisory authority consultation.

**Missing Procedure:** A procedure requiring the EU DPO (Dr. Klaus Weber) to evaluate whether the DPIA indicates unmitigated high risk, and if so, to submit a prior consultation request to the relevant supervisory authority(ies) (likely the Berlin DPA for Meridian's EU establishment) before the model can be deployed, including the specific information required by Article 36(3).

---

## MISSING PROCEDURES — GDPR Article 22 (Automated Decision-Making)

### 9. No Procedure for Identifying Whether Article 22 Applies to Each Model

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 22(1) establishes "the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her." This operates as a general prohibition subject to exceptions in Article 22(2).

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 never references Article 22 or its prohibition. The SOP's scope (Section 1.2) covers "any internally developed or externally procured model that informs consequential decisions about individuals," and Section 4.3 mandates human-in-the-loop for Critical and High-risk models. However, there is **no procedure that systematically determines, for each model, whether the processing constitutes "solely automated decision-making" under Article 22(1)** — i.e., whether there is meaningful human involvement in every decision, or whether the human is merely a rubber stamp. The human-in-the-loop policy (Section 4.3) is a good start but does not operationalize the Article 22 legal test.

**Missing Procedure:** A mandatory Article 22 applicability assessment in Phase 1 (Bias Scoping and Planning) that determines: (i) whether the model makes decisions "solely" based on automated processing, (ii) whether those decisions produce "legal effects" or "similarly significantly affect" individuals, and (iii) if so, which lawful basis under Article 22(2) applies (contract necessity, explicit consent, or Union/Member State law authorization).

---

### 10. No Procedure for Obtaining Explicit Consent for Automated Decisions Using Special Category Data (Article 22(4))

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 22(4) prohibits automated decisions based on special categories of personal data (Article 9(1) — including health data, genetic data, and data revealing racial or ethnic origin) unless: (a) the data subject has given **explicit consent** (Article 9(2)(a)), or (b) processing is necessary for reasons of **substantial public interest** (Article 9(2)(g)), **and** "suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests are in place."

**What's Missing:** Meridian's Clinical AI Platform processes health data (special category under Article 9) for risk scoring, diagnostic imaging, and adverse event prediction. The HealthPay platform processes financial data that may reveal economic vulnerability. The bias detection procedures themselves involve processing protected attributes (race, ethnicity, health status). Yet SOP-AIML-009 contains **no procedure for obtaining explicit consent** from data subjects for automated decision-making based on special category data, nor any procedure for establishing and documenting a "substantial public interest" basis with suitable safeguards.

**Missing Procedure:** For models processing special category data in automated decisions: (i) a procedure to determine the lawful basis under Article 9(2) combined with Article 22(4), (ii) if relying on explicit consent, a procedure for obtaining, recording, and managing withdrawal of that consent (including the Article 7(3) requirement that withdrawal be as easy as giving consent), and (iii) documentation of the "suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests" as required by Article 22(4).

---

### 11. No Procedure for Providing "Meaningful Information About the Logic Involved" (Articles 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g), 15(1)(h))

**What GDPR Requires:** Articles 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g), and 15(1)(h) require that data subjects be informed of "the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject."

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 mandates Model Cards (Section 4.5, 5.4.1) with "detailed sections on performance across sub-groups and known biases." Model Cards are internal governance documents in the MLflow registry. There is **no procedure requiring that Model Card information be translated into externally facing, plain-language privacy notices** provided to data subjects under Articles 13 and 14. There is no procedure ensuring that data subjects exercising their Article 15 right of access receive "meaningful information about the logic involved" in algorithmic decisions affecting them — including how protected attributes or proxies influence outcomes.

**Missing Procedure:** A procedure requiring that for every Article 22-triggering model: (i) the privacy notice (Articles 13/14) explicitly discloses the existence of automated decision-making, the logic involved in accessible terms, and the significance and consequences; (ii) the Article 15 access response procedure includes a mechanism to provide individualized meaningful information about how the model's logic applied to that specific data subject; and (iii) the Model Card content is adapted into a data-subject-facing explainability statement.

---

### 12. No Procedure for Data Subjects to Exercise Article 22(3) Rights (Human Intervention, Express Views, Contest Decision)

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 22(3) requires that where automated decision-making is permitted (under Article 22(2)), the controller "shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision."

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 Section 4.3 mandates human-in-the-loop for Critical/High-risk models, stating the human reviewer must have "authority and competence to override the algorithmic recommendation." However, this is framed as an *internal governance control*, not as a *data subject right*. There is **no procedure** for:

- **Notifying** individual data subjects that an automated decision has been made about them and that they have the right to human intervention, to express their point of view, and to contest the decision.
- **Providing a clear, accessible mechanism** (e.g., a dedicated portal, hotline, or form) for data subjects to invoke these rights.
- **Ensuring the human reviewer is independent** of the model development team and has the authority to overturn the decision — the SOP's human-in-the-loop is an operational reviewer (e.g., a clinician), not necessarily someone responding to a data subject's contestation.
- **Documenting and tracking** contestations, their outcomes, and whether patterns of contestation reveal systematic bias issues.
- **Handling contestations for Standard/Low-risk models**, which under the SOP have no mandatory human-in-the-loop at all — yet may still fall under Article 22 if they produce legal or similarly significant effects.

**Missing Procedure:** A comprehensive Article 22(3) rights-exercise procedure including: (i) proactive notification to data subjects when an automated decision is made about them, (ii) a clear, accessible contestation mechanism (integrated with SOP-COMP-021 — Regulatory Complaints), (iii) guaranteed human review by a qualified person with authority to overturn the decision, (iv) defined SLAs for response (aligned with Article 12(3)'s one-month timeframe), (v) a feedback loop where patterns of contestation trigger bias re-evaluation, and (vi) extension of contestation rights to all Article 22-triggering models regardless of risk tier.

---

### 13. No Procedure for Handling the "Right Not to Be Subject to" Automated Decision-Making (Article 22(1) Prohibition)

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 22(1) establishes a general prohibition: "The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing." Unless an Article 22(2) exception applies (contract, explicit consent, law), the processing is prohibited.

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 assumes automated decision-making is permissible as long as fairness metrics are met and human oversight exists for high-risk models. There is **no procedure for a data subject to simply opt out** of automated decision-making altogether and receive a fully human decision instead. The SOP's exception handling (Section 8) is for internal policy exceptions — not for data subject opt-out requests. If a patient or loan applicant invokes their Article 22(1) right, there is no defined workflow for routing that decision to a fully manual process.

**Missing Procedure:** An opt-out procedure allowing data subjects to decline automated decision-making and receive a manual human decision instead, including: (i) clear communication of this right at the point of data collection, (ii) a mechanism to flag the data subject's preference in the system, (iii) a manual decision workflow with defined timelines, and (iv) a procedure to ensure the quality and consistency of manual alternative decisions.

---

### 14. No Procedure for Documenting the Lawful Basis for Automated Decision-Making Under Article 22(2)

**What GDPR Requires:** Article 22(2) provides three exhaustive exceptions to the Article 22(1) prohibition: (a) necessary for entering into or performance of a contract, (b) authorized by Union or Member State law, or (c) based on the data subject's explicit consent.

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009 does not require any model to document which Article 22(2) exception (if any) authorizes its automated decision-making. The Bias Testing Plan (Section 5.1) captures decision context but not the legal basis for automation. The Model Card (Section 5.4.1) covers intended use, performance, and limitations — but not the GDPR lawful basis for automated processing. For HealthPay lending models, there is no documented assessment of whether automated credit decisions are "necessary for the performance of a contract" under Article 22(2)(a). For Clinical AI, there is no documented assessment of whether explicit consent (Article 22(2)(c)) is the basis, and if so, whether it meets the Article 4(11) and Article 7 standards for being freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous — particularly problematic in healthcare contexts where consent may not be truly "freely given."

**Missing Procedure:** A mandatory legal basis determination for every model performing automated decision-making, documented in the Bias Testing Plan and Model Card, including: (i) identification of the specific Article 22(2) exception relied upon, (ii) for contract-necessity: a documented justification of why automation is necessary (not merely convenient), (iii) for explicit consent: evidence that consent meets Article 4(11)/Article 7 standards and a mechanism for withdrawal, and (iv) for legal authorization: citation of the specific Union or Member State law.

---

### 15. No Procedure Addressing Article 22 Safeguards for Children or Vulnerable Persons

**What GDPR Requires:** While not explicit in Article 22's text, the WP29 Guidelines on Automated Decision-Making emphasize that "controllers should provide appropriate safeguards for vulnerable data subjects, including children." Recital 71 also references safeguards.

**What's Missing:** SOP-AIML-009's scope covers Clinical AI (which may process data concerning children and vulnerable adults) and HealthPay financial services (which may affect economically vulnerable individuals). Yet there is **no procedure** that specifically addresses: (i) whether automated decision-making should ever be applied to children or legally incapacitated adults, (ii) additional safeguards required when it is, (iii) whether the human-in-the-loop reviewer must have specific qualifications for decisions affecting vulnerable populations, or (iv) whether proxy or consent mechanisms for vulnerable persons are adequate.

**Missing Procedure:** A vulnerability assessment within the Article 22 applicability analysis that identifies whether the model's decisions affect children, incapacitated persons, or otherwise vulnerable populations, and if so, mandates enhanced safeguards (e.g., mandatory human review regardless of risk tier, specialized reviewer qualifications, guardian/representative involvement).

---

## Summary Table of Missing Procedures

| # | Missing Procedure | GDPR Article(s) | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mandatory DPIA trigger for automated decision-making systems | Art. 35(1), 35(3)(a) | **Critical** |
| 2 | Systematic description of processing operations in DPIA | Art. 35(7)(a) | **High** |
| 3 | Necessity and proportionality assessment | Art. 35(7)(b) | **High** |
| 4 | Rights-based risk assessment for algorithmic bias harms | Art. 35(7)(c) | **Critical** |
| 5 | DPIA risk-treatment mapping of controls to identified risks | Art. 35(7)(d) | **High** |
| 6 | Data subject / representative consultation | Art. 35(9) | **High** |
| 7 | DPIA review trigger on risk change (drift, retraining, scope) | Art. 35(11) | **High** |
| 8 | Prior consultation with supervisory authority | Art. 36 | **Critical** |
| 9 | Article 22 applicability determination per model | Art. 22(1) | **Critical** |
| 10 | Explicit consent / substantial public interest for special category data ADM | Art. 22(4), Art. 9 | **Critical** |
| 11 | Data-subject-facing meaningful information about logic (transparency) | Art. 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g), 15(1)(h) | **Critical** |
| 12 | Data subject rights exercise mechanism (intervention, views, contestation) | Art. 22(3) | **Critical** |
| 13 | Opt-out from automated decision-making (Article 22(1) prohibition) | Art. 22(1) | **Critical** |
| 14 | Lawful basis documentation for ADM under Article 22(2) | Art. 22(2) | **Critical** |
| 15 | Enhanced safeguards for children and vulnerable persons | Art. 22(3), Recital 71, WP29 Guidelines | **High** |

---

## Conclusion

SOP-AIML-009 is a technically robust bias detection and mitigation framework, but it operates almost entirely within a **statistical fairness and internal governance paradigm**. It lacks the **rights-based, transparency-oriented, and data-subject-empowering procedures** that GDPR Articles 35 and 22 demand. The most critical gaps are: (1) the absence of a mandatory, structured DPIA process integrated with the bias testing lifecycle; (2) the complete absence of Article 22 data subject rights mechanisms (contestation, human intervention, meaningful transparency, opt-out); (3) the failure to address the Article 22(4) prohibition on automated decisions using special category data without explicit consent or substantial public interest; and (4) the absence of any Article 36 prior consultation procedure despite processing that almost certainly crosses the high-risk threshold.

The SOP's reference to SOP-PRI-008 (Conducting a DPIA) suggests Meridian may have a separate DPIA procedure, but SOP-AIML-009 does not integrate with it procedurally — the DPIA is mentioned only as a document the EU DPO "reviews," not as a mandatory, gated step in the model lifecycle with specific bias-related content requirements.

**Compliance level: SOP-AIML-009 — PARTIALLY COMPLIANT with significant gaps.**

## Gap Analysis: SOP-PENG-001 vs. EU AI Act Article 9 (Risk Management System) for High-Risk AI Systems

### Overview

SOP-PENG-001 is a mature, well-structured Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) SOP with strong HIPAA and SOC 2 alignment. However, when measured against **Article 9 of the EU AI Act** — which mandates a *continuous, iterative risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system* — there are **significant structural and substantive gaps**. The SOP was designed for traditional software security risk, not for the AI-specific risk management paradigm the EU AI Act requires.

Below are the specific missing elements, organized by Article 9's requirements.

---

### 1. MISSING: Continuous Iterative Risk Management Process Spanning the Entire AI Lifecycle

**Article 9(2) Requirement:** The risk management system must be "a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- Threat modeling (Section 5.2.2) is conducted **once** at design time (STRIDE workshop) and annually for Tier-1 apps.
- The "Security Impact Rating" (Low/Moderate/High) is assigned once during the Requirements Phase (Section 5.1, Step 5).
- There is no mechanism for **continuous, iterative risk re-evaluation** as the AI model evolves, learns, or encounters new data distributions.

**Gap:** The SOP treats risk assessment as a phase-gate activity, not as a living, iterative process. Article 9(2) requires risk management to be "planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle" — meaning risk identification, analysis, evaluation, and mitigation must be continuously revisited, not just at design time and annually. For AI systems that continue to learn post-deployment (Article 15(4)), this is especially critical.

---

### 2. MISSING: Identification of "Reasonably Foreseeable Misuse" Risks

**Article 9(2)(b) Requirement:** The risk management system must estimate and evaluate risks "when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, **and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse**."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The STRIDE threat modeling (Section 5.2.2) includes "Abuser Stories" — e.g., "As an attacker, I want to brute-force the login API." These are security-focused misuse cases.
- There is no structured process for identifying **non-security, AI-specific reasonably foreseeable misuse** — e.g., a clinician using an AI diagnostic tool on a demographic population it was not validated for, or a deployer ignoring confidence scores.

**Gap:** The SOP's "Abuser Stories" are framed around traditional cybersecurity attack patterns. Article 9(2)(b) requires a broader analysis of foreseeable misuse that could lead to harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights — including misuse that is not malicious but stems from misunderstanding, over-reliance, or off-label deployment.

---

### 3. MISSING: Risk Evaluation Based on Post-Market Monitoring Data

**Article 9(2)(c) Requirement:** The risk management system must include "the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the **post-market monitoring system** referred to in Article 72."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- Phase 6 (Operations) includes continuous vulnerability scanning (Wiz, Snyk), Datadog monitoring for error rates/latency, and a bug bounty program.
- There is **no post-market monitoring system** as defined by Article 72 — i.e., a system that "actively and systematically collect[s], document[s] and analyse[s] relevant data… on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime" to evaluate **continuous compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements**.

**Gap:** The SOP's operational monitoring is infrastructure- and CVE-focused. It does not monitor for AI-specific degradation (model drift, concept drift, data distribution shift, accuracy decay, bias emergence over time). There is no feedback loop from production monitoring back into the risk management system. Article 9(2)(c) explicitly requires that post-market data feeds back into risk evaluation — this closed loop is entirely absent.

---

### 4. MISSING: AI-Specific Risk Categories (Health, Safety, Fundamental Rights)

**Article 9(2)(a) Requirement:** The risk management system must identify and analyze "the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to **health, safety or fundamental rights**."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The STRIDE threat model (Section 5.2.2) categorizes threats as: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege.
- The risk matrix uses "Likelihood x Impact" on a 5x5 scale, but "Impact" is framed in terms of confidentiality, integrity, and availability — not health, safety, or fundamental rights.

**Gap:** STRIDE is a cybersecurity threat model. It does not address risks such as:
- **Algorithmic discrimination** (fundamental rights impact)
- **Incorrect medical diagnosis or triage** (health/safety impact)
- **Over-reliance / automation bias** (safety impact)
- **Psychological harm from erroneous AI outputs** (health impact)
- **Systemic bias against protected groups** (fundamental rights impact)

The SOP needs an AI-specific risk taxonomy that maps to the EU AI Act's protected interests.

---

### 5. MISSING: Residual Risk Acceptability Judgment

**Article 9(5) Requirement:** Risk management measures "shall be such that the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the **overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable**."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The TMD (Section 5.2.2) includes "Residual risk after mitigation" for each threat.
- There is no explicit, documented **overall residual risk acceptability judgment** — i.e., a formal determination that the aggregate residual risk across all identified hazards is acceptable relative to the intended purpose.

**Gap:** The SOP captures residual risk at the individual threat level but does not require a holistic, documented judgment that the overall residual risk of the AI system is acceptable. Article 9(5) requires this at the system level.

---

### 6. MISSING: Risk Elimination Through Design (Hierarchy of Controls)

**Article 9(5)(a)-(b) Requirement:** Risk management measures must ensure "(a) elimination or reduction of risks… in as far as technically feasible through **adequate design and development** of the high-risk AI system; (b) where appropriate, implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures addressing risks that **cannot be eliminated**."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The Design Review Checklist (Section 5.2.3) covers security design controls (encryption, mTLS, input validation, etc.).
- There is no explicit requirement to demonstrate that risks were **first eliminated through design** before resorting to mitigation controls — i.e., a hierarchy of controls approach.

**Gap:** Article 9(5) establishes a clear preference for risk **elimination** through design (e.g., choosing a simpler, more interpretable model architecture; constraining the operational design domain) before layering on mitigation controls (e.g., human oversight, warnings). The SOP does not enforce this hierarchy.

---

### 7. MISSING: Integration with Article 17 Quality Management System (QMS)

**Article 17(1)(g) Requirement:** The QMS must include "the risk management system referred to in Article 9."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The SOP itself functions as a quality/process document with roles, RACI, training, KPIs, and exception handling.
- However, it does not reference or integrate with a formal **Quality Management System** as defined by Article 17 — which requires documented policies for: design control and verification (17(1)(b)), development quality control (17(1)(c)), examination/test/validation procedures before/during/after development (17(1)(d)), **data management systems** (17(1)(f)), post-market monitoring (17(1)(h)), serious incident reporting (17(1)(i)), and an **accountability framework** (17(1)(m)).

**Gap:** While SOP-PENG-001 has many QMS-like elements (RACI, KPIs, training), it is not structured as an Article 17-compliant QMS. Specifically missing: a formal data management system covering data acquisition, collection, labeling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, and retention for AI training data (Article 17(1)(f)).

---

### 8. MISSING: Data Governance for Training/Validation/Testing Datasets

**Article 10 (cross-referenced by Article 9 risk management):** High-risk AI systems must be developed using training, validation, and testing datasets subject to data governance practices including: examination for biases, data origin documentation, assumptions formulation, data gap identification, and ensuring datasets are "relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete."

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- Section 1.2 includes "AI/ML model development artifacts, including training pipelines, feature engineering code, inference endpoints, and model serialization formats."
- Data Scientists are responsible for "security and integrity of ML model training and serving pipelines" (Section 3.2).
- There is **no data governance procedure** addressing: bias examination, representativeness assessment, data origin/provenance documentation, data gap analysis, or statistical property validation of training/validation/testing datasets.

**Gap:** This is one of the most significant gaps. Article 10's data governance requirements are foundational to Article 9 risk management — you cannot identify AI-specific risks without understanding data quality, bias, and representativeness. The SOP is silent on these.

---

### 9. MISSING: Accuracy, Robustness, and Cybersecurity for AI Systems

**Article 15 (cross-referenced by Article 9 risk management):** High-risk AI systems must achieve "an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity" and perform consistently throughout their lifecycle. This includes resilience against errors/faults/inconsistencies, mitigation of feedback loops for continuously learning systems, and protection against AI-specific attacks (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, model evasion, confidentiality attacks).

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The SOP has strong traditional cybersecurity controls (SAST, DAST, SCA, secret scanning, artifact signing, mTLS, encryption).
- There is **no mention** of: adversarial robustness testing, data poisoning defenses, model evasion testing, feedback loop detection/mitigation for continuously learning systems, or accuracy metric declaration.

**Gap:** The SOP's security testing is entirely traditional (OWASP ZAP, CodeQL, penetration testing). It does not address AI-specific vulnerabilities listed in Article 15(5).

---

### 10. MISSING: Serious Incident Reporting Procedure

**Article 73 (cross-referenced by Article 9 via Article 17(1)(i)):** Providers must report serious incidents — defined as incidents leading to death, serious harm to health, critical infrastructure disruption, fundamental rights infringement, or serious harm to property/environment — to market surveillance authorities.

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- References SOP-ITOP-001 (Security Incident Response Plan) for security incidents.
- Vulnerability management (Section 5.6) has remediation SLAs.
- There is **no procedure** for identifying, classifying, or reporting AI-specific "serious incidents" as defined by Article 73 to competent authorities.

**Gap:** The SOP's incident response framework is security-incident-focused. It does not define or operationalize the EU AI Act's "serious incident" concept, which includes non-security events like AI-induced misdiagnosis or discriminatory outcomes.

---

### 11. MISSING: Human Oversight Integration

**Article 14 (cross-referenced by Article 9 risk management):** High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow effective human oversight, including measures to enable human operators to understand, monitor, interpret, and override AI outputs.

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The SOP does not mention human oversight design requirements, override mechanisms, or "human-in-the-loop" design patterns for AI systems.
- The RACI matrix (Section 3.1) covers human roles in the SDLC process, not human oversight of AI system outputs.

**Gap:** Article 14 requires that human oversight measures be built into the system itself — this is a design requirement that should be captured during the Requirements and Design phases. The SOP is silent on this.

---

### 12. MISSING: Transparency and Instructions for Use

**Article 13 (cross-referenced by Article 9(5)(c)):** Risk management measures must include "provision of information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers." Article 13 requires instructions for use covering: intended purpose, accuracy metrics, known/foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, technical capabilities to explain outputs, performance on specific groups, input data specifications, and information to interpret outputs.

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The PRD template (Section 5.1) includes "Regulatory Considerations" and "Functional Requirements."
- There is no requirement to produce Article 13-compliant instructions for use, accuracy metric declarations, or deployer-facing transparency documentation.

**Gap:** The SOP does not require generation of the transparency artifacts mandated by Article 13, which are explicitly linked to the risk management system via Article 9(5)(c).

---

### 13. MISSING: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment Integration

**Article 27:** Deployers must conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA). While this is primarily a deployer obligation, Article 9 risk management by the provider must inform and align with the FRIA process.

**What SOP-PENG-001 Does:**
- The Compliance Officer provides consultation for "HIPAA, EU AI Act, and cross-border data transfer implications" (Section 3.2).
- There is no structured process for the provider to produce the information deployers need for their FRIA (categories of affected persons, specific risks of harm to fundamental rights, human oversight measures).

**Gap:** The SOP does not require the provider to generate the foundational risk information that deployers will need for their Article 27 FRIA obligations.

---

### Summary Table of Missing Elements

| # | Missing Element | EU AI Act Reference | Criticality |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Continuous iterative risk management (not phase-gate) | Art. 9(2) | **Critical** |
| 2 | Reasonably foreseeable misuse risk analysis | Art. 9(2)(b) | **Critical** |
| 3 | Post-market monitoring data feedback loop into risk evaluation | Art. 9(2)(c), Art. 72 | **Critical** |
| 4 | AI-specific risk categories (health, safety, fundamental rights) | Art. 9(2)(a) | **Critical** |
| 5 | Overall residual risk acceptability judgment | Art. 9(5) | **High** |
| 6 | Risk elimination through design (hierarchy of controls) | Art. 9(5)(a)-(b) | **High** |
| 7 | Article 17 Quality Management System integration | Art. 17(1)(g) | **Critical** |
| 8 | Data governance for training/validation/testing datasets | Art. 10 | **Critical** |
| 9 | AI-specific accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (adversarial testing, data poisoning, feedback loops) | Art. 15 | **Critical** |
| 10 | Serious incident reporting for AI-specific incidents | Art. 73 | **High** |
| 11 | Human oversight design requirements | Art. 14 | **High** |
| 12 | Transparency documentation / instructions for use | Art. 13, Art. 9(5)(c) | **High** |
| 13 | Fundamental rights impact assessment alignment | Art. 27 | **Medium** |

---

### Bottom Line

SOP-PENG-001 is a strong **traditional software security** SDLC. However, Article 9 of the EU AI Act requires a fundamentally different paradigm: an **AI risk management system** that is continuous, iterative, lifecycle-spanning, and focused on risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights — not just confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The SOP's STRIDE-based threat modeling, phase-gated security reviews, and CVE-focused operational monitoring are necessary but far from sufficient for high-risk AI systems. **At minimum, Meridian needs a dedicated AI Risk Management overlay** (or a separate SOP) that addresses the 13 gaps identified above, integrated with the existing SSDLC framework.

**Compliance level: GAP — significant structural and substantive deficiencies for high-risk AI systems under Article 9.**

### Article 10: Data and Data Governance

(c) relevant data-preparation processing operations, such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation;

(d) the formulation of assumptions, in particular with respect to the information that the data are supposed to measure and represent;

(e) an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets that are needed;

(f) examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, especially where data outputs influence inputs for future operations;

(g) appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate possible biases identified according to point (f);

(h) the identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance with this Regulation, and how those gaps and shortcomings can be addressed.

3. Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They shall have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. Those characteristics of the data sets may be met at the level of individual data sets or at the level of a combination thereof.

4. Data sets shall take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements that are particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used.
